name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC leaders urge court to reject EPA’s ‘backroom PFAS deal’ with Chemours
description: The EPA and Chemours announced they’d reached a $450 million settlement last month.
text:
An aerial view of the Chemours Fayetteville Works plant in northern Bladen County. For more than 30 years Chemours and its predecessor, DuPont, discharged “forever chemicals” into the Cape Fear River. (Photo: Chemours)North Carolina state leaders are asking a federal court to turn down what they call a “backroom deal” between the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and chemical manufacturer Chemours. 
Chemours, formerly part of DuPont, has been manufacturing chemicals in its Fayetteville plant for decades. In 2017, scientists discovered that PFAS — sometimes known as “forever chemicals” due to their persistence in the environment — were being released from the plant into the Cape Fear river, as well as into other bodies of water from plants in West Virginia and New Jersey. 
More than 2,600 plaintiffs sued Chemours for polluting their drinking water wells, air, soil, and groundwater. The pollution impacted about 500,000 North Carolinians and about 10,000 private drinking wells. 
But plaintiffs won’t get their day in court if a proposed landmark $450 million settlement between the EPA and Chemours, announced last month, moves forward. It requires approval from a federal judge. 
In their public comment on the settlement filed Wednesday, Gov. Josh Stein, Attorney General Jeff Jackson, and Department of Environmental Quality Secretary Reid Wilson criticized the agency for excluding North Carolina from negotiations. 
“For decades, Chemours knowingly contaminated North Carolina’s air and water by discharging PFAS from its Fayetteville plant into the Cape Fear River,” Stein said in a statement Thursday. “Now, the EPA is cutting a deal with Chemours that does next to nothing for North Carolinians and allows polluters to choose what to clean up and where.”
Jackson previously encouraged North Carolinians to submit public comments to the federal government on how the agreement affects them. He shared the letter that he, Stein, and Wilson submitted on Wednesday.
NC AG Jackson calls on residents to weigh in on Chemours’ ‘backroom deal’ over PFAS

“Chemours and the EPA negotiated this deal behind our backs,” Jackson said in a statement. “It does nothing to fix the decades of damage Chemours has done to our state, and it’s offensive to the people who drink this water.”
The state leaders are asking the federal court to reject the proposal. Instead, they want the EPA to work with North Carolina to develop a settlement that benefits the state and its residents. 
While the agreement requires Chemours to spend $90 million over 15 years to fund water cleanup and clean drinking water projects, none of that money is earmarked for the Tar Heel State. 
“This proposed sweetheart deal that was brokered without even consulting North Carolina requires almost nothing more of Chemours than it’s already doing under the consent order it signed with DEQ,” Wilson said in a statement. “It’s offensive and unfair to the people of this state.”
A coalition of nine organizations represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center also filed public comments against the settlement. They say the deal absolves Chemours of responsibility for its actions. 
Attorneys from SELC described the deal as a “remarkably poor bargain” for North Carolina, according to the letter. 
“Rather than holding Chemours accountable, the deal appears designed to shield the company from meaningful consequences for the widespread harm its chemicals have caused,” said Kelly Moser, senior attorney and leader of the Water Program at SELC. “The message is hard to ignore: Chemours gets leniency while families get contamination.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: An effort to boost nature, backed by big-money donors, lands in the middle of Mass.’s ballot question mania
description: As the campaign shifts from ballot-qualifying to general election mode, what the end result will be of all the money raised and spent, all the signatures collected and ads likely to come, and all the potential friction introduced with Beacon Hill — even if the question passes this fall — is for now unclear.
text:
FOR ONE OF THE MOST under-the-radar ballot questions of the nine slated to go before voters this fall, the case is pretty simple. 
A coalition of environmental groups is asking voters to greenlight the innocuous task of setting aside tax revenues that are already collected from the sale of sporting goods and steer them toward conservation.  
Advocates are confident the question can win in November — who in the Bay State is really going to vote against nature, they wonder? — though how much additional money it may ultimately yield for conservation in the coming years is unknown, even if it passes. 
The issue was framed with urgency at a campaign launch event at the Esplanade along the Charles River in Boston on Tuesday, surrounded by boaters on the water and bikers on the trails.  
“This matters more than anything I can think of right now in this moment,” Katie Theoharides, president and CEO of The Trustees who served as energy and environmental affairs secretary under former Gov. Charlie Baker, said at the rally.  
While leaders of the ballot campaign seem confident that it will enjoy broad support from voters, they have relied on just a handful of very deep-pocketed individuals to get the measure in front of voters in the first place, giving critics a fresh example of the ability of wealthy donors to shape the ballot question process.   
In fact, it’s powered in large part by one person. 
Kirsten Waerstad, a Belmont resident who appears to have very little else in the way of political giving, dropped a $800,000 donation to the campaign in September — the third-largest contribution this cycle from an individual donor who isn’t themselves running for office. Waerstad’s donation to this one ballot question is equal to how much money GOP gubernatorial candidate Brian Shortsleeve donated to his own campaign in 2025, according to OCPF data. 
Waerstad, who runs a philanthropic nonprofit called the Humani Foundation and is married to Dharmesh Shah, co-founder of multibillion-dollar Cambridge-based tech firm HubSpot, declined an interview request about her donation but said in a statement that she is “incredibly excited” to be supporting the campaign. 
“I’m inspired by the incredible coalition of conservation organizations and community groups that are working together to pass the Protect Water and Nature initiative this fall, and I’m thrilled to help put nature on the ballot and win in November,” said Waerstad, who received Mass Audubon’s “Nature of Massachusetts” award — the group’s top honor — late last year. “The proposed Nature for All fund will help preserve priceless natural resources for our children, grandchildren, and generations of Massachusetts families to come.” 
Along with Waerstad, two other individuals are financing the ballot measure, forming a trio of donors that combined have contributed all of the almost $1.4 million reported by the campaign through the Office of Campaign and Political Finance at the end of last year, not counting in-kind donations. 
Natasha Grigg, a retired conservationist in Boxford, contributed $420,000. Grigg has only donated to candidates a handful of other times and not since 2021. 
And the campaign reported a $160,000 haul from Jessie Panek, a retired landscape designer who lives in Harvard, on the same September day that Waerstad opened up her checkbook. It appears to be Panek’s first foray into political giving in state politics. 
The campaign didn’t make Panek or Grigg available for comment. There are no limits to campaign contributions for ballot questions in Massachusetts.  
And the ballot question is getting a new corporate boost: David O’Neill, Mass Audubon’s president and CEO, said at the Boston rally that Massachusetts-based company Bemis, an adhesives manufacturer based in Shirley, has pledged $100,000 to the campaign. 
Sam Anderson, senior director of government affairs at Mass Audubon, defended the campaign’s fundraising strategy to date while suggesting the next required financial disclosure, in September, “is going to look a lot different” with “more diverse sets of funding.”  
“These are not mega corporations,” Anderson said in an interview. “These are not out-of-state people. These are not shady interests. These are members of our community,” he said of the campaign’s donors. 
If nothing else, it’s one sign that environmental causes can still churn out big-dollar supporters in Massachusetts during a political moment in which even some Democrats in and out of the Bay State speak more of affordability and “all-of-the-above” energy sources than the perils of climate change and the need to swiftly sever fossil fuels from our power mix.  
Yet as the campaign shifts from ballot-qualifying to general election mode, what the end result will be of all the money raised and spent, all the signatures collected and ads likely to come, and all the potential friction introduced with Beacon Hill — even if the question passes this fall — is for now unclear. 
That’s because the ballot question lacks teeth: It could wind up completely ignored even if passed by voters. State legislators, who have the last word over spending decisions, would still need to appropriate the sporting goods sales tax revenues in line with the goals laid out in the ballot measure. 
Advocates for more funding for nature and conservation rally on the Charles River. (Jordan Wolman/CommonWealth Beacon)
If a majority of voters approve, the coalition projects that the ballot question would direct an estimated $100 million collected from the sales tax of sporting goods purchases annually to a separate fund that would support purchasing land for conservation, improving and adding trails, and bolstering resilience against extreme weather events. Georgia, Texas, and Virginia have already adopted similar models for conservation funding.  
The groups leading the effort, including Mass Audubon, the Trustees, and The Nature Conservancy, say they feel they have no choice but to put the issue directly in front of voters.  
Gov. Maura Healey’s fiscal year 2027 budget cuts the Department of Conservation and Recreation by nearly 4 percent amid broader fiscal headwinds and a continued maintenance backlog the agency was only starting to dig out of. Healey herself, however, has now endorsed the ballot question, telling GBH’s “Boston Public Radio” on Wednesday that it’s a “good thing in Massachusetts to be supporting” a measure that funds nature and water protection and park and trail restoration without raising taxes.  
And while state environmental officials project Massachusetts is on track to meet its goal of conserving 30 percent of state land by 2030, the coalition of more than 90 groups backing the ballot campaign, known as Nature for Massachusetts, argues it will take more money to get there than the state is allocating — and there’s no better way to fund that push than without raising or creating new taxes.   
Funding for nature, said Brad Campbell, the head of the Conservation Law Foundation, is consistently “the last funded and the first cut in the budget scrum that happens every year in the Legislature. It’s time to send a clear message to the Legislature that this is important.” 
Regardless, it’s not clear the ballot question would dedicate as much money to conservation as the $100 million that advocates claim.  
A review by the Tufts University Center for State Policy center estimates the measure would only direct about $65 million into the new nature conservation fund if passed because some of the sales tax revenue counted in other estimates is actually already earmarked for schools and transportation. That’s compared to the roughly $400 million the state spends annually on conservation and recreation, the Tufts analysis found.  
And it’s raised some concerns about the prospect for budgeting via ballot: If advocates of one issue are able to gain voter approval for siphoning off a chunk of General Fund revenues to support their cause, it’s not hard to see how such a method could be abused, further squeezing Beacon Hill’s budgeting powers to set its priorities and fund state programs accordingly. 
There’s some limited precedent for this, including a 1992 ballot question that levied a new tax on cigarettes and directed that money to fund public health programs and more recently the “millionaires tax” that passed in 2022 and is aimed specifically at transportation and public education initiatives.  
But in those cases, new sources of revenue were added into the mix, instead of a tax already in existence that would be drawn from the General Fund. 
“From a public finance standpoint, carving up existing revenue sources into dedicated streams for specific things is a dangerous road,” said Doug Howgate, president of the Massachusetts Taxpayers Foundation. “These are proposals made in a vacuum. The reality is, by definition, spending $1 in one place and not another place has a tradeoff. As folks are assessing this proposal, they’re not going to see those tradeoffs.” 
Then again, how much the ballot question if passed would even upend the normal budget process for conservation spending isn’t clear.  
Legislators could fulfill the proponents’ desire for the tax revenue from sporting goods purchases to act as additional money on top of what is already spent on open spaces, parks, water protection, and coastal resilience projects.  
Or they could subsequently just reduce what is currently dedicated for those purposes so that the new dedicated revenue stream balances out the net total funding for nature, especially as the State House looks poised to pass an environmental bond bill to the tune of more than $3 billion – effectively negating the impact of the ballot question. Either way, passage of the measure in no way guarantees a funding outcome as lawmakers hash out a budget year after year. 
Though lawmakers may feel political pressure not to ignore the earmark  after a majority of voters express a clear desire to see the money spent a certain way, some on Beacon Hill are openly wondering how, exactly, the measure would change the budget process from the status quo — raising questions about what this campaign is practically going to do. 
Rep. Alice Peisch, a Democrat who serves as co-chair for the Joint Committee on Initiative Petitions, made that point at a hearing over the ballot question in March. 
“And hope that we appropriate, is that the idea?” she asked the ballot proponents about the thinking behind the effort. “Seems like a lot of effort to do something that at the end of the day is no different from the process we have right now, which is that you all, and many others, would advocate with the Legislature during the budget process.” 
Theoharides, though, said majority support from voters this fall would still go a long way under the Golden Dome. 
“Nothing is ironclad,” she conceded in an interview, “but this would show that the will of the voters is to direct this money in this way.” 
Advocates insist they are keeping their eyes wide open. 
Part of the decision to go to the ballot in the first place, Anderson said, was a “diagnosis” that this issue “wasn’t going to rise to the top” for lawmakers this session. 
“Of course there’s risks, and we thought very hard about those risks,” he said. “There are other important issues that we need to continue to advocate on with the Legislature. There’s reputational risk — the risk of losing. The best we can do is just be for what we’re for.”

title: Small town in southeast Colorado declared abandoned
description: State officials Wednesday declared a small town in southeast Colorado abandoned after years of turmoil among its residents and local government leaders.  Residents of Hartman, which is near the state’s border with Kansas about a 30-minute drive east of Lamar, have not had elected officials running their town since January, when the entire board of […]
text:
A view of Hartman in southeastern Colorado near the Kansas border. (Google Maps)State officials Wednesday declared a small town in southeast Colorado abandoned after years of turmoil among its residents and local government leaders. 
Residents of Hartman, which is near the state’s border with Kansas about a 30-minute drive east of Lamar, have not had elected officials running their town since January, when the entire board of trustees for the town resigned. The town has 30 residents.
The town government oversaw the local water supply, and without government officials, water infrastructure has drastically deteriorated. Its tower supplies water to about 40 homes, and the town has been on a boil order since October.

“There are no government officials in the Town of Hartman who are authorized to approve contracts, spend funds, appoint replacements, certify elections, or make decisions regarding the Town of Hartman’s water system,” Deputy Secretary of State Andrew Kline’s abandonment order says. 
The Denver Post first reported in March on the tumultuous downfall of Hartman’s town government and its years of water infrastructure challenges. 
The Prowers County Board of County Commissioners will now manage public infrastructure within the abandoned town. The county will also take over the water infrastructure and will direct a water treatment or delivery entity to run it. 
Kline held a hearing earlier this month where town residents and state officials presented evidence in support of and against an abandonment finding. His order that determined the town is abandoned takes into account information obtained through that hearing and relevant Colorado state law. 
“It is clear that there are town residents that ‘remain present, active, and willing to serve,’” Kline said in his order. “The Town of Hartman is not a place that is uninhabited, but rather a place where the resignation of all elected officials effectively prevents its residents from electing a new government.” 
The Colorado Legislature passed a law this year that created an exemption in the state’s process for declaring a town abandoned. Legislators who represent Hartman at the Colorado Capitol sponsored the bill. 
Previously, a town could be deemed abandoned only if it failed to hold an election, elect officers or maintain town government for five years. Now, a town can be deemed abandoned if it has no board of trustees or clerk, is unable to hold an election and owns or operates infrastructure critical for the treatment or delivery of water to residents. 
Officials with the Colorado Department of Local Affairs traveled to Hartman more than 30 times since 2022 to support the town with elections, resignations, budgets, audits and training new officials, Kline’s order said. DOLA officials said the water tower in Hartman was compromised and needed to be repaired or replaced, and the water needs to be tested and treated. No one is operating the town’s water system.
Kline said a decision against determining the town abandoned would place residents in further jeopardy given the health hazards presented by its crippled water infrastructure with nobody to run or fix it. Abandonment is the only mechanism that creates an avenue for residents to access clean water, he said. 
The Department of State also declared the town of Creede abandoned this month, but for more technical reasons, since it was incorporated adjacent to the city of Creede more than a century ago and had not had its own local government for at least five years.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont nonprofit sees $500,000 gift to create youth homelessness services endowment
description:
Leadership at Elevate Youth Services in Barre said the gift provides welcome financial stability for the expanding nonprofit.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont nonprofit sees $500,000 gift to create youth homelessness services endowment.
text:
Favor Ellis, executive director of Elevate Youth Services in Berlin, on Tuesday, July 21, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
Elevate Youth Services in Barre has received a $500,000 endowment gift to support youth homelessness services, the organization announced earlier this month. Leadership said the donation, which comes from the Burlington-based Courtney and Victoria Buffum Family Foundation, will provide the nonprofit a much-needed financial cushion and help enable continued services for young people experiencing housing insecurity.
Elevate operates a number of housing services primarily for youth aged 18 to 24, including 16 emergency shelter beds, six transitional housing placements and a rent voucher program, and also runs a five-bed facility for minors in state custody. The nonprofit serves roughly 400 youths in Washington County each year, said Executive Director Favor Ellis, and leads several statewide programs supporting other providers and assisting current or former foster care charges.
Ellis said that at present, her team is most focused on expanding the suite of services for youth in its care, including mental health and substance use counseling and basic supplies like food.
Youth homelessness is an ongoing concern in Vermont, according to housing advocates. Last year, one statewide count estimated nearly 1,400 youth under 25 were experiencing some form of homelessness. More than 200 children currently reside in time-limited emergency housing placements provided by the state, officials reported last month.
Nearly all the young people Ellis serves present with some form of mental health condition, she said, often connected to trauma earlier in life. That could include domestic violence, or expulsion from a family home due to gender identity or sexuality, she said. 
In general, she added, these young people’s struggles are inherited: “intergenerational poverty, intergenerational homelessness, intergenerational mental illness.” The goal at Elevate, Ellis said, is to build a new sense of community among residents in the nonprofit’s shared living spaces.
“Our mission is to help young people live the lives that they want to live,” she said.
Despite recent expansions, Elevate “almost always” has a waiting list for its shelter facilities, according to Ellis.
The new financial backstop — and annual return of roughly $25,000 — afforded by the endowment is well-timed, Ellis said. Beyond the normal instability of yearly grant renewals, she said, federal grant applications have changed dramatically under the Trump administration.
The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development provides funding for some programs at Elevate, Ellis said, and federal officials have been clear that some services — including harm reduction strategies around substance use and treatment “specific to gender” — are no longer a priority for funding. 
“We serve all youth, regardless of identity,” Ellis said. “It’s hard to talk about that in this current funding environment.”
But now, Ellis is eyeing Elevate’s future projects with new confidence, she said — the Buffum family’s donation is a sign of trust, a valuable gift in itself. 
Elevate added two new eight-bed shelter spaces on the former campus of Goddard College last summer, and is opening a new “drop-in” outreach center for teenagers in Barre, she said. An initial grant of $25,000 from the Buffum foundation while the first year of endowment returns accrue will primarily cover the cost of food for young people in the nonprofit’s care, Ellis added.
Lily Sojourner, who leads the Vermont Department for Children and Family’s Office of Economic Opportunity, said philanthropic gifts can allow service providers to stick to their mission rather than being bound to shifts in public funding priorities. A diverse set of funding streams is always the most stable scenario for this kind of organization, she added, and it’s common for Vermont providers to rely on community donations alongside public money.
“I think Vermont’s really fortunate to have a lot of engaged community members who want to help their neighbors,” she said. “We’ve seen that for years.”

title: A $300 million Fleming County solar project will get state tax refunds
description: A state economic development board voted Thursday to give state tax refunds to an international renewable energy company looking to invest $307 million to build a 188-megawatt solar installation in Fleming County.  The Kentucky Economic Development Finance Authority awards most financial incentives including grants, tax breaks and more to companies through t[...]
text:
Alongside Kentucky Utilities' E.W. Brown power plant in Mercer County, wildflowers help manage vegetation under a solar installation. (U.S. Department of Energy photo by Chad Alkire)A state economic development board voted Thursday to give state tax refunds to an international renewable energy company looking to invest $307 million to build a 188-megawatt solar installation in Fleming County. 
The Kentucky Economic Development Finance Authority awards most financial incentives including grants, tax breaks and more to companies through the Cabinet for Economic Development. Spain-based ACCIONA Energy is receiving a $400,000 a sales and use  tax refund on research and development and electronic processing equipment. 
The refund is through the Kentucky Enterprise Initiative Act, only the second time the board has awarded such incentives to a planned solar installation project in Kentucky, according to a state database of financial incentives. 
The Martin County Solar Project, backed by a company led by former Democratic State Auditor Adam Edelen, received a state tax refund of $600,000 through the Kentucky Enterprise Initiative Act in 2021. That project and Florida-based solar developer BrightNight have also received local bonds as well. 
During the board meeting, members of the state board including board chair Jean Hale, who served as president and CEO of Community Trust Bancorp., questioned a director for ACCIONA Energy about how the electricity from the project would be used, along with decommissioning plans for the project decades in the future. 
Brian Dunneback, director of business development for ACCIONA Energy, said the power generated from the 1,200-acre solar installation would be supplied to East Kentucky Power Cooperative and the larger PJM electric grid, and the company had decommissioning plans. 
“We’ve done a number of environmental studies that include wetlands, critical habitat assessment to make sure that we’re avoiding any impacts to any kind of critical wetlands,” Dunneback said. 
Jeff Noel, the secretary for the Cabinet of Economic Development, thanked the board chair after the vote, saying prospective companies are looking for access to renewable energy. 
“There’s a lot of interdependencies as it relates to these kinds of projects with our ability to attract and even help existing companies grow in those situations where the companies have made a commitment to their shareholders, to their customers, and to their employees that they will have a certain percentage of renewable energy,” Noel said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Rankin County schools released from desegregation order
description: After nearly 60 years, the Rankin County School District has been released from a federal desegregation order put in place to curb racial discrimination.  On Tuesday, U.S. District Court Judge Kristi Johnson declared that racial segregation no longer exists in how students are zoned or transferred to district schools and classes or how staff and […]
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
After nearly 60 years, the Rankin County School District has been released from a federal desegregation order put in place to curb racial discrimination. 
On Tuesday, U.S. District Court Judge Kristi Johnson declared that racial segregation no longer exists in how students are zoned or transferred to district schools and classes or how staff and faculty are assigned to schools. The court also found that students of all races are subjected to equitable discipline practices and have access to extracurricular activities in the district.
“The Court finds that the District’s current policies and practices are race-neutral and comply in good faith with the Court’s orders and the District has done everything practicable to eliminate the vestiges of discrimination,” Johnson wrote.
The court will no longer monitor whether the district is discriminating against Black students and staff. The district no longer discriminates against Black students or operates a dual school system, according to the U.S. Department of Justice. 
At a September hearing, attorneys for the plaintiffs, some of whom were in attendance, argued school desegregation persists in Rankin County schools. Erica Frankenberg, an education professor at Penn State who researches racial desegregation, found in an investigative report that the district missed between 20 and 30 opportunities to diversify its staff, passing on qualified Black applicants in favor of white ones.
Attorneys remarked the district had one Black teacher in the gifted and talented program.
John Hooks, an attorney for Rankin County schools, reminded the court at the September hearing that Brandon Elementary was designated a National Blue Ribbon School for closing the achievement gap for Black students in 2021.
Black students post higher graduation grades and lower drop-out rates in the district, he added.
Rankin County schools join the Copiah County School District, which was released from its desegregation order in August. In Mississippi, 28 school districts remain under desegregation orders. 
Only two other southern states, Alabama and Georgia, have more districts that are monitored for vestiges of segregation by a federal judge.
The federal monitoring of Rankin County schools came about as a result of a lawsuit brought by local Black students. In 1967, Kenneth Adams and other Black children sued the district for discriminating against Black students and operating a dual school system for them. The court ordered a freedom of choice plan for students within the district, and later, in 1970, ordered the district to desegregate its schools across six metrics, ranging from how students are zoned to district schools to staff assignments to schools.
Thad Cochran US Courthouse in Jackson, Miss., Tuesday, July 19, 2023.  Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
For the subsequent decades, district officials provided the court with annual reports on the racial composition of staff assignments and student enrollment, among other data. District officials were tasked with ensuring no schools in the district had a student population that was overwhelmingly Black or white. White student populations at schools had to be between 46.59% and 86.59% in the 2023-24 school year. 
The goal was that each school roughly represented the diversity districtwide. Rankin County schools are approximately 27% Black and 62% white.
The court ensured compliance through district data. Since the September hearing, the court received at least five reports from the district detailing the racial demographics of students at each school and among student transfers between schools. The district also gave the court the racial breakdown of its teachers and administrators.
Twelve schools fell outside of the range set by the court to determine racially identifiable schools over the past five years.
In October 2019, the court stopped monitoring whether new construction and building closures disproportionately disadvantaged Black students or staff. That year, the court also stopped monitoring the race of all district bus drivers. Both decisions came after the court ruled that district leaders no longer discriminated in decisions related to district expansion, school construction and abandonment of buildings and supplies.
Rankin County’s release from its desegregation order has followed several others in the region. The Department of Justice under President Donald Trump has signaled willingness to release more school districts from desegregation orders. More school districts were released from desegregation orders during Trump’s first administration than under the past four presidents.
“From the very first, federal supervision of local school systems was intended as a temporary measure to remedy past discrimination,” Johnson cited a prior ruling. “Now, after almost 60 years, the Court concludes its supervision.

title: Trump administration rules out mass ICE enforcement at the polls in midterms
text: WASHINGTON — U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is not planning an aggressive campaign at voting sites during the upcoming midterm elections, the Department of Homeland Security said Thursday in response to a States Newsroom inquiry about a letter from U.S. Senate Democrats voicing concerns about armed federal agents at polling places.ICE, an agency within DHS that has sustained intense criticism since the start of the second Trump administration for its aggressive and sometimes deadly tactics, has no plans to target polling sites in November, a DHS official told States Newsroom in an email. The official left open the possibility, though, that the agency’s plans could change based on available intelligence.“ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” the DHS official said. “ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action.”The email came from a general DHS media account and did not name the official. The statement did not specify anything about DHS agencies other than ICE.While DHS made similar statements earlier this year, this one responded to a request for comment about a letter this week from a dozen U.S. Senate Democrats to three Cabinet members demanding to know more about the administration’s possible plans to send federal law enforcement officers to polling places across the country. The group, led by Sen. Edward Markey of Massachusetts, sent a letter Tuesday to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in which the lawmakers asked whether armed federal agents would be deployed at election sites, which they said would be prohibited under federal law. “Congress has enacted longstanding criminal prohibitions against sending federal personnel to polling places and using federal power to interfere with elections,” they wrote. “Americans should never have to wonder whether the federal government intends to police the ballot box with armed agents.” Democrats have voiced increasing worries that President Donald Trump is seeking to control elements of election administration, which is a state responsibility under the U.S. Constitution. The issue is at the center of lawsuits brought by Democratic campaign and nonpartisan voting-rights groups challenging an executive order restricting mail-in voting. And U.S. House Democrats say the administration is withholding disaster relief funds as leverage to force states to change their election laws.“The letter reflects my and my Senate colleagues’ deep concerns that Donald Trump appears to be planning to steal the upcoming election, which Republicans cannot win on the merits,” Markey said in a Thursday statement to States Newsroom. “We know that no unlawful, illegal, and unconstitutional act is beyond him and we must be ready for it.”Joining Markey on the Tuesday letter were Sens. Chuck Schumer of New York, Gary Peters of Michigan, Tammy Duckworth of Illinois, Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, Andy Kim of New Jersey, Chris Van Hollen and Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Bernie Sanders of Vermont, Raphael Warnock of Georgia, Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Maria Cantwell of Washington.Growing concern The senators’ concerns, they said, arise partly from findings revealed earlier this month that came out of an investigation launched in 2025 by the Democratic National Committee. Last October, the committee sought records regarding the possible deployment of federal law enforcement officers to polling stations, ballot-drop sites and election offices. The departments of Justice, Homeland Security and Defense initially did not produce any documents, and during ensuing litigation, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement represented it had found “no responsive records,” according to the July 28 letter. But after the DNC challenged the search results, ICE admitted to finding “more than 11,000 potentially responsive pages,” while U.S. Customs and Border Protection, another DHS agency, said it located nearly 117,000, lawmakers wrote. The Department of Defense declined to comment Thursday on the senators’ letter, telling States Newsroom that it will instead follow its typical protocol of responding directly to the authors themselves. The Department of Justice did not respond to a request for comment.Trump’s focus on elections  Democrats’ inquiries into the administration’s plans also stem from comments President Donald Trump has made in recent months about election integrity.When a PBS Newshour correspondent asked Trump in May if he would send ICE agents or National Guard troops to polling sites for the midterms, he said he would “do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections.”  And earlier this month, during a nationwide primetime address, he again reiterated claims about the country’s voting systems being vulnerable to hacking and disputed his 2020 presidential loss, sowing doubts about the entire election process despite having a lack of evidence to back up his words.  “President Trump’s statements, coupled with his repeated threats to invoke the Insurrection Act — which authorizes the president to deploy military forces inside the United States to suppress rebellion or domestic violence — only heighten concerns,” the senators added in their letter. “The Administration now has a choice,” they wrote. “It can continue to fuel the appearance that it is laying the groundwork for an unprecedented federal intrusion into state-run elections, or it can finally provide Congress and the American people with the transparency they deserve.”The lawmakers requested that Blanche, Mullin and Hegseth provide details about any possible plans to deploy federal troops at election sites in November and identify who may have authorized such deployments, setting a deadline of August 11. They also asked that the federal agency leaders produce records “concerning the possible deployment of federal law enforcement personnel or troops to polling places or other election sites.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana moves to set up homelessness courts, with critics saying it won’t help
description: Advocates and service providers for the homeless worry a new Louisiana law that criminalizes unauthorized sleeping outdoors will make it even harder for people who struggle to find permanent housing.
text:
A makeshift campsite for people experiencing homelessness in downtown Salem, Oregon, is pictured on Jan. 29, 2024. (Ben Botkin/Oregon Capital Chronicle)Advocates and service providers for the homeless worry a new Louisiana law that criminalizes unauthorized sleeping outdoors will make it even harder for people who struggle to find permanent housing.
Act 788, sponsored by Rep. Debbie Villio, R-Metairie, was dubbed the Streets to Success Act. It prohibits public camping or sleeping overnight in public areas without permission. It also allows local judges to create homelessness courts where defendants can be connected with housing and other support services rather than punished with fines or jail time.
Penalties in the new law include fines up to $500, jail time up to six months or both. It also allows for the option of court-ordered participation in drug treatment or mental health programs.
Defendants would be required to either pay the cost of their treatment in rehabilitation programs or, if they can’t afford it, perform unpaid community service. A judge could also waive these costs.
Successful participation in a homelessness court program could allow those charged to have their conviction set aside and prosecution dismissed.
The law has been widely criticized. The National Homelessness Law Center called it “one of the cruelest anti-homeless bills in the country.” Advocates for unhoused people have spoken out against the law, saying it would do more harm than good to people living on the streets.
“When folks have nowhere else to go, they do have to sleep outdoors,” said Joe Heeren-Muller, coordinator for the Louisiana Advocacy Coalition on Homelessness.
“It’s not, generally speaking, because of a stubborn insistence that living outdoors is in their best interest, but it’s simply because they lack the opportunity and the means to secure a safe and affordable indoor habitation,” he added.
Defenders of the new law argue it creates a pathway to access needed services, such as substance abuse rehabilitation and mental healthcare, for people experiencing homelessness.
In a written statement to the Illuminator, Villio said the law doesn’t criminalize homelessness but instead creates “necessary external pressure to compel individuals into critical mental health and addiction treatment services rather than leaving them unassisted on the street.”
Advocates disagree, saying the problem is driven by lack of access rather than the lack of a law that compels people to get the help they need.
“There’s a lack of accessible and affordable treatment for people. There’s no reason to think that the courts are going to make that more accessible,” Heeren-Muller said.
Under the new law, local governments can vote on whether they will allow outdoor sleeping and camping in specific, publicly-owned areas, and they would have to approve any designated areas annually. But in order to first approve it, the governing body needs to show there aren’t sufficient beds available in homeless shelters and that nearby property values wouldn’t be affected.
The majority of the new law went into effect when Gov. Jeff Landry signed it June 9. The portion that allows designated outdoor sleeping zones will go into effect Jan. 1.
Louisiana’s new law follows on the heels of a recent U.S. Supreme Court decision in an Oregon case, Grants Pass v. Johnson, that allows municipalities to penalize unauthorized sleeping in public areas. Justices decided, in a 6-3 vote, the law didn’t constitute cruel and unusual punishment.
There are 3,688 people experiencing homelessness in Louisiana, according to the latest counts from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. That represents about eight out of every 10,000 people in the state. The count found 42% of those people were unsheltered, meaning they were on the streets or living in vehicles, while the rest were in shelters or transitional housing.
The HUD report didn’t include people staying with family or friends, or in similarly unstable housing situations that could lead to becoming unsheltered or in need of more direct assistance.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV Treasurer Pack says it’s ‘unacceptable’ clothing voucher closed amid $370M surplus
description: State Treasurer Larry Pack says it’s “unconscionable” that West Virginia's school clothing assistance program for low-income children has already stopped taking applications due to a funding shortfall.
text:
West Virginia State Treasurer Larry Pack addresses reporters about his 2026 legislative priorities during a news conference Nov. 17, 2025, in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)State Treasurer Larry Pack says it’s “unconscionable” that West Virginia’s school clothing assistance program for low-income children has already stopped taking applications due to a funding shortfall.
“I think it is unacceptable that a state where we celebrate millions of dollars of surpluses, and we announced a program and a week later stop a program that is designed to help low-income school children have new clothes to start school in just two weeks,” Pack told West Virginia Watch on Thursday.
“It is just really hard to understand the priorities are of this administration. It does appear that children are not part of it,” he added.
Applications for the school clothing assistance program were open for seven days before funds ran out Monday.
According to Gov. Patrick Morrisey’s office, 52,000 children in West Virginia applied for the school clothing assistance program in that window. 
“This year, demand for the benefit was extraordinarily high, and the available funding was exhausted before the application period ended,” Lars Dalseide, the governor’s communications director, said earlier this week.
Eligible families receive $200 through the program to shop for shirts, pants, shoes, coats and more at retail stores before school starts.
West Virginia pays for the program through the federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Family, or TANF, program. 
Earlier this year, lawmakers authorized $177 million in TANF funding for DoHS to spend this current fiscal year on programs that help low-income children and families.
In May, Morrisey told reporters that his administration discovered a projected $43 million TANF deficit, prompting a review of the state’s use of those federal dollars. The review caused a delay in launching the school clothing assistance program. In the past, the program typically began accepting applications July 1.
The governor’s office hasn’t publicly released documents showing the TANF deficit.
Pack called on the Morrisey administration to have “full disclosure” on the use of TANF funds and noted the state is only in month one of the current fiscal year yet dealing with funding questions.
“It needs to be a document that people can look at and peruse and ask questions about,” Pack said. “And then, if in fact there’s not enough money, I am quite sure the Legislature would love to give suggestions on where we can find a million dollars in a budget that has all these tremendous surpluses.”
Last year, West Virginia’s school clothing assistance program served more than 57,000 children, according to the governor’s office. In the past, the program has served more than 80,000 kids. 
There are ongoing concerns about how other programs funded by TANF, including family support centers and child care assistance programs, could be impacted by Morrisey’s review of the federal anti-poverry funds.
DoHS announced on July 16 that the department was nearing completion of the review of TANF dollars. 
“Today, West Virginia receives approximately $98.8 million in federal dollars each year to support TANF-funded state activities but spends approximately $137 million annually on TANF programs,” DoHS said in a news release. “The difference has been covered using TANF reserve funds – essentially savings accumulated over previous years. At the current expenditure rate, those reserve funds will be exhausted in about 13 months.”
Pack said TANF funding concerns are “not going away.” 
“I think there will absolutely be more transparency, more clarity. It’s the question whether we’re going to get it really soon, or the Legislature will mandate over time,” he said. “When you think about the safety net population, you know we have a duty to do the right thing. I don’t think the state of West Virginia is doing the right thing with this population.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Attorneys for former police chief who led Kansas newspaper raid want to drop him as a client
description: TOPEKA — The attorneys for former Marion Police Chief Gideon Cody have asked the court to withdraw from his criminal case because of a broken relationship between the attorneys and their client. Cody faces a low-level felony charge of interfering with judicial process and is set to go on trial Aug. 24. He led the […]
text:
Former Marion Police Chief Gideon Cody enters the Marion County Courthouse on Oct. 7, 2024, with attorney Sal Intagliata for his first appearance in a low-level felony case. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The attorneys for former Marion Police Chief Gideon Cody have asked the court to withdraw from his criminal case because of a broken relationship between the attorneys and their client.
Cody faces a low-level felony charge of interfering with judicial process and is set to go on trial Aug. 24. He led the police raid on the Marion County Record, the newspaper publisher’s home, and the home of a city councilwoman in August 2023.
Special prosecutors Marc Bennett, of Sedgwick County, and Barry Wilkerson, of Riley County, cleared Cody and other law enforcement officers of wrongdoing in carrying out the raids, even though they were based on a made-up crime and violated both state and federal laws that protect journalists and their sources. The raids spawned five ongoing federal lawsuits.
The criminal charge stems from Cody telling a witness, after the raids became the topic of intense scrutiny, to delete text messages that could give someone the wrong idea about the nature of their relationship. If convicted, because he has no criminal history, Cody’s sentence would be presumptive probation.
On Wednesday, Wichita defense attorneys Sal Intagliata and Audra Asher filed a motion to withdraw from the case.
“Effective assistance of counsel has been undermined by a breakdown in the attorney-client relationship and attorney-client communication,” they wrote.
They requested a hearing on their motion. A motion hearing for the case was already scheduled for Aug. 5.
If the attorneys are allowed to withdraw, Cody’s trial could be delayed for a second time. It previously was set for Feb. 2.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: BREAKING: Mandela Barnes drops out of primary for Wisconsin governor
description: UPDATE: This story has been updated with additional details. Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes announced he is suspending his campaign for governor Thursday in a video posted to social media, narrowing the field to four as state Rep. Francesca Hong has expanded her lead in polls.  “We’re incredibly proud of all the things that we’ve […]
text:
Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes in his launch video for his 2026 gubernatorial campaign. | Photo courtesy Mandela Barnes for Wisconsin campaignUPDATE: This story has been updated with additional details.
Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes announced he is suspending his campaign for governor Thursday in a video posted to social media, narrowing the field to four as state Rep. Francesca Hong has expanded her lead in polls. 
“We’re incredibly proud of all the things that we’ve accomplished and all the resources that we have raised to spread our message, but it’s become very clear who our nominee is going to be,” Barnes said in the video without naming a candidate. 
Mainstream Democrats in recent weeks have been seeking a candidate to consolidate behind to stop Hong, a democratic socialist many fear cannot win the general election against Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, but her lead has only grown in the last week. 
Barnes had faced doubts since he launched his campaign last Dec., in part due to his failed U.S. campaign against U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson in 2022, but he has largely been considered to be among the  frontrunners in the race. The latest Marquette University Law School poll showed him with 16% support among likely primary voters, second to Hong’s 38%, but way ahead of the rest of the field, with Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley placing third at 7%. In recent weeks, Barnes has been competing most directly with Crowley, who exited the race a few weeks ago, but restarted his campaign with the endorsement of Gov. Tony Evers after Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez dropped her bid.
According to a Politico report, Barnes’ announcement comes as damaging media reports about him were expected to hit in coming hours. His exit leaves it a four-way race between Hong, Crowley, former Department of Administration Secretary Joel Brennan and state Sen. Kelda Roys. 
The winner of the Aug. 11 Democratic primary will likely face U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, the presumptive GOP candidate in November. 
“Now, we have to do everything we possibly can to defeat Tom Tiffany, and that’s exactly what I’m committed to do for the next 96 days,” Barnes said.
According to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel, Barnes’ decision also comes amid reporting by the outlet on allegations that Barnes took advantage of his role in the party to have sexual encounters with young adult women. He has not been accused of any crimes. According to the Journal Sentinel report, in 2025, the Democratic Party of Wisconsin hired a law firm to look into similar claims but the allegations they received were anonymous and unspecific and nothing actionable was found.

Thank you, Wisconsin. pic.twitter.com/FKDjCaPdJZ
— Mandela Barnes (@TheOtherMandela) July 30, 2026

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Advocacy group criticizes U.S. Marshals after four-day sweep of arrests
description: Escucha Mi Voz Iowa, an immigrant-led advocacy group, is calling for more transparency after the U.S. Marshals Service carried out enforcement operations across Iowa from July 21-24, arresting 61 people, including a vehicle stop amid Iowa City traffic that the group characterized as “reckless.” According to a news release from the U.S. Marshals Service, only[...]
text:
U.S. Marshals performed an operation at the intersection of Highway 1 and South Riverside Dr. in Iowa City, July 23, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Escucha Mi Voz Iowa's Facebook)Escucha Mi Voz Iowa, an immigrant-led advocacy group, is calling for more transparency after the U.S. Marshals Service carried out enforcement operations across Iowa from July 21-24, arresting 61 people, including a vehicle stop amid Iowa City traffic that the group characterized as “reckless.”
According to a news release from the U.S. Marshals Service, only 12 out of the 61 people detained were accused of being “violent criminals.” Escucha Mi Voz Iowa questioned why so many people were arrested, despite the stated purpose of the operation being to remove “dangerous individuals from the communities of central Iowa.”
The Iowa City enforcement involved armed U.S. marshals carrying out an operation at a busy intersection on July 23. They detained Coralville resident Lattieny Lockett, who was accused of failing to register as a sex offender. Lockett is currently being held in the Johnson County Jail.
Eyewitnesses told Escucha Mi Voz Iowa that U.S. marshals were driving recklessly, weaving between vehicles in stopped traffic while carrying “long guns” and wearing tactical vests, the organization stated in a news release.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Paul Cornelius, chief of staff for the Iowa Department of Corrections, said the agency assisted U.S. marshals with their enforcement in Iowa City, describing the incident as a “routine arrest.”
According to Escucha Mi Voz Iowa, eyewitnesses recalled observing a female passenger in the vehicle with Lockett during the arrest, describing her as an “African immigrant wearing an ethnic headwrap.” The organization says the woman’s whereabouts are still unknown as of Wednesday, and her identity is unverified.
Witnesses who spoke to Escucha Mi Voz Iowa also said many citizens were “caught in the middle” of the operation, “endangering” residents at the intersection of Highway 1 and South Riverside Drive, the organization stated.
“That was reckless as hell. Federal agents were waving guns around and running between cars at one of the busiest intersections in Iowa City. Somebody could have been shot. Somebody could have crashed. A family could have been caught in the middle,” Clinton Dimambu, Escucha Mi Voz Iowa member and naturalized citizen from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, said in a news release. “I came to this country believing the government was supposed to keep people safe, not turn a public intersection into a war zone. The U.S. Marshals need to explain why they thought this was acceptable.” 
David Goodner, Escucha Mi Voz executive director, said he reached out to Deputy U.S. Marshal Joshua Finnis, who heads the Davenport Sub-Office for the Southern District of Iowa’s U.S. Marshals Service. Goodner said in a release he was told that the arrest was for a “run of the mill state offense.” The U.S. Marshals Service Davenport Sub-Office was contacted by Iowa Capital Dispatch but declined to comment.
Organization calls for transparency
The operation, named “Operation Heatwave,” was coordinated with the Iowa Department of Corrections, along with assistance from local law enforcement and Homeland Security Investigations. In addition to 61 fugitives being arrested, 97 felony arrest warrants were cleared.
Escucha Mi Voz said it wanted more information about the involvement of local law enforcement personnel in the operation.
A news release from the U.S. Marshals Service lists the Coralville Police Department as part of Operation Heatwave’s task force.
Coralville Chief of Police Kyle Nicholson said in an interview the police department was not directly involved in Operation Heatwave, but a detective from Coralville was involved with a task force that led to multiple arrests in Des Moines.
“We have a detective whose duties include being a task force officer with the U.S. Marshals,” Nicholson said. “He was involved in the warrant operation last week. “However, he was in the Des Moines metro area and not involved in the arrest of Mr. Lockett here in Johnson County.”
Escucha Mi Voz Iowa is calling for “full transparency” regarding the incident, and to immediately release:


The identities, charges, and arrest locations for all 61 people arrested during Operation Heatwave.


The agency affiliation of every federal, state, and local officer assigned to the task force.


The identities of every officer and agent present during the Riverside Drive traffic stop in Iowa City.


The operational plans governing the use of high-risk traffic stops and other tactical enforcement methods during “Operation Heatwave.”


A complete accounting of every participating agency’s role, including Homeland Security Investigations and local law enforcement officers assigned to federal task forces.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico state agency CFO files lawsuit alleging $83M budget shortfall from universal childcare
description: The New Mexico Early Childhood Education and Care Department’s chief financial officer is suing the department and alleging that its leaders retaliated against her for raising concerns that the implementation of the universal childcare program late last year caused an $83 million budget shortfall.
text:
A new lawsuit alleges that the New Mexico Early Childhood Education and Care Department chief financial officer voiced concerns about the financial impacts of the state’s universal childcare program to department Secretary Elizabeth Groginsky, pictured right, alongside Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on Sept. 8, 2025, before being placed on leave. (File photo/Source NM)The New Mexico Early Childhood Education and Care Department’s chief financial officer is suing the department and alleging that its leaders retaliated against her for raising concerns that the implementation of the universal childcare program late last year caused an $83 million budget shortfall.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Carmel Pacheco-Aragon filed the whistleblower protection lawsuit in the state’s First Judicial District Court late Wednesday evening. In the lawsuit, she alleges that ECECD leaders illegally shuffled funding between programs to cover the shortfall.
The lawsuit says she told ECECD Secretary Elizabeth Groginsky that state law requires written authorization and legislative approval for such budgetary adjustments — and alleges that ECECD leaders had only secured verbal authorization from the state Department of Finance and Administration.
“The law doesn’t take this position of, ‘Do whatever the hell you want. We’ll figure it out next session.’ That’s not how the appropriation statutes work,” Jacob Candelaria, an attorney and former state lawmaker who’s representing Pacheco-Aragon, told Source NM Thursday. “That’s what’s happening, from what we can tell.”
Candelaria previously represented a trio of Republicans who unsuccessfully challenged the legality of the state’s universal childcare program. After a Second District Court judge denied their claim in June, Candelaria appealed to the New Mexico Supreme Court, where he similarly lost.
The Early Childhood Education and Care Department did not respond to Source NM’s request for comment Thursday morning prior to publication.
Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham first announced the program in September. The state lifted income restrictions on free childcare in November. Earlier this year, she signed a bill into law that provided a framework for the program, such as requiring co-pays from high-earning families during economic downturns.
Pacheco-Aragon’s lawsuit contends that she was “abruptly put on administrative leave” in early July and that department leaders did not provide her with specific allegations. Days after going on leave, the suit says a department official told Pacheco-Aragon she was suspended because she had BCC’d a longtime personal friend on an email that reflected her “deep anxieties regarding the agency’s handling of the childcare assistance program budget shortfall.”
As of the filing of the lawsuit, she is still on leave and “believes her termination from employment at ECED is imminent,” it says.
“That is textbook whistleblower protection retaliation,” Candelaria said.
Her lawsuit seeks reinstatement to her job and two times the amount of her backpay plus interest.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Stevens dismisses PAC focus as ‘campaign finance zoomies’
description: As U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham) makes her closing arguments to August primary voters across the state, the congresswoman, who is seeking the Democratic nomination for the U.S. Senate, met with business leaders in Lansing on Wednesday for a question-and-answer session. Questions regarding campaign finance and the amount of outside money being raised[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham), a Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate, speaks during a candidate meet and greet with the Lansing Regional Chamber in downtown Lansing, Mich. July 29, 2026 | Photo By Ben Solis/Michigan AdvanceAs U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham) makes her closing arguments to August primary voters across the state, the congresswoman, who is seeking the Democratic nomination for the U.S. Senate, met with business leaders in Lansing on Wednesday for a question-and-answer session.
Questions regarding campaign finance and the amount of outside money being raised and spent on her behalf continue to follow her across campaign events and in key debates. It has been a major focus for the campaign rhetoric of her opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, but also as a concern among undecided voters who might see Stevens’ connections to corporate and advocacy PACs, such as the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, as a liability.
That issue surfaced again during her appearance before the Lansing Regional Chamber this week, as the first question posed by a business leader at the event centered squarely on campaign finance. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Stevens was asked about the tens of millions of dollars she’s received from corporations and other super PACs, which El-Sayed has repeatedly criticized. The ire, one business leader said, was an especially important issue for Democratic primary voters who are shifting more toward progressives.
When asked for her take on that, Stevens invoked former U.S. Sen. Debbie Stabenow and retiring U.S. Sen. Gary Peters, who have both endorsed her.
“I’m fundraising in the exact way that they always did,” Stevens said. “There’s deep frustrations that I think we all share. We’re that swing state now. With all the money that’s coming in from campaign committees and party committees, and things along those lines.”
Although Stevens did not directly answer the question, she used it as a springboard to pivot toward attacking El-Sayed.
“It’s important to recognize my record. I’m not lip service. I want to overhaul our system. I’m the only person in this race with an A grading from End Citizens United. I have a record of taking on this dark money,” Stevens said. “But my only focus is people here in Michigan. … That’s how I do my work. My opponent in this race also has a Super PAC that is funded by his father in law. I am proud of my record and I’m proud of what I am standing for, and I’m proud of why I’m running for this seat.”
She also accused El-Sayed of accepting dark money and asserted that he was doing some of the exact same things he was accusing Stevens of.
Later, another business leader asked Stevens for specifics on how she would attack the campaign finance problem facing U.S. elections, noting she didn’t answer the previous question on the matter. A bill by U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) was also referenced, which would abolish super PACs, and Stevens was asked if she would support it.
Stevens responded by saying that something like that should start in the Senate, and that the upper chamber of Congress should “put big ideas down.” She also said she would entertain a constitutional amendment to curb corporate influence on campaign finance.
“We are running stagnant as a nation. Michigan has been losing proportional representation for the last 50 years,” Stevens said. “It’s not in the Constitution. … I’ve got a stronger legislative record for Michigan. Senator Sanders, with all due respect, he’s got a campaign platform. He’s in the independent party. I haven’t talked to him about it. I’m not trying to do any division.”
U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (center) speaks at meet and greet event in Detroit with Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (right) and U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina (left). July 24, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
Stevens, who again did not address the question directly, quickly pivoted to her work on the auto industry rescue during the Obama administration and raised concerns about El-Sayed’s financial disclosures. She eventually landed back to the question at hand.
“Maybe something is breaking. I have the pledge. I have the commitment. I have the voting record,” Stevens said. “I would love a constitutional amendment to get rid of money in politics and maybe make our elections shorter. … I’ve even talked to the colleagues on the other side of the aisle. We need them to know that we’re in a moment of reckoning.”
As Stevens grapples with questions on super PACs and questions about her own connections to dark money in the race, some of her endorsers have come out in support of PAC spending and outside money as having a positive impact in elections.
Astead Herndon of the “America, Actually” podcast, produced by Vox, recently hosted Democratic U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina, who has endorsed Stevens. He told Clyburn that some 80% of Americans oppose dark money and support getting it out of elections.
Clyburn was asked if he did not think the Congressional Black Caucus was on the wrong side of history due its members’ stances on using PACs and advocacy dollars to help boost their political operations. The dynamic of dark money and PACs giving Black candidates a leg up in key races was also the subject of a recent report in Politico.
Clyburn said “no.” He framed the use of dark money in elections as a civil rights issue.
“You know, as well as I do, that no white person in this country came out of slavery,” Clyburn said. “I’m not that far removed from it. I know how my parents grew up. They didn’t grow up with wealth. They couldn’t pass that wealth onto their children because they never had it. I served with people here who are multimillionaires. If they decide that, ‘I’m not going to take any kind of corporate PAC money, because my mommy and daddy are writing the checks.’ So are we just supposed to stay out of politics because we don’t have the family wealth to support it? Or do we sit down and find common ground?”
Clyburn challenged Herndon to “find one vote that I have ever cast that pharma supported and my constituents didn’t.”
Michigan Advance asked Stevens where she really stands on campaign finance reforms given Clyburn’s comments, and how his comments squared away with her saying that she supports a constitutional amendment to get money out of politics.
Stevens said she wants to be bold, but also said that she thinks some voters have “the campaign finance zoomies.”
“The first vote I took was for campaign finance reform. It stalled in the Senate. It was deeply frustrating. I remember we were planning strategies around that in Mitch McConnell’s Senate with regard to changing that,” Stevens said. “But here’s the other thing I’ll tell you: it seems like we got the campaign finance zoomies. We’ve got to be really honest here. Who’s benefiting from this level of infighting? It’s the Republicans who already have all their dark money all lined up ready to go.”
Stevens then said that she’s more focused on kitchen table issues, like affordability, because of what she’s hearing from voters on the ground.
“This is what my campaign is about. My opponent has done a great job talking about campaign finance. It’s an educated issue,” Stevens said. “I even had someone who’s got a law degree asking me about some of the campaign finance stuff today. That’s totally fine, but you know what else? These families on paid leave? They need affordable daycare. They need good public schools to go.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Judiciary commission members criticized for not revealing campaign contributions to ex-House speaker
description: More than half of the Judicial Nominating Commission members who voted to advance former House Speaker K. Joseph Shekarchi’s bid to fill an opening on the Rhode Island Supreme Court have donated to his political campaigns in recent years, state finance records show. Four of the panel’s nine members collectively contributed over $30,000 to the […]
text:
Zachary Mandell, chairman of the Rhode Island Judicial Nominating Commission, prepares to begin the  panel's meeting on Tuesday, July 28, 2026. Mandell donated $10,835 to former House Speaker K. Joseph Shekarchi’s campaigns between 2015 and 2026, according to state finance records. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current) More than half of the Judicial Nominating Commission members who voted to advance former House Speaker K. Joseph Shekarchi’s bid to fill an opening on the Rhode Island Supreme Court have donated to his political campaigns in recent years, state finance records show.
Four of the panel’s nine members collectively contributed over $30,000 to the Warwick Democrat’s campaign account since he first ran for office in 2012.
“The fact that four members of the Commission have contributed more than $30,000 to that account, and none of the four disclosed that at the public meeting is disappointing,” John Marion, executive director of Common Cause Rhode Island, said in a statement to Rhode Island Current. Marion has been an outspoken opponent of Shekarchi’s nomination.
The donations were first reported Wednesday by GoLocal Providence, one day after the commission recommended five finalists to fill the vacancy created by Rhode Island Supreme Court Justice Maureen McKenna Goldberg’s retirement in March.
All nine members voted in favor of four of the candidates: Assistant Attorney General Christopher Bush, Family Court Judge Laureen D’Ambra, Superior Court Judge Luis Matos and attorney John Roberts.
Commission members David Holley and Lamel Moore, both of whom were appointed by the General Assembly’s Republican leaders, declined to advance Shekarchi’s application to the governor for consideration.
The commissioners who donated to Shekarchi were Chairman Zachary Mandell, Thomas Casale, James Lepore and Raffaele Liguori.
Thomas Dickinson, Shekarchi’s attorney, said the former House speaker has complied with campaign finance reporting requirements since his first election in 2012.
“All donations have been posted by the Board of Elections, and they are online and available for public review,” he said in an emailed statement Thursday.
Shekarchi makes the list of Rhode Island Supreme Court potential nominees. But will he make the cut?

Mandell, a personal injury attorney who was appointed chairman of the commission by Gov. Dan McKee in February, donated $10,835 to Shekarchi’s campaigns between 2015 and 2026 — most recently contributing $1,000 on Jan. 12, according to filings made with the Rhode Island Board of Elections.
Casale, a Johnston auto body shop owner who was appointed to the commission in 2020 by then-Speaker Nicholas Mattiello and then-Senate President Dominick Ruggerio, has donated $10,400 to Shekarchi since 2017. Records show a $2,000 contribution was made Jan. 22.
Lepore, a criminal defense attorney appointed to the commission in 2019 by Ruggerio, has given Shekarchi $4,050 since 2012. He contributed $500 on Jan. 2, records show.
Liguori, a personal attorney who was appointed by McKee in June, has donated $4,750 to Shekarchi since 2017, including $500 on Jan. 12.
Neither of the four members immediately responded to requests for comment from Rhode Island Current. Casale told WPRI-12 Wednesday he hadn’t considered recusing himself and that he’s given “to the whole General Assembly.”
The state’s Code of Ethics exempts campaign contributions from factoring into the analysis of whether a conflict of interest exists. But good government advocates like Marion argue the four commissioners’ lack of disclosure during Tuesday’s meeting “reflects a profound lack of judgment.”
“Rhode Islanders have every reason to question the independence of those commissioners who chose not to disclose their donations to Rep. Shekarchi,” Marion said.
Shekarchi stepped down as House speaker May 7 as he announced his application for the lifetime spot on Rhode Island’s highest bench. Questions about what he will do with his $4.7 million campaign account lingered throughout the process, including during his interview before the Judicial Nominating Commission Tuesday.
The Rhode Island Code of Judicial Conduct prohibits judges and judicial nominees from making contributions to political organizations and candidates. Judicial applicants can still spend the money as they please before their name is submitted by the governor to the General Assembly for confirmation.
Shekarchi has pledged not to touch his campaign account and, if nominated, would seek guidance on how to properly dispose of the money. His application also raised ethical concerns that an immediate leap from the legislative branch to the judiciary violates the state’s revolving-door rules that bar a lawmaker from taking a state job within a year of leaving office.
Superior Court Judge Richard Licht ruled otherwise Monday, siding with Shekarchi’s legal arguments that the Supreme Court is a constitutional position exempt from the state’s ethics law.
“This controversy is exactly why a revolving door is so important,” Marion said. “When someone no longer holds elected office, no one can question whether they are being influenced by campaign donations and no one can question whether the donation will buy access or influence with the elected official.”
The governor has until Aug. 18 to pick one of the five finalists as his nominee, who must then be confirmed by the House and Senate.
