text: WASHINGTON — For the second time in as many weeks, a War Powers Resolution aimed at curbing President Donald Trump’s war with Iran failed to pass the U.S. Senate Thursday.The vote breakdown, 49-50, fell along familiar lines as previous War Powers votes, with Republican Sens. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Rand Paul of Kentucky and Susan Collins of Maine supporting the measure. Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania voted no, as he’s done in just over a dozen similar measures.Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., continues to be absent while in medical rehab.A similar War Powers Resolution to rein in Trump’s military conflict in Iran passed in the U.S. House on July 23, but failed in the Senate — both led by Republican majorities.War heats upThe regional war reignited yet again this week after Trump ordered retaliatory strikes Tuesday, along with Saudi Arabia’s armed forces, on Iran-backed militias in eastern Iraq. The strikes on “multiple terrorist logistics and weapons sites” were in response to Iranian drone attacks on U.S. forces in the region, according to U.S. Central Command.Trump told Fox News on Wednesday, “We are going to beat the f—-- s—- out of them.”The United States launched a “heavy wave” of strikes on Iranian military sites beginning at 10 p.m. Eastern Wednesday “in response to yesterday's attempted missile attacks on U.S. forces,” according to U.S. Central Command.The cost of oil jumped to just over $90 a barrel Wednesday in response to renewed fighting and a continued chokehold on traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, where one-fifth of the world’s petroleum traveled prior to the U.S. and Israel launching the war in late February. This means Americans are again paying more for fuel. According to AAA, the U.S. national average for a gallon of regular gasoline rose to $4.09 Thursday.Before the volley of strikes began again, Trump had announced a pause, after the U.S. and Iran traded rocket fire for nearly two weeks following the collapse of ceasefire talks. Service members killedThe president on July 22 attended the dignified transfer, in which the remains of soldiers are transferred from an aircraft arriving from the theater of operations back to the United States, for four U.S. service members killed as a result of the conflict with Iran.Three of the service members were killed July 17 and July 18 in an Iranian strike at a U.S. airbase in Jordan, and a fourth was killed during a controlled detonation of an Iranian drone July 19 at a U.S. base in Iraq. The most recent deaths of U.S. soldiers in the conflict bring the total killed to 18, while the number of injured increased to 653.But the Pentagon does not recognize the four most recent deaths among those in the Iran war, dubbed by the administration as Operation Epic Fury. Instead, the Pentagon is categorizing the latest deaths and injuries as casualties of “overseas operations starting July 7, 2026.”The administration is asking Congress for an additional $67 billion for the war in Iran. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Senate appropriators July 21 that the war has already cost $37.5 billion.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Nearly 18,900 CT children have lost SNAP benefits over past year
description: CT's 15.7% rate of children losing SNAP benefits is worse than the 13% rate reported in a survey of 19 states where data was available.
text:
Nearly 18,900 Connecticut children have lost access to federal nutrition benefits since July 2025, when Congress and President Donald Trump ordered a wide array of human services cutbacks, state officials reported this week. 
Connecticut’s erosion rate of 15.7% is worse than the 13% average rate that a nationally recognized policy group recently found in a survey of 19 states where Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program enrollment data was readily available.
“There are severe consequences, not just for the children but for society at large” with these enrollment trends, said Luis Nuñez, a research analyst for the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan policy institute based in Washington, D.C.
Enrolling households in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits long has been recognized to improve birth and other health outcomes. Losing SNAP benefits also can cost a family access to free school meals.
Nuñez also noted the federal government’s own agricultural research service estimates every $1 spent on SNAP boosts overall economic impact by $1.50.
Finding data about declining SNAP enrollment isn’t always easy
Equally concerning, according to the center, is that many states fail to make SNAP data easily accessible online.
The center could discover the decline in child participation since July 2025 using online resources in just 13 states, though six others provided data that normally isn’t published.
Many states in the Northeast and mid-Atlantic regions did provide SNAP information for the report, including Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Vermont.
Still, the center didn’t report receiving any information from Connecticut, where anti-hunger advocates have pushed to use state dollars to supplant vanishing federal resources for nutrition programs.
The state Department of Social Services operates an online dashboard that provides aggregate information, but not monthly totals, about adults and children who have entered the SNAP program each year. Families and individuals can join and leave the program rolls multiple times annually.
Jalmar De Dios, chief external affairs officer for the Department of Social Services, said the department strives to provide timely and easily accessible information about the many programs it manages amid a rapidly changing human services environment.
“We are always calling other states to see what best practices they have,” De Dios said. “We know that there’s a lot of things we still need to learn.”
The department and Gov. Ned Lamont’s administration have felt pressure from legislators and others to mitigate big cutbacks in federal spending on healthcare and social programs.
State officials have made $550 million in surplus funds since last November available for this effort.
Over the past year, Lamont and legislators have tapped these funds several times since November to combat hunger, committing:

$8.5 million to provide $300 grocery store gift cards to assist an estimated 25,000 residents who have lost access to SNAP benefits.


$4.7 million to regional community action agencies and to the United Way of Connecticut’s 2-1-1 information line. These nonprofits help households navigate new SNAP eligibility rules or identify other forms of nutrition assistance.


Millions of dollars in supplemental payments to bolster Connecticut Foodshare and affiliated pantries.

They also included $12 million in the state budget adopted in May to provide universal free breakfast at Connecticut schools starting this fall.
Still, other members of the General Assembly’s Democratic majority say Connecticut needs to do more, and the first step is getting more information about declining SNAP enrollment and the problems it creates.
“I think we need vastly more data on the human toll … and the changes to SNAP in particular,” said Sen. Matthew Lesser, D-Middletown, who co-chairs the General Assembly’s Human Services Committee.
“We cannot do everything,” he added, “but we can do something.”
Lesser’s inquiry about the center’s analysis, and Connecticut’s absence from it, prompted state officials Tuesday to generate the latest estimate of child participation in SNAP.
The enrollment numbers led state Sen. Cathy Osten, D-Sprague, co-chairwoman of the Appropriations Committee, to renew her push this week to create an ongoing state-funded nutrition benefit to help those pushed off SNAP who cannot otherwise obtain enough food.
Osten proposed such a program last spring, but legislative leaders and Lamont didn’t include it in the budget. More readily available hard numbers could be the key to getting something passed, she said.
“I know the legislature would like to have more data on the participants of SNAP,” Osten said, adding that enrollment relative to age, race ethnicity and regions within the state all are important.
Rep. Jillian Gilchrest, D-West Hartford, the other co-chair of Human Services, is running this fall for Connecticut’s 1st Congressional District seat. But she predicted Tuesday state lawmakers will demand more data about and options to assist those who’ve lost SNAP benefits once the 2027 General Assembly session begins Jan. 6.
“I think it’s going to continue to get louder,” she added, “because the need continues to grow.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Democrat Jim Priest talks tariffs, bipartisan problem-solving ahead of Oklahoma Senate runoff
authors: Sabrina Thaler, KOSU, Natalie Armour, KOSU
description: In an Aug. 25 runoff election, Oklahoma voters will choose the Democratic nominee to replace Markwayne Mullin in the U.S. Senate after his March appointment to lead the Department of Homeland Security. In the June primary, N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas led the five-way Democratic primary with 45% of the vote, and Jim Priest followed with nearly […]
text:
Jim Priest, one of two Democratic candidates to take Markwayne Mullin's seat in the U.S. Senate, sits for an interview in the KOSU studio on July 6. (Photo by Natalie Armour/KOSU)In an Aug. 25 runoff election, Oklahoma voters will choose the Democratic nominee to replace Markwayne Mullin in the U.S. Senate after his March appointment to lead the Department of Homeland Security.
In the June primary, N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas led the five-way Democratic primary with 45% of the vote, and Jim Priest followed with nearly 24%. State law requires a runoff when no candidate in a primary earns more than half the vote.
The winner of the runoff will face Republican Kevin Hern in the general election in November. Hern has served as the Congressman for Oklahoma’s first district since 2018 and swept the Republican primary in June.
Neither Thomas nor Priest has held elected office before. Priest, a lawyer and nonprofit executive, ran in 2010 to serve as state Attorney General and lost to Republican Scott Pruitt. Thomas is a nurse.
Both candidates would face an uphill battle in November. Oklahoma has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1990, and Hern alone received more votes in the Republican primary than every Democratic candidate combined. President Donald Trump endorsed Hern shortly after Mullin’s cabinet appointment, a decision the New York Times wrote “all but assured” Hern would take the seat.
Hern has also raised significantly more money than either Democratic candidate, including more than $5 million he personally loaned his campaign.
KOSU interviewed Priest and Thomas about how they would approach a race against Hern, their attitudes toward the President and what their priorities would be in Congress. KOSU’s interview with Jasmine Thomas will be published on Wednesday.
Sabrina Thaler, KOSU reporter: Why are you running for Senate?
Jim Priest, Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate: It was probably watching the chaos in Washington on TV and news feeds that began to eat at me. I wrote an editorial in The Oklahoman back in November, and I said, ‘We can’t give up. We’ve got to keep fighting for democracy in this time when the danger is that democracy might not survive.’
Then I got to thinking about my grandson, James. He’s eight years old, and I thought someday when he’s older, James may turn to me and say, ‘Papa, what did you do when our democracy was in danger?’ And I need to have a good answer. So I’ve told James, ‘I’m going to run for United States Senate, James.’ And with your help and with the help of your listeners, I’ll succeed, and maybe I can make a difference and bring some sanity and thoughtfulness back to Washington.
Thaler: You don’t have conventional political experience. What experience of yours does make you a qualified candidate for Congress?
Priest: Well, I was a lawyer for 35 years in both federal and state court, so I’ve handled a wide variety of issues. But in particular, I spent a lot of time in civil rights cases and employment law cases, reading the law, reading the Constitution, understanding constitutional concepts. And then I did run for attorney general back in 2010, and when I came in second, I learned that you don’t get a consolation prize or a participant trophy. You just have to go pick up your signs. But that loss really became a pivot point for me, because I knew I wanted to serve people in a bigger way than just in my law practice.
So I pivoted into the nonprofit world, and for the next 15 or so years, I led three different organizations here in central Oklahoma, including Sunbeam Family Services, that provides a wide variety of social services to those in need. And, then I went on to be the ‘Chief Encouragement Officer,’ the CEO, at Goodwill Central Oklahoma, where I really was able to put my experience to work in workforce development, training and trying to help people find jobs or better jobs. So I think that whole experience, both in the nonprofit world and in the legal world, has prepared me well.
In addition, at one point during my law career, I went back and became ordained. And I’d always felt like maybe there’s something I could do in the church community that would be helpful. So I became an ordained minister, and I’ve pastored a church for a short period of time and then helped other churches in a part-time capacity. And, you know, when you’re in the ministry, you’re helping people in some of the most critical times of their lives. Sometimes they’re joyful, but sometimes they’re very sad. And so experiencing those highs and lows, I think, has also prepared me not just from a brain standpoint, but from a heart and a head standpoint.
Thaler: Oklahoma has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate since 1990, and the state has also struggled with low voter turnout. In June, less than a quarter of registered voters cast ballots. If you win the August runoff, how do you plan to reach Republican and independent voters?
Priest: I think this is a great opportune time for Democrats to be true to themselves and to tell the real story about what Democrats stand for. Democrats stand for working people, and we’ve got a lot of working people in Oklahoma. But even if people don’t consider themselves working folks, I’d say the vast majority of Oklahomans are tired of what they see going on in Washington: the opportunism, the people who are taking advantage of inside positions with insider trading and corruption, the people that are reckless and out of control as ICE agents. All of these are creating a spirit of unhappiness and discontent in the state.
We’ve got to motivate Democrats to get out and vote. Low voter turnout is one of the awful things about our state. We have so many great things, but people have either given up on voting or don’t see their vote as important. And so we’ve got to encourage them and urge Democrats, independents and Republicans to get out and vote. I think independents are naturally inclined this year to go with Democrat candidates because they recognize what’s happened in our state and in our nation when Republicans have an overwhelming majority.
I’ve had the good fortune of having many friends who are Republican come up to me and say, ‘Thank God you’re running. We need you in Washington.’ They recognize the failings of not their party, per se, but people in their party, and the current resident of the White House, who has failed to live up to true Republican ideals. I think all of that combines to give Democrats a real chance this year.
Thaler: How will you translate Oklahomans’ day-to-day concerns into federal policy? What exactly will you propose?
Priest: I think what Oklahomans are, above all else, is they are practical problem solvers, whether it’s fixing a tractor that’s broken down in the field or trying to come up with a solution for homelessness in the city. I go as a Democrat to the US Senate, but when I get there, I want to be a collaborator with whoever wants to be a problem-solver, whether that’s Senator Lankford or somebody in the Democratic ranks or in the Republican ranks. Let’s set aside the partisan bickering. Let’s set aside the name-calling, which really doesn’t move the ball down the field, and let’s get to the solutions for the American people.
Thaler: What are some of those solutions?
Priest: I think one of the biggest backsteps that this current administration has taken was the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill, which is not very beautiful for those in need. What we have found is that it has cut back on health care for all Americans, particularly rural areas. It’s decimating rural health care. And so we’ve got to get in there and reverse the bad effects of the ‘big ugly bill.’
And then Congress has to reclaim authority over tariffs. Tariffs are a tax on the American people. They’re not a tax on other countries. And so one of the reckless things that this administration has done is imposing tariffs in a willy-nilly fashion. You know, it’ll be 10% one day, but then if they look at the president funny or they offend him in some way, well, it’s going to get raised 100%. That kind of unpredictability in foreign relations not only affects our relationship with other countries, but it becomes a tax, through tariffs, on the American people. That’s why people in rural areas and farm areas are finding it difficult to get fertilizer that’s affordable, to find parts for tractors and farm equipment. The tariffs have been a terrible blight on the American people, and Congress has the authority over those. The Supreme Court has cut back a little bit on the president’s authority in that realm, but he’s still trying to find a way to get around the Supreme Court ruling.
Thaler: If you win August’s runoff, you would face Representative Kevin Hern in the general election, who is a sitting congressman and swept the Republican primary. His campaign has also raised over $9 million, and that includes $5 million of Mr. Hern’s own investments. How are you planning to bridge that gap and defeat Kevin Hern in the general election?
Priest: When I was a lawyer and went into the courtroom, I would always think, ‘what is the strength of the other side and how can I use that to my advantage?’ I think the great wealth that Kevin Hearn has accumulated, both in his campaign coffers, but in his personal wealth as well, is really a sign of what’s wrong with America today. Politics is being influenced, to a sinister effect, by money. And we know about the Supreme Court case that needs to be reversed, that allowed dark money into politics. What I would do is just shine a light on Kevin Hern, on his finances, on how he’s financing his committee.
It would be great to have $9 million in our campaign coffers. You could do a lot of communications that way, but money doesn’t win elections. Money helps in getting your word out, but what wins elections is credibility, sincerity, integrity. And so I think if we just shine a light — ‘here’s my track record, here’s my experience, here’s my history helping people and solving problems’ — and here’s Congressman Hern. What legislation has he passed? How has he helped the people of Oklahoma? And what about all these allegations of insider trading and accumulation of wealth? I think if we shine a light on those things, people will come to a common sense solution when they vote.
Thaler: Representative Hern has been a fierce champion of President Trump and received the president’s endorsement in this election. And your potential predecessor, Markwayne Mullin, left his post in the Senate to join the president’s cabinet as a senator. How would you approach a working relationship with the president?
Priest: I am willing to work with people from a wide divergence of opinions. It will be challenging to work with President Trump if he continues on the reckless path that he’s on. Perhaps cooler minds will prevail; people will speak wisdom into his ear instead of just telling him what he wants to hear. And as long as there are areas where we can collaborate, I look forward to working with President Trump. I don’t know how many of those areas he’s interested in. He’s already told us he doesn’t think affordability is a real thing. He called it a hoax. Well, if that’s job one, which I think it is, then President Trump is either going to have to come around and recognize that maybe it doesn’t affect him and his billionaire friends, but it affects most of America’s working people. And he either needs to get concerned about that and roll up his sleeves and work with us, or he needs to get out of the way and let Congress enact legislation that will address those needs.
Thaler: What differentiates you from Jasmine Thomas, your opponent in this runoff?
Priest: Jasmine is a young woman who has a licensed practical nurse background. But I think the thing that distinguishes us is our approach to problem solving. I have a history in all my different careers of solving problems for people, being involved in the community consistently, for the past three, four decades. Miss Jasmine doesn’t have that kind of a track record. She’s young, so she hasn’t had the same opportunities, but she’s not looked for those opportunities either. So I think in terms of what we see wrong in Washington, we both agree things need to change. The difference happens with looking at the track record and who has the best chance not only to solve problems in Washington, but to win the fall election. And I think I’m the best candidate to beat Kevin Hern in November.
This transcript has been lightly edited for clarity and brevity.
This article was originally published by KOSU.

Starting this fall, nursing students at Mercy College of Health Sciences will train under a new clinical model through MercyOne. (Photo courtesy of Mercy College of Health Sciences)Mercy College of Health Sciences has partnered with a medical center that was also created by the Sisters of Mercy to develop a new method of providing clinical training to nursing students.
The Des Moines private college stated in a news release that it will collaborate with MercyOne Des Moines Medical Center to launch a new framework for clinical education this fall for students pursuing their bachelor’s degree in nursing. The program is called a “Dedicated Education Unit.”
“This partnership represents a significant step forward in how we prepare nurses for the realities of practice,” said Vincent Salyers, dean of the Joyce E. Lillis School of Nursing at Mercy College, in the release. “The Dedicated Education Unit model allows our students to build genuine competence and confidence within a real care team, not just rotate through it. That difference matters, both for the students and for the patients they will one day serve.”

According to the release, this education unit will have nursing students remain at MercyOne for the majority of their clinical training, rather than rotating between different systems each semester. text:
Members of the Colorado House of Representatives work on the final day of the 2026 legislative session on May 13, 2026, at the Colorado Capitol in Denver. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)Colorado Democrats hope to flip four state House seats and one state Senate seat this fall to widen their majority power in the Legislature, the national party’s state legislative campaign committee announced this week.
Democrats currently hold a 43-22 majority in the House and 23-12 majority in the Senate. If the strategy announced Wednesday by the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee is successful, it would push Democrats into a supermajority in both chambers. That would make it possible for the caucuses to refer state constitutional amendments to the ballot and override vetoes from the governor with a party-line vote. A party attains a supermajority when it holds at least two-thirds of a chamber’s seats.

The DLCC is eyeing House Districts 16, 19, 50 and 51 and Senate District 30 to flip. It also wants to defend House Districts 25, represented by Evergreen Rep. Tammy Story; 43, represented by Highlands Ranch Rep. Bob Marshall; 46, represented by Pueblo Rep. Tisha Mauro; and 59, represented by Durango Rep. Katie Stewart.
It also wants to protect seats in Senate Districts 3, currently represented by Pueblo Sen. Nick Hinrichsen, who isn’t seeking reelection; 11, represented by Colorado Springs Sen. Tony Exum; 15, represented by Loveland Sen. Janice Marchman; and 27, represented by Centennial Sen. Tom Sullivan.
All of the districts the committee wants to flip and protect involved some of the closest races in the 2024 election. In the Colorado Springs-based House District 16, for example, Republican Rep. Rebecca Keltie defeated then-incumbent Steph Vigil by three votes. Vigil is running to regain that seat against Republican Jill Haffley.
There will be a rematch in House District 19 against Republican Rep. Dan Woog of Frederick, who defeated Jillaire McMillan by a little over 100 votes in 2024. In House District 50, Tommy Butler is running against Republican Rep. Ryan Gonzalez of Fort Lupton, who won the seat in 2024 by a little under 600 votes. Democrat Jacki Marsh is running against Republican Amy Parks in House District 51, a seat currently held by Loveland Rep. Ron Weinberg. Weinberg is not seeking reelection and won the seat in 2024 by about 5 percentage points.
‘Once-in-a-generation opportunity’
In the Senate, Democrats are hoping to flip District 30, currently represented by Republican Sen. John Carson of Highlands Ranch. Carson was appointed to the seat, and the last Republican to win the seat, Kevin Van Winkle in 2022, won with about 54% of the vote. Democrat Kevin Leung is facing Carson in the general election.
In a statement, DLCC President Heather Williams noted that since Democrats won control of the Colorado Senate in 2018, they have passed policies protecting abortion rights and expanding firearm restrictions. The last time the committee spent heavily in Colorado legislative elections was in 2022.
“We are prepared to capitalize on this once-in-a-generation opportunity to expand Democratic power across the map and get this group of strong candidates across the finish line in November,” she said.
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: VTDigger
title: The U.S. can’t ignore its own human rights law on Israel
description:
Federal law bars aid to human rights violators. The U.S. keeps arming Israel anyway.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  The U.S. can’t ignore its own human rights law on Israel.
text:
Dear Editor, 
Accountability is a foundational pillar of government that ensures political leaders are fulfilling their duties honorably and legally. As a 14-year-old student from Waterbury observing the world’s political actions today, what frightens me most is the federal government’s lack of accountability. This is especially highlighted in the conflicts in the Middle East. 
The Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, requires that any security assistance or arms provided by the United States to any country must advance internationally recognized human rights and avoid identification of the United States with any violations of those rights. The act prohibits assistance to any government that engages in a consistent pattern of human rights violations. 
The United States’ continued military and financial support of Israel despite actions in Gaza that the United Nations’ own commission of inquiry has concluded constitute genocide, and its military actions in Lebanon, suggests a violation of this policy. To uphold the ideals our country was founded on, we must hold the government to its own laws and policies. That is why Senate Resolution 797, introduced to the U.S. Senate by Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., is so important. This resolution requests a report on Israel’s human rights practices, and questions whether the United States should continue supporting it. 

READ MORE

Since this is a privileged resolution, Welch can force it to a floor vote, which he has not done yet. It is extremely important to me that my senator sees this resolution through, because the obscene acts being committed against innocent people of Gaza and Lebanon are unacceptable and should not be supported by the U.S. This is not just a morally driven opinion, but a fact that, under law, the United States cannot assist governments that continually commit human rights violations. 
From a young age, children have been given rules to follow and expected to abide by them. It is only right that the federal government is held to these same standards. 
Zoya BianchiWaterbury, Vt.

text:
UNC Chapel Hill. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NCNewsline) “Publish or perish” is a well-known saying among university professors, reflecting the pressure to have their research published to continue advancing in their field.
Academic programs face a similar mandate: Attract students or perish.
That was the case this week, when University of North Carolina Provost Magnus Egerstedt told the UNC-Chapel Hill Board of Trustees that four degree programs had been placed on pause.
Addressing the University Affairs committee Wednesday, Egerstedt said after reviewing UNC-Chapel Hill’s 275 degree programs, 28 stood out for low enrollment or low rates of degree completion.
Programs were judged in part by UNC system office thresholds for the number of degrees awarded over a five-year period. Programs were flagged if they experienced a 20% or greater decline. In the second phase of the review, the provost said broader quantitative metrics were used to assess the programs, including enrollment, admissions, student credit hours, and the time-to-completion of a degree.
A deeper dive into the 28 flagged programs identified programs that were sustainable based on their importance, programs with low enrollment where active restructuring was underway, programs where the drop in enrollment was temporary or the result of a data anomaly, and programs that should be paused and admissions halted.
Egerstedt said four graduate programs fell into the category of degrees “on pause” to allow time to substantially revamp or consolidate the degrees. In some cases, the programs may be formally discontinued once all enrolled students have completed.
Programs currently on pause include:

Digital Curation and Management in the School of Information and Library Science – According to a report, faculty voted to eliminate this program because of low enrollment, and will repackage it as a concentration for existing master’s degrees, rather than a free-standing degree. Two students involved will be allowed to complete their coursework as the program winds down.
Curriculum and Instruction in the School of Education – All doctoral students have finished this program, and zero students are enrolled for the coming year.
Environmental Sciences and Engineering in the Gillings School of Public Health – All students have completed classwork and no new students have enrolled. The school is rethinking this Master of Science in Public Health degree “given a larger context of engineering at UNC.”
Health Policy and Management in the Gillings School of Public Health – This Master of Science in public health has two students enrolled who will be able to complete their coursework. One student is expected to graduate in Dec. 2026, and the other is a dual MSPH/MBA candidate expected to graduate in May 2027. UNC is considering a pathway to allow undergraduate students to earn a Bachelor of Science in Public Health (BSPH) and a Master of Science in Public Health (MSPH).

Among the four graduate-level programs that could be discontinued, only four students are currently enrolled.
Egerstedt said he was surprised that the review only turned up four programs out of 275 at UNC-Chapel Hill that needed to be paused.
“We are actually in a rather unusual situation as a university. We’re growing our enrollment, which means there are more students on campus, which means a lot of our degrees are growing,” said Egerstedt. Other programs such as clinical specialties were intended to be small, explained the provost.
Trustee Marty Kotis said the academic program review did not go far enough and should have included the cost for degrees conferred.
“We’ve got to do a better job of considering the dollars involved,” Kotis told the committee.
At Thursday’s full Board of Trustees’ meeting, Kotis reiterated the need for UNC-Chapel Hill leadership to look at student outcomes to make sure that degrees offer “meaningful value.”
The academic review process is ongoing.
“I just want to make sure we’re doing everything we can to invest in the areas where it’s going to make the most difference in people’s lives,” said Kotis.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana Medicaid will cover GLP-1s for obesity
description: Hoosiers insured through Medicaid will soon gain access to GLP-1 medications for obesity. Gov. Mike Braun on Thursday directed the Indiana Family and Social Services Administration, which administers Medicaid benefits to 1.9 million Hoosiers, to participate in a federal initiative to cover GLP-1 medications for obesity. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid In[...]
text:
Gov. Mike Braun commits to join federal initiative to cover GLP-1 medications for obesity through Medicaid. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Hoosiers insured through Medicaid will soon gain access to GLP-1 medications for obesity.
Gov. Mike Braun on Thursday directed the Indiana Family and Social Services Administration, which administers Medicaid benefits to 1.9 million Hoosiers, to participate in a federal initiative to cover GLP-1 medications for obesity.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Innovation Center is working with drug makers like Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk to make GLP-1 medications more affordable — for state Medicaid programs and beneficiaries alike.
States that opt into the BALANCE model can access GLP-1 medications at a lower cost. Indiana Medicaid will pay $85.16 of the $245 monthly cost per person, thanks to contributions from the federal government and manufacturer discounts.
Manufacturers agreed to provide free lifestyle support as well.
“Indiana is proud to expand access to essential treatment for eligible Hoosiers,” Braun said in a news release Thursday. “This agreement reflects our commitment to Make Indiana Healthy Again by pursuing practical solutions that increase healthier lives.”
Exact details about eligibility criteria and timing are not yet available, as the agreement is still being finalized.
A news release from the governor’s office said access to obesity treatment could allow more Hoosiers to remain or return to the workforce and limit reliance on public assistance.
“Obesity is a serious, chronic disease, and addressing it can open the door to better health,” David A. Ricks, chair and chief executive officer of Eli Lilly, said in the release. “Here in Indiana, 71% of adults are living with obesity or overweight. This toll on our state’s health is also a toll on our economy, costing an estimated $10.7 billion a year, or nearly 2% of GDP.
“Indiana opting into the BALANCE model is a meaningful step forward,” he said, “and we’re grateful for the Governor’s leadership in making breakthrough medicines like Foundayo and Zepbound available to eligible Medicaid patients. We’re proud our home state is taking action to expand access to obesity treatment, so more Hoosiers can get the care they need.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Democratic senator asks TN governor for details about potential federal nuclear partnership
description: A Tennessee state senator is asking Gov. Bill Lee to disclose the location of any new nuclear energy and waste sites as part of a potential partnership with the federal government.  Sen. Heidi Campbell, a Nashville Democrat, sent a four-page letter to Lee Thursday asking for the disclosure and for the administration to let the […]
text:
Sen. Heidi Campbell, a Nashville Democrat, asked Gov. Bill Lee to provide more transparency about Tennessee's any potential future nuclear energy partnership. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A Tennessee state senator is asking Gov. Bill Lee to disclose the location of any new nuclear energy and waste sites as part of a potential partnership with the federal government. 
Sen. Heidi Campbell, a Nashville Democrat, sent a four-page letter to Lee Thursday asking for the disclosure and for the administration to let the General Assembly provide review and comment before any deal is made. 
The United States Department of Energy announced earlier this week that Tennessee was one of five states under consideration for partnership as part of the Trump administration’s attempt to boost nuclear energy production. 
The federally designated Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus would allow Tennessee to create an industrial-like zone near Oak Ridge that could support “the full nuclear fuel lifecycle, including fuel fabrication, enrichment, reprocessing used nuclear fuel, and disposition of waste.”
Campbell said that, aside from saying the campus would be centered around Oak Ridge, the Lee administration has kept most of the details quiet. 
“You simply can’t make our state a nuclear dumping ground without public awareness, input, and participation,” she said in the letter to Lee. 
Tennessee named finalist for federal partnership involving nuclear energy sites

 
Tennessee has long been at the forefront of nuclear energy because of Oak Ridge, which served as a federal research site for the initial production of the atomic bomb in World War 2. The Tennessee Valley Authority today operates two nuclear energy plants in the state. 
Gov. Bill Lee has been a strong advocate for revitalizing Tennessee’s nuclear energy, praising the federal Department of Energy’s choice of the state as a finalist.  He has also created a state investment fund that, as of 2025, was offering $70 million in incentives for companies in the nuclear energy industry.
Part of the reason for the lifecycle campus concept is that currently there is no approved place to store high levels of radioactive waste, which the Trump administration hopes to get around through the new program, according to a White House memo obtained by Politico.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi businesses have the power to slow the brain drain, new study shows
description: Chrishanna Wragg reads a story to toddlers at the 3 Steps Daycare, Thursday, April 23, 2026, in Kosciusko.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Mississippi could grow its population, strengthen its workforce and boost its economy if employers offered more family-forward policies – and doing so wouldn’t be that hard, researchers argue in a new report by the Mississippi Early Learning Alliance. 
Those policies include paid leave, childcare assistance, flexible scheduling and health-related benefits. Even modest changes could increase employee retention and productivity and put millions more dollars into the state’s economy, said researchers for the nonprofit group, which is dedicated to improving early learning and child development outcomes in the state. 
Biz Harris, who said she and her family were aided by paid family leave, reads to her son Elliott. Credit: Courtesy photo
“Too often, family-forward workplace policies are seen as nice-to-have benefits or feel-good ideas,” Biz Harris, executive director of the Mississippi Early Learning Alliance, told Mississippi Today. “But the reality is that they’re some of the most effective tools employers have to address the workforce challenges they’re already facing.” 
Mississippi has the nation’s second-lowest workforce participation rate, with nearly half of its adults unemployed. Childcare challenges cost the state an estimated $673 million a year, including $553 million in employer losses from absenteeism and employee turnover. More than half of Mississippi parents report missing work because of childcare access, and some leave their jobs altogether. 
And Mississippians are leaving more than just their jobs. The state’s population has declined or remained unchanged nearly every year since 2014, leading to what policy analysts have dubbed “the brain drain.” Jackson is one of the fastest-shrinking U.S. cities. Meanwhile, neighboring states such as Alabama and Arkansas are growing. 
The good news, according to the report, is that employers don’t have to look out of state for solutions. Several Mississippi companies are already implementing strategies that help attract and keep working parents. 
Mississippi Power, a utility company headquartered in Gulfport, offers up to 12 weeks of paid maternity leave, two weeks of paid parental leave and 12 weeks of paid adoption leave, according to the report. 
Toyota Mississippi, a manufacturing plant in Blue Springs, includes an on-site childcare center offering 24/7 services to align with employees’ shifts. 
Many family-forward policies don’t require significant financial investments, the report noted. Offering flexible workday start and end times costs employers nothing and can help employees navigate school or daycare drop-off and pick-up times. A private lactation space in an existing area of the workplace can improve employee satisfaction without requiring major structural shifts for an organization. 
The report also encouraged employers to invest in health benefits that are specifically geared toward supporting families, such as a low-deductible family insurance plan. 
Mississippi Early Learning Alliance helped develop a childcare tax credit for businesses that contribute to the cost of childcare for their employees. The group created an economic impact calculator to help businesses understand how much money they could save by investing in childcare. 
Family-forward policies can start small but have profound impact, Harris said. And not just for working parents, but for the next generation. 
Studies show that when working parents have access to robust paid leave and affordable, high-quality childcare, children bond better and benefit cognitively and emotionally. Those children grow up and become stronger contributors to the communities where they’re raised. 
“Supporting caregivers and parents during the earliest years of a child’s life isn’t separate from building a stronger economy,” Harris said. “It’s how we build one.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Democrats, confused by ethics rules, restricted interactions with federal candidates
description: TOPEKA — The Kansas Democratic Party stoked confusion and frustration by issuing restrictive guidelines to county party leaders about ethics rules surrounding candidates for federal office, saying county parties couldn’t include the candidates in events or printed materials. The guidance sent in early June was based on a misunderstanding between Democrats an[...]
text:
Jeanna Repass, chair of the Kansas Democratic Party, appears at an April 26, 2026, event at the Aztec Shawnee Theater. Repass said the party was trying to follow ethics rules when it restricted county parties from interacting with federal candidates. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The Kansas Democratic Party stoked confusion and frustration by issuing restrictive guidelines to county party leaders about ethics rules surrounding candidates for federal office, saying county parties couldn’t include the candidates in events or printed materials.
The guidance sent in early June was based on a misunderstanding between Democrats and the state agency that governs ethics violations, the Kansas Public Disclosure Commission, and stems from the Johnson County Democratic Party’s attempt to promote select candidates for U.S. Senate and disregard U.S. Rep. Sharice Davids’ primary challenger, Sarah Preu.
The disclosure commission informed Democrats that state law forbids them from spending money to promote “a single candidate” for federal office, but that it was OK to “provide information for all candidates in a race.” The Kansas Democratic Party then sent a statewide directive that said county parties weren’t allowed to hold forums for federal candidates, print materials that reference them, or spend money on anything that would aid them.
As a result, the party unnecessarily blocked candidates from participating in parades and other events that could have boosted their public awareness in the weeks ahead of the primary. The Johnson County Democratic Party deleted federal candidates from its website and reprinted its voter guide.
Democrats say they were just following the rules, based on correspondence with ethics regulators who approved their flawed guidance before it was sent.
Candice Wilson, general counsel for the disclosure commission, told Kansas Reflector the agency became a “sacrificial lamb” for those who were upset by the party’s misunderstanding of the rules.
“We are committed to being nonpartisan and fair, and any insinuation that we have put our thumb on the scale of any particular party or candidate is not true,” Wilson said. “We just want to engage in educational efforts with groups to ensure that everyone is obeying the law and that our elections are transparent and fair.”
Jeanna Repass, chair of the Kansas Democratic Party, said Johnson County Democrats made a mistake by trying to promote just five of the 11 Democrats running for U.S. Senate.
“There was a kerfuffle involving Johnson County, and it got what I would call very aggressively heated,” she said.
But, she added, “we have done nothing but try to broker this correctly.”
“So this idea that they were the sacrificial lamb is outrageous,” Repass aid. “I’ve been taking the bullet.”
 
Kansas Sen. Patrick Schmidt, D-Topeka, talks to reporters during a May 27, 2026, news conference at the Statehouse in Topeka, where he accused Adam Hamilton of mishandling a report of child sex abuse at a church camp in 2005. Schmidt and Hamilton are both seeking the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
The kerfuffle
Deann Mitchell, chair of Johnson County Democratic Party, said the county party’s 50-member board decided to promote select candidates based on fundraising, cooperation with the party and, in one case, a candidate’s conduct.
The party printed 70,000 voter guides and planned a candidate forum for the U.S. Senate race before the disclosure commission intervened. Mitchell said she had to claw back the voter guides, which were already in canvassers’ hands, and reprint them at a cost of $13,000. The party chose not to include federal races in the reprinted voter guide or on the website, and to cancel the forum.
Mitchell said the decision was based on Wilson telling her she wasn’t allowed to spend money on “a” federal candidate.
“So from that, I took it that we could not have ‘any’ federal candidates on our voter guide, website, anything,” Mitchell said.
The real constraint was that the county party’s board was unwilling to be all-inclusive with the candidates.
Wilson said the commission heard from “multiple federal candidates” who said they wanted to be included in the Johnson County voter guide.
“Instead,” she said, “the Johnson County Democratic Party had framed it to us that the candidates had asked not to be included. So we certainly know about candidates’ frustration.”
Mitchell disputed that assessment. She said one candidate, Michael Soetaert, asked the party not to promote him. She said another candidate, Damon Anderson, was nonresponsive. The board excluded Anne Parelkar, Jason Hart and Kevin Latz because of fundraising, she said.
The board also refused to support the candidacy of state Sen. Patrick Schmidt, a Topeka Democrat who had attacked the frontrunner in the race, Church of the Resurrection pastor Adam Hamilton, with accusations about how he handled a report of child sex abuse at a church camp two decades earlier.
Mitchell said the board’s decision was based on Schmidt’s “conduct,” which she explained as him recruiting candidates to run against incumbent legislators.
Schmidt said he encouraged one individual to run in Democratic Rep. Susan Ruiz’ district in Johnson County. But, he said, the decision to exclude him was really about protecting Hamilton.
“Whoever the deciders are within that organization were angry about trying to call attention to Adam Hamilton covering up sex abuse at his church,” Schmidt said, referencing an accusation that Hamilton denies.
 
U.S. Rep. Sharice Davids, D-Kansas, files for reelection on May 11, 2026, at the Kansas Secretary of State’s Office in Topeka. She faces a primary challenge from Sarah Preu. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)
How the law works
There is a two-part test under state law.
Is a county party spending money, and does it benefit a particular candidate?
If the answer to both parts is “yes,” the party is violating the law and could be subject to fines from the disclosure commission.
Wilson provided Kansas Reflector with written memos issued by the commission dating to 1998 to show the law has been interpreted consistently for decades.
Democrats, who have seldom had contested primaries for federal races in recent years, believed the law was being applied differently this year. That’s because there was confusion over the second part of the two-part test.
Alex Fall, political director for the Kansas Democratic Party, provided Kansas Reflector with emails he exchanged with Wilson in early June. He asked Wilson to review a draft of the guidance the party planned to send to county chairs.
“This guidance looks good,” Wilson replied on June 9.
It wasn’t.
Wilson provided Kansas Reflector with a clarification memo she sent to the party the next day. The memo outlines the two-part test and says it is OK to invite “all federal candidates for a particular election to attend/speak at an event.”
The memo is consistent with guidance Wilson provided to Mitchell on June 8 in a back-and-forth exchange, which Mitchell provided to Kansas Reflector.
“If you wish to provide information for federal candidates, you may do so only so long as you do not expressly support a single candidate and instead, provide information for all candidates in the race,” Wilson wrote.
Mitchell asked as a “point of clarity” whether the party “CAN promote the federal candidacy if we list ALL candidates.”
Wilson responded: “You cannot spend money to promote a federal candidate, even if you list all the candidates.”
The distinction — the word “promote” — was lost on Mitchell.
Later, as confusion and frustration escalated, Wilson provided further clarity. She said in a June 24 email that her previous communication meant  “you may not circumvent the law to support/favor a federal candidate by listing all candidates.”
For example, Wilson wrote, the party can’t promote Davids just because it lists Preu as a candidate.
“I just want to reiterate that in no way is our agency prohibiting you from including federal candidates on voter guides or at events,” Wilson wrote.
That was more than a month ago. The Johnson County Democratic Party still doesn’t list federal candidates on its website. Instead, it provides a note saying the disclosure commission prevents them from listing federal candidates, which isn’t true. The county party could list all of the candidates if it wanted to.
Ironically, the Johnson County Republican Party briefly listed Schmidt, the Topeka Democrat, as a candidate alongside Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall and his primary challenger, Arch “Pond” Naramore.
Mitchell said the experience has been “a growing pain” for a county party that has expanded over the past eight years.
“I am attempting to follow the rules,” she said. “I reprinted 70,000 pieces of lit. Had my website scrubbed. Our office was scrubbed. We have done everything that we thought we were required to do, and then we get told, ‘Well, you’re being mean,’ or whatever, because we’re trying to follow the rules that we were given directly from Candice.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Petitions for Arkansas direct democracy proposal fall short, secretary of state says
description: All signatures submitted in favor of putting on the November ballot a proposal to strengthen Arkansas’ initiative and referendum process were tossed because none of them were countable under state law, the secretary of state’s office announced Thursday. Secretary of State Cole Jester wrote in a letter to the proposed constitutional amendment’s sponsors that[...]
text:
A supporter of the Arkansas Abortion Amendment holds up a sign in an Arkansas Capitol hallway where petitions to put the amendment on the November ballot were delivered Friday, July 5, 2024. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)All signatures submitted in favor of putting on the November ballot a proposal to strengthen Arkansas’ initiative and referendum process were tossed because none of them were countable under state law, the secretary of state’s office announced Thursday.
Secretary of State Cole Jester wrote in a letter to the proposed constitutional amendment’s sponsors that 19,924 petition pages submitted to his office had an incorrect ballot name on them. The popular name approved by the Arkansas Attorney General’s Office was “The Arkansas Ballot Measure Rights Amendment.” Jester said the name attached to the signature pages was “The Ballot Rights Amendment of 2026.”
“No petition part had attached or on its face the ballot title approved by the Attorney General,” Jester wrote. “Therefore you have submitted zero countable signatures” under state law. 
At least 90,704 valid signatures from registered voters must be submitted for a proposed constitutional amendment to qualify for the ballot.
Even if the correct name had been attached and submitted properly, Jester said Protect AR Rights, the group behind the measure, would have only had 83,211 signatures, falling short by 7,493 the number required for his office to begin checking whether they were valid. 
But that figure doesn’t include signatures on 2,453 pages that he said could not be counted due to “notary and canvasser defects.” An additional 87 pages submitted to his office also did not count because they were attached to an unrelated proposed ballot measure on education.
Gennie Diaz, the spokesperson for Protect AR Rights, said the group was meeting with its legal team today to determine next steps and declined to comment further. 
Jester, a Republican, added that even if those reasons did not disqualify the proposal, state law prohibited him from counting signatures from canvassers who have violated state laws regarding petition signatures. Arkansas law says that the secretary of state cannot count the signatures if it determines those laws were broken by a “preponderance of the evidence.”
“The petition submitted to my office contains evidence of such laws being violated,” he wrote, pointing to several examples he provided of canvassers printing their name but not signing it on petitions, among other issues his office said were present.
Jester said in a statement his office has “a legal obligation” to apply state law equally to proposed changes to the state constitution.
“Our responsibility is not to determine the merits of the proposal, but to ensure the constitutional and statutory requirements established by the people and the General Assembly have been satisfied before a measure is certified,” Jester said.
Protect AR Rights was one of three groups collecting signatures this spring for their proposed constitutional amendments. Protect AR Rights was the only group to submit signatures to the secretary of state’s office by the July 3 deadline. 
All three groups are involved in a lawsuit against the secretary of state that’s challenging a number of state laws restricting the state’s initiative and referendum process. 
Opponents of the laws have said they make it nearly impossible for Arkansans to propose their own laws or constitutional amendments and place them to a statewide vote. Supporters of the laws argue they protect the integrity of the process. 
U.S. District Judge Timothy Brooks issued a preliminary injunction in November that temporarily blocked the state from enforcing some of the laws against parties involved in the suit, including two that require canvassers to request a photo ID from potential signers and inform them that petition fraud is a criminal offense.
Earlier this month, Brooks deemed some of the challenged laws unconstitutional, but took no additional action. He held a two-day bench trial in the case in Fayetteville this week.
Aug. 2 was the deadline for the secretary of state’s office to review the signatures. Aug. 20 is the deadline for the secretary to certify ballot measures to the counties for inclusion on the ballot for the General Election on Nov. 3. 
Election officials in 2024 rejected signatures submitted in favor of an abortion rights amendment, saying the group behind it did not comply with state law regarding documentation of paid signature gatherers. The state Supreme Court upheld that rejection.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri governor fills long-vacant teacher seat on state education board
description: Gov. Mike Kehoe appointed a former mayor of St. Louis and a Kansas City math teacher to the State Board of Education Thursday, filling a voting seat representing the 1st Congressional District and an advisory position reserved for a classroom teacher that has been vacant since lawmakers created it eight years ago. Vince Schoemehl, who […]
text:
Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe announced two appointments to the State Board of Education Thursday, saying his office supports "efforts to modernize and improve Missouri's public schools" in a news release (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Gov. Mike Kehoe appointed a former mayor of St. Louis and a Kansas City math teacher to the State Board of Education Thursday, filling a voting seat representing the 1st Congressional District and an advisory position reserved for a classroom teacher that has been vacant since lawmakers created it eight years ago.
Vince Schoemehl, who served three terms as mayor from 1981 to 1993, will succeed Pamela Westbrooks-Hodge until the expiration of her term in July.
Schoemehl’s career is marked by public service and charitable work, leading a nonprofit called Grand Center Inc. which worked on revitalization of a St. Louis arts district for 14 years.
His experience in education began in 2003, when he joined the St. Louis Public Schools board before resigning in 2005. His time on the board was divisive, with Schoemehl among four members who pushed to consolidate district schools and hire a private management team.
After leaving the school board, Schoemehl helped launch the St. Louis Language Immersion School, a public charter school sponsored by his alma mater, the University of Missouri-St. Louis. He currently serves as treasurer of the school’s board of directors. It is unclear whether he plans to step down before joining the State Board of Education.
Current state board member Kerry Casey, who is from Chesterfield, was influential in the development of KIPP charter schools in St. Louis and served on KIPP’s board until her appointment to the state board.
The State Board of Education, which oversees the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education, has governor-appointed members from each of the state’s eight congressional districts. State law says members may not be “connected, either as an official or as an employee, with any public, private, or denominational school, college or university.”
The Independent asked Kehoe’s office whether Schoemehl plans to continue his role on the charter school’s board but has not received a response. Schoemehl did not return a request for an interview.
State law makes an exception for an advisory position lawmakers created in 2018 for “an active classroom teacher.” The role does not have voting authority. 
But the position has remained vacant since it was created. The issue came before the state board last year during its annual retreat.
Westbrooks-Hodge said at the time that it was strange to have the seat vacant for so long.
“I would hope there’s a sense of urgency,” she said to the education department’s then-chief legal counsel.
Educators have volunteered for the role over the years, and teacher advocacy groups have supported filling it.
On Thursday, Kehoe appointed Michael McDonald, a math teacher at Park Hill High School in the Kansas City area, to the position.
“We are proud today to appoint two new members to the State Board of Education, including an active classroom teacher,” Kehoe said in a press release. “Our administration will continue to support and work with the board on efforts to modernize and improve Missouri’s public schools for the benefit of families and communities across our state.”
Since his election in 2024, Kehoe has appointed members to seven of the eight voting member spots on the board. His appointees have moved quickly to consider changes to Missouri’s education policies. 
Schoemehl and McDonald join the board at a critical time. Following the retirement of former Education Commissioner Karla Eslinger in May, the board has begun a nationwide search for the department’s next leader.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Democrats are destroying New England’s local governance tradition
description:
Regional planning commissions now hold sweeping authority over local land-use decisions that used to belong to town voters.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Democrats are destroying New England’s local governance tradition.
text:
This commentary is by Todd Heyman, a co-owner of Fat Sheep Farm & Cabins, who lives in Hartland.
The Vermont Democratic Party is off course. In the shadows of highly technocratic laws, New England’s cherished wisdom tradition of direct democratic rule is being destroyed, even though Vermont remains a predominantly rural state with no signs that it has outgrown its chosen form of local government. 
Under Act 181, the Democratic leadership dramatically increased the power of regional planning commissions to control decisions about local communities that have always been decided by our town governance structure. Under Vermont law, land-use rules, whether zoning bylaws or town ordinances, passed by selectboards have always been subject to a direct democratic vote of all citizens, if enough citizens petition to take action. No longer.
Regional planning commission staff who are neither elected nor subject to any ethical enforcement regime are now passing rules with the force of law that will trump a wide array of local decisions. Act 181 has also delegated to RPCs the power to draft what amount to statewide zoning maps subject only to state bureaucratic approval. RPCs not only get to make the rules for certain projects now, but they have been allowed to define the scope of their own jurisdictional limits. Yes, Act 181 tells the courts that they must defer to the RPCs — which write the very definitions that decide when their plan overrides a town’s. Talk about the fox guarding the henhouse.
It would be difficult to design a governmental unit with less accountability. This power shift away from trusted local officials and Australian ballot town voting is heretical to New England, and exactly the type of addiction to unnecessary and so-called expert regulation that has created the blue states’ affordability crisis.
As New York Times columnist and liberal Democrat Ezra Klein has bluntly explained, “You cannot be the party of working families when the places you govern are places working families cannot afford to live.” In his book “Abundance,” co-authored with Derek Thompson, Klein writes that the affordability crisis is largely due to Democrats’ misplaced trust in complex regulatory processes over elected politicians. He urges the party to confront its regulatory addiction to stop stifling the building of things we need, like housing.
Just like previous well-intentioned environmental measures Klein discusses, Vermont passed Act 181 to address concerns with forest fragmentation and wildlife habitats. Its proposed solution was to impose the existing Act 250 commercial permitting regime on rural residents seeking to build a single house if their property was designated as Tier 3 land. This would have been a minor inconvenience for the rich but a deal-breaker for anyone else, exacerbating the housing and affordability crisis in a single stroke.
It was also an intellectually lazy move. The Legislature tried to slap a commercial regulatory regime on residential Vermonters to achieve something that regime was never designed to do. And if the Legislature lacked the imagination to come up with a custom-designed solution, it could have chosen a better existing state law to address the issue. Rewarding landowners with lower property taxes for voluntarily not developing these lands through the current use program, for example, would have made these lands more affordable, not less.

READ MORE

The lesser-known and understood provisions of Act 181 that survived are being implemented right now, and very few Vermonters know anything about it. New rules are being drafted by unelected RPC staff, subject only to a supervisory network of unelected board members and state bureaucrats. If you happen to be paying attention and wanted to have input on these rules in, for example, the Two Rivers-Ottauquechee region, where I live, you would have to work across more than a dozen different communities to persuade enough appointed board members to take action to veto the decisions of RPC staff. Good luck.
If you have watched these public meetings online, you would see a member of the Two Rivers-Ottauquechee staff deny public involvement in violation of both Act 181 and Vermont’s Open Meeting Law, and then publicly disparage and make false statements about the person whom they unlawfully refused to allow to speak. 
And these new rules are entirely unnecessary and overbroad. They are written for large commercial chains, not the family-scale businesses that seek to operate in our sparsely populated rural areas. In the Two Rivers-Ottauquechee region, any commercial project that triggers Act 250 review — no matter how small — must install electric car chargers. If the business is deemed to have “substantial regional impact,” such as serving two towns near a town boundary, it must provide transportation impact studies for each phase of development to get its Act 250 permit. If it is a rural business engaged in principal retail, it must also conduct transportation impact studies.
In the aggregate, all these new regulations will drive up the costs of desperately needed housing and other new economic activity in rural communities, if not deter them altogether. While not every RPC has seized these powers as aggressively, there is no real obstacle to their doing so.
The next legislative session must revoke the doctrine of regional and state supremacy over local land-use decisions. Regional plan rules should require municipal approval by means of warned votes in every affected community. RPCs should require municipal approval to participate in Act 250 appeals, which can hold up projects for years. And the law granting them the power to assume jurisdiction over virtually any project they choose, and implement rules that trump municipal ones, must be repealed. 
If you are a Democrat voting in the primaries, make sure your chosen candidates understand that our democratic tradition is at stake.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Democrats are destroying New England’s local governance tradition.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota mammoth dig unearths ‘rare’ array of bones from beneath garage
description: A mammoth excavation under a northwest North Dakota garage is unearthing a more complete prehistoric beast than paleontologists had hoped for when the discovery was made in the 1980s. The excavation in Burke County is being spearheaded by the North Dakota Geological Survey, which has used its team, summer interns and some geology students from […]
text:
Team members excavate mammoth bones under the supervision of the North Dakota Geological Survey beneath a garage in Burke County in June 2026. (Photo courtesy of North Dakota Geological Survey)A mammoth excavation under a northwest North Dakota garage is unearthing a more complete prehistoric beast than paleontologists had hoped for when the discovery was made in the 1980s.
The excavation in Burke County is being spearheaded by the North Dakota Geological Survey, which has used its team, summer interns and some geology students from the University of North Dakota since June to carefully dig out the iconic animal.
“When you dig something up, you never know if it’s going to be one bone and the whole thing is going to be over,” North Dakota State Geologist Clint Boyd said. “Very quickly it became clear, no, there is a reason we are digging here.”  
Boyd said this mammoth skeleton is a rare find and the most complete mammoth from North Dakota, though not as encompassing as the mammoth site in Hot Springs, South Dakota.
He said the team is still working to determine the type of mammoth, either woolly or Columbian. The team is also trying to determine the sex of the mammoth. 
Boyd said the excavation underneath the garage could wrap up in September so the garage can be reconstructed for the home owner this fall. He added the excavation team plans to return in spring 2027 to excavate areas outside of the garage.
So far, he said the team has recovered bits of the skull, lower jaw and some ribs. They are beginning to find the limbs of the animal and are hopeful to find the mammoth’s tusks waiting to be uncovered outside of the garage. The timeline to complete the mammoth excavation remains fluid.
A mammoth may be hiding below a North Dakota garage

The bones were discovered on a northwestern North Dakota property in 1988 while the owner was digging a foundation for a garage. The family sent a couple of teeth to North Dakota State University, which verified that the teeth had come from a mammoth that lived during the Pleistocene Epoch, commonly called the Ice Age. 
However, by the time the North Dakota Geological Survey was notified of the verified discovery, the garage foundation had already been poured, and the garage, attached to the home, had been constructed. The Geological Survey was not able to fund the demolition of the garage, excavation and construction of a new garage in an agreed timeline with the owner.
For about 35 years, the mammoth stayed under that garage until former North Dakota State Geologist Ed Murphy reexamined his old notes from the 1988 discovery and learned the property had changed hands over the years. He reached out, spoke to the new owner and agreed to conduct site testing around the garage.
“They’ve been wonderful to work with,” Boyd said.
In 2025, state lawmakers allocated $150,000 for the excavation as part of Senate Bill 2014.
Andrew Clark, deputy state historic preservation officer, told members of the State Historical Society Board at their July meeting that a team from the Historical Society convinced the landowner to rip up the garage floor and used ground penetrating radar to evaluate the mammoth site.
Team members excavate mammoth bones under the supervision of the North Dakota Geological Survey beneath a garage in Burke County in June 2026. (Photo courtesy of North Dakota Geological Survey)The North Dakota Geological Survey works to excavate mammoth bones in Burke County in June 2026. (Photo courtesy of North Dakota Geological Survey)A mammoth hyoid bone is uncovered during an excavation in Burke County under the supervision of the North Dakota Geological Survey in June 2026. (Photo courtesy of North Dakota Geological Survey)A mammoth spinal vertebra is uncovered during an excavation in Burke County under the supervision of the North Dakota Geological Survey in June 2026. (Photo courtesy of North Dakota Geological Survey)A team member excavates mammoth bones under the supervision of the North Dakota Geological Survey beneath a garage in Burke County in June 2026. (Photo courtesy of North Dakota Geological Survey)Team members excavate mammoth bones under the supervision of the North Dakota Geological Survey beneath a garage in Burke County in June 2026. (Photo courtesy of North Dakota Geological Survey)A mammoth tooth plate is uncovered during an excavation in Burke County under the supervision of the North Dakota Geological Survey in June 2026. (Photo courtesy of North Dakota Geological Survey)Team members excavate mammoth bones under the supervision of the North Dakota Geological Survey beneath a garage in Burke County in June 2026. (Photo courtesy of North Dakota Geological Survey)A team member excavates mammoth bones under the supervision of the North Dakota Geological Survey beneath a garage in Burke County in June 2026. (Photo courtesy of North Dakota Geological Survey)
Clark said radar results showed the mammoth skeleton may have been damaged by the construction of the garage due to some “pushing around” of the bones. 
The excavation team discovered when the property’s former owner dug the 3-foot foundational footings for the garage, some of the bones were severed, removed as part of the construction process and then returned to the site as part of soil backfill, Boyd said.
He added the situation is unique because if the construction crew hadn’t struck the bones, they would have never known they were there.
“But, you’d prefer less of it had gotten hit than actually did,” Boyd said
The skeleton may be at the Burke County property because water carried it from the location it died, he said. Though Boyd said they don’t think the water carried the mammoth far, most likely yards instead of miles.
The property owner has indicated the mammoth will become part of the North Dakota state fossil collection though a formal agreement has not yet been finalized, he said.
“Ideally, it will eventually go on display upstairs in the Heritage Center,” Boyd said.
If a display at the museum is not possible, he said they would look to display the mammoth near the place it was discovered. Any display is still years away.
Boyd said the excavation should not need any additional state funding until they are ready to prepare an exhibit, which might not be until the 2029-31 biennium.
He said his team’s first mammoth excavation was in the Freedom Mine near Beulah in 2023, which yielded a large tusk, part of a hip and some ribs from what was likely a Columbian mammoth. 
If a fossil discovery is made on private land, there are no mandatory reporting requirements in the state for encountering fossils. Residents will not lose their rights to fossil finds on private land if they alert the Geological Survey, Boyd said.
“We’re mostly coming there to give the landowner information, and if they decide that they want to keep it, that’s their right,” Boyd said. “But, if we get to see it, where it was found, that adds to our information about the state.”
Rare T. rex find in North Dakota, mammoth fossil digs ‘significant’ for research

The team is working with the property owner to finalize a name for the skeleton.
Meanwhile, about 160 people have participated in public fossil digs this year supervised by the Geological Survey. The digs this year are being held in the Pembina Gorge, Dickinson and Bismarck areas. 
In July, one dig participant found a 3.5-inch T. rex tooth.
The 2026 events are sold out, but a wait list is available through the department’s website. Fossil events in 2027 are expected to be posted this fall with sign-ups occurring in January or February.
