name: Maine Morning Star
title: Scarborough calls on Congress to investigate activities at local ICE facility
description: Members of the Scarborough Town Council voted Wednesday to pass a proclamation calling on Maine’s congressional delegation to look into the operations of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement processing facility in the town after a federal agent shot and killed a man in Biddeford earlier this month.  But residents who spoke at the town […]
text:
A Scarborough resident addresses the town council before they voted unanimously on a proclamation calling on Congress to investigate ICE activities in the town. (Photo by Lauren McCauley/ Maine Morning Star)Members of the Scarborough Town Council voted Wednesday to pass a proclamation calling on Maine’s congressional delegation to look into the operations of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement processing facility in the town after a federal agent shot and killed a man in Biddeford earlier this month. 
But residents who spoke at the town council meeting said the proclamation doesn’t go far enough.
“We’re not in charge of federal immigration policy, but all eyes in Maine are on us as the only town that hosts a facility,” said Mary Ellen Galante, a Scarborough resident and retired nurse midwife, who objected to the proclamation because it “places all of the responsibility for action on our federal delegation and not on our town.” 
Galante was among the roughly 70 people who attended the packed meeting, while more than 50 others braved the rain outside holding signs calling to get ICE out of Maine.
New restrictions on state involvement in immigration enforcement take effect Wednesday

The killing of 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero on July 13 has renewed scrutiny of federal immigration enforcement in Maine and many residents have called for local and state leaders to do more to protect communities in the state. 
The question of how much power a community has to challenge federal activities within its jurisdiction is one that has wracked the state since President Donald Trump’s administration launched its enhanced enforcement operation in January. Several new laws took effect Wednesday that limit local cooperation with federal immigration agencies.
ICE in Maine
Unlike many other states, Maine does not have a standalone ICE detention center. The Scarborough processing facility is an administrative building for routine check-ins with three small, short-term holding cells. Detainees have historically been held in local jails or transferred to detention centers in Massachusetts or New Hampshire, or as far as Texas.
But during the meeting, several speakers raised concerns that ICE was misrepresenting what was occurring at that location.
“I think there are legitimate questions about whether the ordinances and the plans that have been put into place are consistent with what is happening in practice there,” Maine Rep. Sophie Warren, a Democrat who represents Scarborough, told Maine Morning Star. Warren presented a petition signed by more than 370 Mainers, 175 of which are Scarborough residents, calling on the council to take specific actions, including formally investigating the operations at the ICE facility and enforcing local laws and other municipal tools to rein in unlawful activities, which she said has precedence in Oregon.  
The U.S. General Services Administration, which manages federal real estate, leased the facility from owner AEY, LLC. According to the agency’s lease inventory, the current 15-year lease began in 2021. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Since ICE arrived at the site, local community members have regularly demonstrated outside the facility, and hundreds demonstrated in Scarborough the day after Guerrero was killed.
U.S. Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts made an unannounced visit to the Scarborough facility on July 17, during which he confirmed that is where the officer who shot Guerrero works.
In December, U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree also visited the Scarborough facility after concerns were raised about attorneys not being permitted to accompany their clients to routine check-ins. 
Josh Soley, the leasing and property manager for the building, said the GSA has the authority to sublease the facility to whichever agency they choose and that neither the state nor landlord has a say in who occupies the building.
Soley said he’s in support of the protests but believes the facility has nothing to do with what happened in Biddeford. He said people are “trying to find a place to put their voice, but I think it needs to be better targeted.” 
But Scarborough councilmember Jon Anderson said that he believes Soley “must be part of this conversation.” Anderson said residents should know whether the company intends to extend the lease when it expires, and said Soley should also explore whether there’s a “mutually agreeable path” to end the lease arrangement with GSA early, “given the tragedy that occurred from the ICE agent employed at that facility.”
GSA declined to comment on the proclamation or the terms of the current lease agreement. 
“I have a 20-page lease that I need to re-sign every single year and it asks me not to do unlawful activity,” Scarborough resident Sarah Lunt told the council. She added, “I would assume that that includes murdering someone in cold blood.” 
Dozens of people braved the rain outside the July 29 Scarborough town council meeting to protest the ICE facility in the town. (Photo by Lauren McCauley/ Maine Morning Star)
Proclamation details
The proclamation asks Maine’s congressional delegation to engage with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and other agencies to review the facility and evaluate alternatives, “including the relocation or discontinuation of such operations at that location.” 
It further asks for transparency and community engagement regarding federal immigration enforcement activities and for the delegation to “ensure that federal actions conducted within Maine respect human dignity, civil rights, public trust, due process, and community safety and commit to raising concerns with federal officials should evidence emerge that these standards are not being upheld.”
The town notes that proclamation should not be interpreted as opposition to lawful immigration enforcement but rather, the “expectation that such enforcement be conducted in a manner consistent with the values of safety, transparency, accountability, and respect for all people.”
While a handful of residents expressed concern that the resolution was beyond the purview of the council and would open the town to lawsuits from the federal government, the vast majority who spoke said they supported the proclamation as a first step for the town to take.
Congressional support
Ahead of the meeting, Pingree, who represents the southern Maine district that includes Biddeford and Scarborough, told the Scarborough council that the town “has every right to ask whether continuing to host this facility serves the interests of the community.”
“In my view, that question deserves serious consideration from the Department of Homeland Security,” Pingree wrote in a letter. “When a federal facility reaches the point where its very presence undermines the public confidence and leaves residents feeling less safe, the federal government has a responsibility to reconsider if that facility belongs there at all.”
Pingree added that she’s “exploring every available avenue to address enforcement operations and the continued presence of ICE in Scarborough.”
Sens. Angus King and Susan Collins, and Rep. Jared Golden did not comment on the proclamation. They previously sent a joint letter to the DHS Inspector General calling for a full, transparent investigation into the shooting and King has called for a review of ICE protocol.
Emma Davis contributed reporting to this story.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Judicial selection amendment could ravage rural Kansas communities. School funding is at stake.
description: As former elected officials with 16 years of experience in the Kansas Legislature and more than 50 years working with parents and children in our public schools — from Belle Plaine to Stafford and from Haviland to Garden City — we want to highlight how Kansas school children and rural communities could be affected by […]
text:
The Kansas Supreme Court is the last bulwark defending our state's constitutional requirement that all kids receive an adequate and equitable education, write our columnists. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)



As former elected officials with 16 years of experience in the Kansas Legislature and more than 50 years working with parents and children in our public schools — from Belle Plaine to Stafford and from Haviland to Garden City — we want to highlight how Kansas school children and rural communities could be affected by the constitutional amendment on the ballot Aug. 4.

This amendment would establish direct elections of Kansas Supreme Court justices, without any limits on campaign funding, conflicts of interest, or political activity by the justices.
Discussions about changing judicial selection in Kansas started about 15 to 20 years ago because of court decisions requiring the Legislature to adopt constitutional funding for schools. The debate heated up again recently because the current school finance formula is set to expire next year.
Debate about the court’s makeup did not begin due to some lofty goal of promoting democracy, but because the Kansas Supreme Court is the last bulwark defending our state’s constitutional requirement that all Kansas kids receive an adequate and equitable education, regardless of where they grow up.
Over the years, legislators from both parties resisted overthrowing the state Supreme Court. Last year, legislative leaders twisted enough arms to put an amendment on the ballot. Instead of providing voters with a compromise such as adding more members to the vetting panel or Senate confirmation, Legislative leaders took the most extreme path — direct judicial elections with no limits other than what will be “provided by law” in the future, when the public no longer has a say.
The amendment explainer doesn’t mention it, but if you look closely, near the end of the struck-out language, the proposed amendment specifically removes prohibitions that prevented judges from wielding their position and influence to engage in political campaigns and partisan activities.
Kansas public school children could suffer if the next time a school finance case is decided, justices are more concerned about soliciting $1 million campaign checks from out-of-state special interests than protecting every kid’s right to an education.
When both of us were in the Legislature, the Supreme Court forced legislators from across the state and political spectrum to work together to achieve a school funding formula that provided every student a suitably funded education regardless of their ZIP code.
This was not an easy task. Legislators first had to fix our state’s budget after the disastrous tax experiment, which left schools reeling and considering major reductions in services. That could have meant cuts to school transportation funding and cuts to schools with lower enrollment, both of which would have devastated rural communities.
The current, merit-based selection method preserves the fairly good chance that lawyers who grow up and have experience working in rural communities are selected for Supreme Court seats. Right now, the primary qualifications for Supreme Court justices are lawyers’ reputation, their legal career and their judicial service record. Under these conditions, a lawyer with a rural Kansas background can compete with anybody.
And they have.
Since Kansas adopted merit-based selection in 1958, more than 30% of justices appointed under this system have had roots in Kansas towns with a population of less than 10,000 people, and more than 60% of justices have had roots in communities with a population of fewer than 50,000 people.
A recent opinion piece by a law professor criticized a decision the Kansas Supreme Court made in 2013, saying the court was “urban-dominated.” For most of the court’s history during the school finance cases — and for the past 20 years — the court has actually been “rural-dominated.” In 2013, the hometowns of five of the seven justices were Caldwell, Tipton, Goodland, El Dorado and Salina.
Salina and El Dorado may be getting pretty cosmopolitan, but the law professor may want to get out a little more before claiming Goodland, Tipton, or Caldwell are “urban-dominated.”
If the amendment becomes law, the No. 1 qualification for any candidate will not be their legal career or service, but rather how many “friends” can write $1 million checks for a statewide campaign. That will include a few big donors in Wichita and Kansas City, but mostly, that type of donor lives in New York City, California and wherever Elon Musk or George Soros call home for tax purposes.
In addition to rural justices’ service record, geographic representation is built into the current system. Every congressional district in the state is guaranteed two out of the nine seats on the vetting panel — one lawyer and one non-lawyer.
Regardless of the selection panel’s membership, Kansas governors have always made the ultimate selection under the current system, and governors of both parties have routinely spread out their appointments geographically because they know this will widen their appeal to voters.
The state lost two rural justices over the past 18 months due to unexpected health issues (Chief Justice Marla Luckert from Goodland and Justice Evelyn Wilson from Smith Center), but we retain K.J. Wall from Scott County, and the next governor will immediately have the opportunity to select two new justices because of the current system’s mandatory retirement provision.
The Legislature is going to be renegotiating our school finance formula next year. Over time, the current system has ensured we have rural Kansas voices on the court, and it has protected rural Kansas kids from severe funding cuts that would forever harm our rural communities.

John Doll served in the Kansas Senate from 2017 to 2025 and the Kansas House from 2013 to 2017. Before that, he taught government for 20 years at Garden City public schools. Mary Jo Taylor served in the Kansas Legislature from 2017 to 2021 and served as a teacher, principal and superintendent in Kansas public schools for 34 years. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Trump admin’s endangered species rule change could leave Georgia’s wild places unprotected
description: A federal rule change set to go into effect this fall could cause big changes to Georgia’s landscape, and environmental groups are sounding the alarm. “It’s probably the worst action that’s ever been taken in the history of the Endangered Species Act,” said Will Harlan, southeast director of the Center for Biological Diversity in Asheville, […]
text:
Female red-cockaded woodpecker at a nest cavity at Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge, Saturday, June 1, 2024. Experts worry a new rule change could put species like the red-cockaded woodpecker at risk of habitat loss. Larry Woodward/U.S. Fish and Wildlife ServiceA federal rule change set to go into effect this fall could cause big changes to Georgia’s landscape, and environmental groups are sounding the alarm.
“It’s probably the worst action that’s ever been taken in the history of the Endangered Species Act,” said Will Harlan, southeast director of the Center for Biological Diversity in Asheville, North Carolina. “It is absolutely devastating for not just listed species, but all wildlife. It will wreak havoc upon the ecosystems that both wildlife and humans depend upon.”
The change rescinds the definition of “harm” in the Endangered Species Act. Under the new rule, intentionally killing a protected species remains forbidden, but indirectly killing a species by altering or destroying its habitat is not.
The federal government describes the rule change, which is set to take effect Sept. 14, as aligning enforcement with the original intent of the 1973 Endangered Species Act.
But Georgia Wildlife Federation President Mike Worley said protecting species from only direct killing misses the point.
“The hazards to animals aren’t just the direct killing,” he said. “The hazard to a lot of our species today are indeed the habitat conversions, habitat destruction. We are at a place where roughly 80 to 90% of species that are on our endangered list aren’t there because people are shooting them or killing them intentionally.”
A unique woodpecker
Red-cockaded woodpecker. Chuck Hess/U.S. Forest Service
Worley said the red-cockaded woodpecker, a feathery critter who once was common throughout the southeast, could be emblematic of species under threat by the new rule.
“Nobody shoots a red-cockaded woodpecker – I doubt they’re very good table fare,” he said. “Nobody hunts them. Nobody does a direct take of them.”
But in the last century, their numbers dwindled as the longleaf pine forests they once thrived in were reduced to about 3% of their former area due to logging and development.
“That’s why the red-cockaded woodpecker was on the endangered species list, because we had done away with their habitat, not because we had killed too many of the individuals with a gun,” Worley said.
The longleaf pines of the Jones Center at Ichauway, a 29,000-acre research and conservation institute near the southwestern corner of the state, are home to about 200 red-cockaded woodpeckers, up from just one in 1999, thanks to relocation efforts from around the southeast and careful management.
The red-cockaded woodpecker was one of the first species to receive protection under the Endangered Species Act in 1973, and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service changed its status from endangered to threatened in 2024 after conservation efforts led to its numbers starting to bounce back.
A North Atlantic right whale with propeller scars. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
Jones Center outreach and education coordinator Rachel McGuire said the birds are the only woodpeckers in North America that make their homes in living trees rather than dead ones.
One advantage of that is it allows them to bore holes around the tree, causing sticky resin to leak out and gum up the plans of snakes that climb up trees to eat woodpeckers. They also have a symbiotic relationship with a type of fungus that makes the core of the tree soft and easier to excavate.
Still, even in ideal circumstances, with help from other woodpeckers, it can take at least a year to build a nest, so the loss of an excavated tree can be devastating.
McGuire said highly adapted species like the red-cockaded woodpecker could be among the most vulnerable to the type of habitat loss conservationists worry the rule change will cause.
“The species that stand probably the most to lose are going to be those that need more specialized habitat, species that utilize larger home ranges, so they need simply more habitat, more connectivity,” she said, adding that it’s not unusual for red-cockaded woodpeckers to use up to a few hundred acres for foraging.
Harlan with the Center for Biological Diversity said he’s worried not just for the woodpeckers, but for species across the state, from humongous North Atlantic right whales that calve on protected sites off Georgia’s coast to credit card-sized bog turtles in the Blue Ridge Mountains.
“The protections for sea turtles and shorebirds protect a bunch of other marine species that maybe aren’t listed but are declining or need protections,” he said. “Same with endangered bats and forest birds and hellbenders and mussels and fish. They protect rivers that protect brook trout, which aren’t federally listed but are vital to the fly fishing trout industry of north Georgia, for example. So really all wildlife will be affected if habitat like rivers and forests are allowed to be degraded. Those Endangered Species Act protections were really umbrella protections for all of Georgia’s wildlife.”
Next steps
Red-cockaded woodpecker with bug snack. Photo credit: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
In a letter to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service during a public comment period, Georgia Department of Natural Resources Wildlife Division manager Ted Will criticized the change as contrary to the language of the Endangered Species Act and potentially harmful.
“We believe that the proposed interpretation of ‘harm’ is incorrect, and could do much to inhibit effective wildlife management and conservation. Habitat management is an integral part of Georgia DNR’s Strategic Plan, and permeates virtually every aspect of what we do as a state wildlife agency.”
Department of Natural Resources manager of external affairs Haley Chafin said in a statement that the department will continue to protect wildlife while following the law.
“Georgia has a reliable track record of conserving and preserving the state’s natural wonders and assets while also promoting greater opportunity for individuals and communities, and it will continue to balance those important objectives in the future,” the statement reads in part.
The Center for Biological Diversity is part of a lawsuit seeking to overturn the rule change. Harlan argues that the change exceeds the Trump administration’s authority.
“Congress passed the ESA, and they made it very clear in the language of the law itself that a species and its habitat are protected under the law,” he said. “Trump is trying to circumvent that by changing how the regulations are implemented, but that doesn’t change the law.”
The U.S. Department of the Interior and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service did not respond to requests for comment.
Harlan said Georgia could decide to impose some of its own protections. The state Department of Natural Resources is reviewing recommended revisions to its own protected species list.
“It’s proposing to potentially add new species and maybe strengthen protections for state-listed species,” he said. “That’s different than the federal Endangered Species Act, but Georgia could put some more teeth in its state endangered species act to protect the habitat, to make up for what’s currently being lost federally, so that might be one path.”
But states don’t have the same authority – or the same budget – as the federal government.
“Georgia has in some ways laid a foundation, but the challenges of enacting an endangered species act and the resources that go into overseeing and managing that are enormous,” Worley said.
“I cannot imagine, as a national developer, having to face fifty different endangered species acts across the nation,” he added. “You’ve got to address each one individually and how that state effectively addresses those problems.”
Catherine Wannamaker, an attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center, which is also suing over the proposed rules change, said the court actions are “hoping to keep this at bay until a new administration has a chance to revisit it.”
But she said the rule change could mean big changes to Georgia’s wild places before that has the chance to happen.
“This is a rule change that has landscape-scale impact, and everyone should care about it,” she said. “Not just for endangered species but because of habitat and common species we all see as we walk around our neighborhoods and drive through our back roads, and it’s just a really, really big deal.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: State of the Race: Michigan’s competitive congressional primaries will draw November battle lines
description: Voter Guide: 2026 Michigan Primary Election In just a few days, Michigan voters will make their way to the polls for the Aug. 4 primary election, bringing weeks of absentee and early voting to a close. With a consequential general election on the horizon, Democrats and Republicans across the state are making their final pitches […]
text:
Former Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink, retired Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam and Lansing-area political organizer William Lawrence at a candidate forum hosted by Eaton County Democratic Party and Indivisible Michigan 7th District. April 8, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan AdvanceVoter Guide: 2026 Michigan Primary Election

In just a few days, Michigan voters will make their way to the polls for the Aug. 4 primary election, bringing weeks of absentee and early voting to a close.
With a consequential general election on the horizon, Democrats and Republicans across the state are making their final pitches on why they should represent their party in November and how they would win over undecided voters. 
As primary election day draws near, here are the candidates and races to watch: 
 
7th Congressional District
One of the most politically competitive seats in Michigan, if not the nation, Michigan’s 7th Congressional District has been declared a major target for Democrats looking to grow their ranks in the U.S. House.
While Barrett, the incumbent, is unopposed in the primary, Democrats must choose between former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink, retired Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam and political organizer William Lawrence. 
Among the biggest questions heading into the general election is how the candidates will appeal to independent and undecided voters within the politically purple district.
The nonpartisan Cook Political Report has said the district is a “toss up,” meaning both Barrett and the Democratic nominee will have their work cut out for them in the months following the primary.
Michigan 7 encompasses all of Clinton, Ingham, Livingston and Shiawassee counties, most of Eaton County and parts of Genesee and Oakland counties.
 
Bridget Brink
Former Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink speaks at a candidate forum for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District hosted by the Eaton County Democratic Party and Indivisible Michigan 7th District. April 8, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance
A 28-year foreign service veteran, Brink has pitched herself as the only candidate in the race who directly stood up to Trump, referencing her decision to resign as ambassador to Ukraine in 2025 over the administration’s decision to place pressure on Ukraine instead of Russia to end the war following Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion.
While speaking with voters, Brink has pledged to take action on healthcare costs, calling for a rollback to federal Medicaid cuts, expanding Medicare to cover vision and dental and capping prices for drugs such as insulin and EpiPens. 
Lowering costs for constituents is also a key priority for Brink, as is defending American rights and Democracy from the Trump Administration.
As of July 15, Brink had raised $2.98 million with $841,459 cash on hand.
 
Matt Maasdam
Retired Navy SEAL and Democratic Congressional Candidate Matt Maasdam (center) visits with members of the United Association of Plumbers and Pipefitters Local 333 at its training center in Lansing. March 17, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance
A former Navy SEAL and military aide to President Barack Obama, Maasdam carries the endorsement of U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly), who previously served as the district’s representative, defeating Barrett in 2022.
As far as his priorities if elected, Maasdam emphasizes affordability, banning stock trading in Congress, seeking to end the revolving door of politicians becoming lobbyists and cracking down on dark money, or political spending from undisclosed donors.
Maasdam has also pledged to hold the Trump Administration accountable for abuse of the Constitution, calling for an overhaul of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, including an end to mass raids, warrant requirements for arrests and searches and the prosecution of agents who break the law.
According to his pre-primary report, Maasdam has raised $2.13 million with $464,028 in cash on hand.
 
William Lawrence
U.S. House candidate William Lawrence speaks at a rally with U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in Lansing, Mich., on July 19, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
Born in East Lansing, Lawrence cofounded the Sunrise Movement, a youth-led political action group focused on advocating for climate justice. When he later returned to Lansing, Lawrence advocated for housing access and tenants’ rights, co-founding the Mid-Michigan Tenant Resource Center and leading the MI Rent is Too Damn High Coalition. 
Backed by U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Detroit) and other prominent progressives in Congress, Lawrence has sought to set himself apart from his more moderate opponents, repeatedly noting that he is the only candidate in the race to support a 12-month federal moratorium on data centers. 
Lawrence has prioritized ending “endless wars,” opposing the war in Iran and U.S. arms sales to Israel, while arguing that the resources the U.S. spends on military operations abroad could be better spent on healthcare, housing and other areas to support American families.
As of July 15, Lawrence had raised $1.12 million and reported $383,115 cash on hand.
 
10th Congressional District
With John James running for governor, Michigan’s competitive 10th District is open. Cook Political Report rates it Republican-leaning. The district, which covers southern Macomb County and parts of eastern Oakland County, was a key target for Democrats in 2024.
 
Christina Hines
Courtesy of Christina Hines
Hines previously served as an assistant prosecutor in Wayne and Washtenaw counties and made an unsuccessful run for Macomb County prosecutor in 2024. 
She has pledged to strengthen and expand the Affordable Care Act, Medicare and Medicaid and has taken the Political Integrity Project’s pledge to support anti-corruption measures in Congress, receiving an endorsement from End Citizens United, a political action committee focused on campaign finance reform.
Former Macomb County Prosecutor Carl Marlinga, who unsuccessfully ran against James in 2022 and 2024, has also endorsed Hines as the Democratic nominee.
According to her campaign’s pre-primary report, Hines has raised $1.21 million with $158,196 in cash on hand.
 
Eric Chung
Courtesy of Eric Chung for Michigan
A former Commerce Department attorney who helped implement the CHIPS and Science Act, Chung said he’s running for Congress to “fight for Michigan against Donald Trump’s attacks on our rights, our healthcare, and our democracy.”
On his campaign website, Chung said he would work to roll back Trump’s tariffs. He has also promised to address rising health costs, by restoring Medicaid funding cut by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, and restoring Enhanced Affordable Care Act premium tax credits which expired at the end of 2025.
Like Hines, Chung has taken the Political Integrity Project’s pledge to support anti-corruption measures.
If he prevails in the primary, Chung could go on to be the first openly LGBTQ+ person to represent Michigan in Congress.
As of July 15, Chung’s campaign had raised $1.9 million, with $621,397 cash on hand.
 
Tim Greimel
Tim Greimel, mayor of Pontiac. | Photo courtesy of Tim Greimel for Congress
Former Pontiac mayor and state House Democratic leader Tim Greimel has built up a strong coalition of labor support, including endorsements from the Michigan Education Association, Michigan Professional Fire Fighters Union, the Utility Workers Union of America and more.
Greimel says he’s focused on working families, pledging to stand up to the Trump Administration, protect Social Security and Medicare, and lower the cost of living.
As of July 15 Greimel’s campaign had raised $1.26 million, with $328,004 on hand.
 
Michael Bouchard Jr.
Michael Bouchard Jr. | Campaign photo
A U.S. Army Veteran who has pledged to push for the completion of the southern border wall and support parental rights in their child’s education, Michael Bouchard is Trump’s hand-picked candidate to succeed James. 
The son of Oakland County Sheriff Mike Bouchard, the younger Bouchard has also drawn support from House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) and members of Michigan’s Republican Congressional Delegation including Lisa McClain (R-Bruce Township), Jack Bergman (R-Watersmeet) and Tim Walberg (R-Tipton). 
As of July 15, Bouchard’s campaign had raised $1.41 million, with $958,230 cash on hand.
 
Steffan Demetropoulos
Steffan Demetropoulos | Campaign photo
A U.S. Army Veteran and construction project manager, Demetropoulos has pitched himself as an everyday American looking to restore trust in Washington. 
On his campaign website, Demetropoulos lists fiscal responsibility, government transparency and protecting the future of children among his priorities.
“That means reducing wasteful spending, strengthening economic opportunity for working families, and ensuring parents have a voice in their children’s education,” Demetropoulos wrote.
As of July 15, Demetropoulos had raised $6,870 with $3,641 cash on hand.
 
Justin Kirk
Justin Kirk | Campaign photo
An attorney who previously interned for U.S. Rep. Paul Mitchell, Kirk has listed retaining Republican control of the U.S. House of Representatives as a top priority for his campaign.
On his campaign website Kirk said he would work to make Michigan a hub for supply chain, warehousing logistics and distribution and promote responsible data center development. 
If elected, Kirk also said he would work to improve Michigan’s education system amid declining math and reading scores, promote trades and champion Michigan’s role in supporting national security.
According to his pre-primary filing, Kirk’s campaign raised $463,208 with $238,376 on hand.
 
Robert Lulgjuraj – Suspended
While his name still appears on the ballot, former prosecutor Robert Lugjuraj announced on July 14 that he was ending his campaign for U.S. House following Trump’s endorsement in the race.

 
11th Congressional District
With U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens’ decision to run for U.S. Senate, several Democrats have stepped up to the plate to succeed the four-term representative. 
As a safe Democratic seat, whoever emerges victorious in the primary will likely take home another win in November. However, Troy Mayor Ethan Baker, who is unopposed in the Republican primary, is set to challenge Democrats for control of the district
The 11th Congressional District encompasses municipalities in central Oakland County, including Farmington Hills, Ferndale, Pontiac and Troy. 
 
Aisha Farooqi
Aisha Farooqi | Campaign photo
An Attorney and appointed member of the Michigan Child Abuse and Neglect Prevention Board and the child of immigrant parents, Farooqi’s campaign says she is focused on fighting for a New American Dream, available to every working family and community across the U.S.
Like many other Democratic candidates heading into the midterm, Farooqi is focused on addressing the rising cost of living, promising to fight for higher wages and fair compensation for workers while reducing regulatory burdens on companies providing essential goods. 
She also supports Medicare for All, a universal childcare system, abolishing ICE and creating a pathway to citizenship for undocumented immigrants.
As of July 15, Farooqi had raised $421,142, while reporting an on-hand deficit of $352 dollars.
 
John Paul Torres
John Paul Torres, a candidate for U.S. Congress, at an event hosted by the Southfield Neighbors Action Committee about ICE presence in metro Detroit. July 22, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Torres serves as the vice president of the Waterford School District’s Board of Education and is a former member of the team of court administrators who implemented juvenile justice reforms for the Michigan Supreme Court.
“I’m a father, a husband, and a public servant. I’ll fight for the working people who built this country, not the billionaires driving up the cost of living,” Torres said on his campaign website. “Our campaign is 100% grassroots. I will never take corporate or utility PAC money.”
Torres supports Medicare for All, universal childcare, abolishing ICE and comprehensive immigration reform, noting that he’d worked on the DREAM Act as a Congressional Fellow.
According to Torres’ pre-primary report, his campaign has raised $147,385 with $3,841 cash on hand.
 
Jeremy Moss
Sen. Jeremy Moss (D-Bloomfield) presented his resolution to put language lifting Michigan’s same-sex marriage ban on the ballot to the Senate Committee on Civil Rights, Judiciary and Public Safety. March 19, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
A state lawmaker first elected to the state Legislature in 2015, Moss is the first openly gay member of the Michigan Senate and its only Jewish state senator. If he prevails in the primary, Moss could also be the state’s first openly LGBTQ+ representative.
Moss told Michigan Advance he’s been a demonstrated fighter for the district, pointing to his work in the Legislature supporting gun safety reforms passed after the 2023 Michigan State University shooting, an expansion to Michigan’s Civil Rights Law, and working to implement a constitutional amendment improving access to the ballot box. 
Moss supports a robust public health option as a pathway to universal health coverage, and has called for dismantling ICE, arguing the agency cannot be reformed under the Trump Administration.
Both Farooqi and former Ford Engineer Don Ufford have criticized Moss for his support for Israel.
Ufford’s campaign has accused Moss of taking money from donors and organizations with ties to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, also known as AIPAC. Moss said that’s not true, chalking up the overlap in contributions to his campaign from individuals who also gave to AIPAC as  support from Jewish residents.
“This is a district with the highest concentration of Jewish residents in our state and I’m obviously a proud Jewish Michigander,” Moss said. “It’s really shameful to mischaracterize all of my Jewish supporters as a part of a PAC conspiracy.”
As of July 15, Moss’ campaign has raised $1.49 million, with $352,516 in cash on hand.
 
Don Ufford
Don Ufford | Campaign photo
The former head of global engineering for Ford Motor Company, Ufford’s campaign has described him as a “political outsider with real-world experience” frequently drawing critical comparisons with Moss’s campaign. 
Ufford has been endorsed by End Citizens United and supports Medicare for All, an end to the war in Iran and abolishing ICE.
While Ufford has criticized Moss for previously accepting political contributions from organizations like DTE Energy, Consumers Energy and Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan while campaigning for the Legislature, Moss has pointed to reporting from the Detroit News noting that Ufford had identified as a Republican in 2022 while participating in a bipartisan political leadership fellowship at Michigan State University.
“Don Ufford is a Democrat who proudly served in the Biden White House, where he worked to bring manufacturing jobs back to Michigan,” Ufford Campaign Manager Mark Goldenberg told Michigan Advance, later explaining Ufford served in the Made in America Office under the Office of Management and Budget, working on the EV transition and manufacturing development.
Ufford’s campaign had raised $1 million as of July 15, with $289,619 cash on hand.
 
13th Congressional District
While two U.S. representatives hold Detroit within their district, the majority Black city hasn’t had a Black representative in Congress since U.S. Rep. Brenda Lawrence’s term ended at the start of 2023. However, the primary elections in Michigan’s 13th Congressional District could change that. 
As a reliable blue seat, whoever prevails this coming Tuesday is all but certain to win in November. Only one candidate is listed on the Republican Ballot: T.P. Nykoriak, who in 2016 was sentenced to 16 months in federal prison for stealing U.S. savings bonds from a church. 
Michigan’s 13th Congressional District is made up of portions of Detroit, and its suburbs, including Allen Park, Hamtramck, Romulus and Wyandotte.
 
Shri Thanedar
Running for his third term in Congress and facing yet another primary challenge, U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Detroit) is once again defending his record of showing up for his constituents.
U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Detroit) speaks to press at Detroit’s Riverside Park to demand President Donald Trump allow the Gordie Howe bridge to open. July 7, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
In the 2024 campaign cycle, then-Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan and other officials living within Thanedar’s district argued that he was not responsive to the district’s needs, criticisms that Thanedar’s primary opponent continues to echo in 2026. 
 In a text message to Michigan Advance, Thanedar noted that his office had delivered $45 million in federal work project funding for communities within his district, including support to help Detroit seniors age in place, home repairs for veterans and grant funding to establish a center to provide support services to survivors of human trafficking and exploitation.
“The federal government sends hundreds of billions of dollars to Michigan every year,” Thanedar said. “Things like ARPA funds and the Infrastructure bill are what allows Michigan to invest in local communities. But in addition to that, I’m proud to get funding approved for specific projects throughout the entire 13th District.”
Thanedar also cited his opposition to the previously-planned ICE facility in Romulus, noting that he’d held a town hall meeting outside the facility and participated in the collective effort that resulted in the plan being scrapped. 
If Democrats regain their majority in the U.S. House, Thanedar, who serves as the ranking member of the U.S. House Committee on Homeland Security’s Oversight, Investigations and Accountability Subcommittee, said he’d like to chair that subcommittee.
“As chair of Oversight in the Homeland Security Committee, I will make sure we subpoena and prosecute ICE and this administration for all their crimes,” Thanedar said.
As of July 15, Thanedar had raised $390,276 over the course of this campaign cycle, with $5 million cash on hand.
 
Donavan McKinney
Taking office in the Michigan House in 2023, McKinney has centered his congressional campaign on three core issues: getting corporate dollars and cash from undisclosed donors out of politics, backing Medicare for All and providing free universal childcare.
Michigan state Rep. Donavan McKinney (D-Detroit) speaks at a rally advocating against a proposed 24% wholesale tax on marijuana for the next fiscal year. Sept. 30, 2025 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
While speaking with Michigan Advance, McKinney noted that Thanedar was elected to Congress the same year McKinney was elected to the Michigan House. During that same period of time, McKinney argued he’d delivered more funding for Detroit as a member of the Michigan House Appropriations Committee than Thanedar had as a congressional representative.
During his campaigning Thanedar has slammed McKinney for taking $2,000 from Ambassador Bridge owner and Trump donor Matthew Moroun for his state House Campaign in 2022-2023.
McKinney told Michigan Advance those dollars had gone to support food programs and community events. 
“I never personally benefited from those contributions. I just gave it straight to the community,” McKinney said, pointing to his record in the Legislature of supporting efforts to ban utility companies and state contractors from donating to political campaigns.
Although Thanedar has won the support of U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York), McKinney has been endorsed by multiple members of the Congressional Black Caucus, including Reps. Steven Horsford (D-Nevada), Ayanna Pressley (D-Massachusetts), Ilhan Omar (D-Minn) Lateefah Simon (D-Calif.) and Summer Lee (D-Pa.). McKinney also has the support of fellow Detroit-area Rep. Tlaib and Bernie Sanders.

As of July 15 McKinney had raised $1.37 million, with $142,853 in cash on hand.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio Haitians lose jobs, face terror — and impossible choices
description: With Ohio’s Haitian refugees losing their protected status Monday, Springfield’s large population has begun being terminated from their jobs, a pastor who works with the community said on Tuesday. They face being forced to return to a nation that the International Rescue Committee says is “in the grip of an overwhelming humanitarian crisis.” Right now, […]
text:
A mural is displayed in an alley downtown in Springfield, Ohio. (Photo by Luke Sharrett/Getty Images.)With Ohio’s Haitian refugees losing their protected status Monday, Springfield’s large population has begun being terminated from their jobs, a pastor who works with the community said on Tuesday.
They face being forced to return to a nation that the International Rescue Committee says is “in the grip of an overwhelming humanitarian crisis.” 
Right now, gangs control Haiti. Kidnapping, murder, and rape are rampant. And the pastor, Carl Ruby, said one Springfield 12-year-old faces having to return to a place where he saw animals feeding on murdered corpses when he was just five.
‘Thousands of people are now going to die violent deaths,’ says attorney for Ohio Haitian community

“They’re just terrified for their physical safety,” Ruby said during a virtual press conference. “Many of them have already been traumatized… Some of them have been in prison. Some of them have been tortured. Some have been beaten. Some had been raped. Nearly all of them have seen friends or family members killed.”
And some of those families — those who have had children since coming to the United States — face an excruciating choice: whether to take their children with them into the violent chaos that is Haiti or leave them behind in a relatively peaceful, prosperous place where their children’s citizenship gives them the right to stay.
More than 330,000 Haitians have received temporary-protected status since an earthquake devastated the impoverished Caribbean country in 2010. Once in the United States, their status has been renewed as conditions in Haiti continued to deteriorate.
Early last year, Ohio’s then-Attorney General Dave Yost and 27 other Republican state AGs wrote a letter to the Trump administration stressing the word “temporary” in temporary protected status. 
They claimed without evidence that it was safe for some with protected status to return to those home countries and urged a review.
Then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem in November announced that she was terminating protected status for Haitians who had qualified, including about 45,000 in Ohio and roughly 15,000 in Springfield.
Lawyers for the Haitians sued, arguing that Noem had failed to follow the 1990 law creating temporary protected status. It requires that the government conduct a mandatory review of conditions in a group’s home country to certify that it’s safe to return before forcing them to go.
Lower courts blocked the termination. 
But in June, in a 6-3 ruling the U.S. Supreme Court reversed them, ruling that the TPS law itself barred most court challenges to the way its provisions were or were not applied.
Attempt to halt imminent deportations of Haitians and Syrians blocked in US Senate

The court didn’t bar constitutional challenges, however, and SCOTUS Blog on Tuesday reported that some of those are in the works.
But for Haitians in Ohio, that might seem a thin reed on which to lean. They and many others are bracing for a mass-deportation such as those conducted by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in other regions.
 Ruby, the Springfield pastor, said no such operation has happened yet. 
“It could happen as soon as this week,” he said. “What we’re hearing from other reporting is that they’re planning on deporting them directly back to Haiti. There have been cases in the community where they have been picked up one day. Sent to a detention center the next day. And on the third or the fourth day they’re back in Haiti. It’s obviously not safe for them to go there.” 
The pastor added that jobs and support services are almost nonexistent when deportees get to Haiti.
In addition to terror over what might happen in Haiti are worries about what’s next for Springfield.
Ruby said that he and his colleagues have been working for the past 18 months to build “a very large coalition of faith leaders not only here in Springfield, but across the state of Ohio and across the nation who will stand with us if we have anything like what took place in Minneapolis.”
He was referring to a mass-enforcement operation last winter in which masked ICE officers shot and killed two protestors, both of them citizens. Analysis of videos taken at the scene showed that neither protester posed the threat that Trump administration officials claimed after the shootings.
Ruby stressed that he and other faith leaders want any protests of ICE enforcement actions to be peaceful, and that protesters have to be ready for the possible consequences of civil disobedience, such as going to jail.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Gov. Mike DeWine has criticized some of his Republican colleagues for falsely demonizing Springfield’s Haitian immigrants. 
On Tuesday, his spokesman reiterated a statement DeWine issued last month when the U.S. Supreme Court issued its ruling that effectively revoked their protected status.
“Today’s decision is a legal decision,” DeWine said. “As I have stated in the past, the policy to remove these individuals from this country is a mistake.”
DeWine later added, “The situation in Haiti could hardly be much worse. The violent gangs run most of the country. The government barely functions. And, the economy is in shambles.”
Lynn Tramonte, founder of the Ohio Immigrant Alliance, questioned whether DeWine would instruct the Ohio Highway Patrol not to assist ICE in enforcement operations. 
In the past, the Highway Patrol has worked with U.S. Border Patrol to apprehend undocumented immigrants, the American Immigration Council reports.
Dan Tierney, DeWine’s press secretary, didn’t answer directly when asked if the Highway Patrol would assist ICE with enforcement operations in Springfield.
Tramonte said DeWine could do more to help Haitians who suddenly find themselves without status.
“The governor might claim he is powerless to do anything in the face of federal agents invading our state to take our people, but here are two things he can do,” Tramonte said in a text message. 
“He can instruct the Highway Patrol not to assist ICE in the enforcement of civil immigration laws. That’s not their job and they shouldn’t have to get involved. He can also underscore the same point for local police who often seem to think they should be on the hunt for immigrants instead of focusing on crime.”

title: Federal government will put 2,840 acres of Ohio’s only national forest out to bid for fracking
description: Nearly 3,000 acres of land in Ohio’s only nation forest will be auctioned for fracking in September.  The Bureau of Land Management announced 41 parcels totaling 2,840 acres in Wayne National Forest will go up for a bid on Sept. 15. The announcement was made earlier this month and these parcels are in Monroe and […]
text:
Lake Vesuvius Recreation Area at Wayne National Forest in Ohio. (Getty Images file photo.)Nearly 3,000 acres of land in Ohio’s only nation forest will be auctioned for fracking in September. 
The Bureau of Land Management announced 41 parcels totaling 2,840 acres in Wayne National Forest will go up for a bid on Sept. 15. The announcement was made earlier this month and these parcels are in Monroe and Washington counties. 
“Leasing is the first step in the process to develop federal oil and gas resources. Before development operations can begin, an operator must submit an application for permit to drill detailing development plans,” the Bureau of Land Management said in a statement.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“The BLM reviews applications for permits to drill, posts them for public review, conducts an environmental analysis and coordinates with state partners and stakeholders.”
Fracking is the process of injecting liquid into the ground at a high pressure to extract oil or gas.
There were approximately 2,000 incidents associated with oil and gas wells in Ohio from 2015-2023, according to FracTracker Alliance, a nonprofit that collects data on fracking pipelines. 
Evidence shows increased exposure to fracking impacts health, in particular children’s health, including low birth weight, preterm births, congenital anomalies, and asthma, according to Yale School of Medicine. 
The Ohio Capital Journal recently published a story about how Washington County residents are concerned injection wells leaking brine waste could contaminate Marietta’s drinking water. 
‘The precipice of an emergency.’ Marietta residents worry drinking water could become contaminated.

Ohio Environmental Council Senior Attorney for Land and Water Nathan Johnson said putting out bids to frack Wayne National Forest is concerning. 
“It’s unfortunate that the feds keep trying to push this,” he said. “We really need to take good care of our public lands.”
The BLM’s overall plan is to lease out 40,000 acres for fracking in Wayne National Forest, Johnson said. 
 “That’s a huge amount of land for Ohio,” he said. “That’s more than 30,000 football fields.” 
As required by law, the BLM is currently in the middle of a 30-day public protest to receive additional comments which will end Aug. 17. The BLM scoped out the 41 parcels in January.
Ohio state Rep. Tristan Rader, D-Lakewood, urged people to post comments.  
“This is just continued exploitation of the people and resources of Ohio by large corporations,” Rader said in a statement. “For generations, the people of this region and this state have been sidelined by the interest of extractive industries.” 
The Wayne National Forest was established in 1935 and comprises 244,000 acres spanning 12 counties with three units in Athens, Ironton, and Marietta in Southeast Ohio. 
More than 200,000 people annually visit Wayne National Forest, which is known for its hiking, biking, horseback riding trails, and off-road vehicle trails. 
“If development occurs on this scale … you’re going to have heavy truck traffic,” Johnson said.
“You’re going to see well paths. One of the the major concerns if you’re visiting the area is health, safety, truck traffic, but the air pollution is just always a constant. It does not respect boundaries.”
There are already 1,200 conventional wells operating in Wayne National Forest, Ohio Oil and Gas Association spokesperson Mike Chadsey noted.
But Johnson said there are very big differences between the two.
“This project, it’s all shale development with these huge, massive well pads, massive pipeline developments,” Johnson said. “So totally different ball game than what the Wayne has seen in the past with these much smaller operations.”
A national forest is managed by the U.S. Forest Service under the Department of Agriculture and blends conservation with public service and resource extraction like logging and mining. 
A national park is managed by the National Park Service under the U.S. Department of Interior and the goal is to protect and preserve natural lands in their natural state. 
Ohio has one national park, Cuyahoga Valley National Park in Northeast Ohio.

title: Smart policy, not online storefronts, is the cure for Ohio’s obesity crisis
description: More than 3 million adults in Ohio (nearly 37% of our population!) live with obesity. This is not a personal failing; it is a complex, chronic disease crisis that is worsening each year and demands a focused, statewide intervention. Fortunately, we are entering an era of unprecedented medical advancement. The advent of GLP-1 receptor agonists is a […]
text:
A woman takes out an Ozempic pen. (Photo by Shalina Chatlani/Stateline.)More than 3 million adults in Ohio (nearly 37% of our population!) live with obesity. This is not a personal failing; it is a complex, chronic disease crisis that is worsening each year and demands a focused, statewide intervention.
Fortunately, we are entering an era of unprecedented medical advancement. The advent of GLP-1 receptor agonists is a game-changer. As an obesity care physician, I see firsthand how these innovative medications transform lives by reducing the risk of diabetes, heart disease, and stroke while supporting weight management.
Ohio is uniquely positioned to leverage these FDA-approved treatments to improve population health, provided we lead the way in ensuring their safe and appropriate use to improve metabolic health of those affected.
In Ohio, pediatric obesity care is anchored by our world-class children’s hospitals, as it should be. Our state’s pediatric health centers carefully evaluate patients, recognizing that mental health and disordered eating behaviors must be considered before prescribing GLP-1s to anyone under 18.
For adults, however, a critical barrier remains: when insurance coverage is denied or unavailable, patients are often driven to seek alternative, unverified options.
This lack of legitimate, affordable access to GLP-1 medications has turned the online landscape into a digital Wild West. This will lead to highly variable care, that could have more risk and is not connected to a patient’s primary provider.
At the same time, Ohio has a golden opportunity to expand access to safe, equitable GLP-1 coverage through Medicaid for our most vulnerable citizens.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Innovation Center recently established the BALANCE (Better Approaches to Lifestyle and Nutrition for Comprehensive hEalth) Model.
Under this five-year demonstration project, participating states directly receive significant, federally negotiated manufacturer rebates without any effort.
BALANCE will also provide patients with no-cost lifestyle and nutrition support programs to maximize the drug’s effectiveness.
The registration deadline for the BALANCE model is Jan. 1, 2027.
Integrating coverage of FDA-approved obesity medications into Medicaid is a critical step toward ensuring that lower-income Ohioans have access to affordable, science-based obesity treatments — in the same way that Medicaid beneficiaries have access to proven therapies to manage other chronic diseases, such as hypertension or asthma.
While some policymakers hesitate over the upfront cost of these medications, the fiscal and human toll of inaction is far higher.
However, other states such as Missouri and Louisiana recognize obesity as a chronic disease that demands a comprehensive battle plan, and both have taken steps to provide Medicaid coverage for these critical treatment tools.
Obesity is a medical condition that increases the risk of costly chronic conditions, including diabetes, heart disease, and stroke. It requires evidence-based treatment, and Ohio’s health systems are prepared to deliver it.
By joining the BALANCE program and tightening regulations on reckless online providers, we can reverse the rise in obesity rates and chart a healthier future for all Ohioans.

title: Most states temporarily house foster children in hotels, offices
description: More than 9,000 children in foster care had to temporarily stay in hotels, office buildings and other potentially unsafe settings when states couldn’t find suitable places for them, according to a new federal audit. The inspector general’s office of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services found that states had an especially difficult time […]
text:
Margie Quin, commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Children’s Services, has been named as a defendant in two proposed class action lawsuits alleging DCS warehouses and mistreats children. Tennessee fared poorly in a new federal audit examining the number of foster children placed in hotels, office buildings and other potentially unsafe settings. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)More than 9,000 children in foster care had to temporarily stay in hotels, office buildings and other potentially unsafe settings when states couldn’t find suitable places for them, according to a new federal audit.
The inspector general’s office of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services found that states had an especially difficult time placing older children and children with complex behavioral and mental health needs. The pandemic and the opioid abuse epidemic also created challenges during the period covered by the audit, which was January 1, 2022, to June 30, 2023.
When a court determines that a child should be removed from a home because remaining would be a risk to the child’s well-being, the responsibility for placement and care of the child is transferred to a state child welfare agency. The preferred option in most cases is kinship care, or placement with relatives.
When kinship care is not available, states may place children with nonrelative caregivers, or in child care institutions. Licensed foster care locations must meet certain safety and health standards and be approved by the state.
But of the 49 state agencies (including the District of Columbia) that responded to the inspector general’s questionnaire, 34 reported that they had to temporarily place children in unlicensed settings that are not designed to care for children. Of those, 30 provided enough information for the agency to associate the stays with individual children.
Of the 15,705 temporary emergency placements tracked by HHS, 59% lasted four or fewer days and 28% lasted for five days or longer. The longest stay, in a hotel, lasted 251 days. The average length of stay across all reported placements was one week.
Seventeen states reported a total of 1,922 hotel room stays; 22 reported a total of 2,698 office stays; and 16 reported 4,412 stays at other unlicensed facilities, such as cabins in state parks.
States shift toward kin-first foster care

Arizona and Texas alone accounted for nearly half of all the reported temporary stays. Arizona reported 3,907 placements involving 3,481 children, while Texas reported 3,923 temporary placements involving 1,977 children.
Other states with a high number of emergency placements included Tennessee (1,845), Illinois (812) and Washington state (612).
Eight states (Alaska, Hawaii, Indiana, Missouri, Nebraska, New York, Ohio and Pennsylvania) did not track their use of emergency temporary placements, and Delaware and Montana did not submit any data.
Seven states (Connecticut, Iowa, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Rhode Island, Utah and Wyoming) said they did not place any children in emergency temporary settings.
