name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio citizens showed power by stopping state EPA approval for data center pollution of waterways
description: “You can’t fight city hall.” Resistance is futile. The powers that be always win. Pick one. If you need an excuse to justify inaction with a cynical shrug, there are plenty. But there are also plenty of examples of people who give enough of a damn to battle bureaucracy, to push back because they must. […]
text:
The Ohio River on July 7, 2026. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).“You can’t fight city hall.” Resistance is futile. The powers that be always win. Pick one. If you need an excuse to justify inaction with a cynical shrug, there are plenty. 
But there are also plenty of examples of people who give enough of a damn to battle bureaucracy, to push back because they must. 
They make calls, send letters, show up. They challenge “city hall” and rules too hard to change even if they cannot win. Because sometimes they do. 
Thousands of Ohioans took on the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency over a quality-of-life threat. They won. For now. 
In December enraged citizens got wind of the Ohio EPA’s outrageous proposal to make it easier for massive data centers to pollute local waterways with impunity and they mobilized to table the blanket approach under consideration. 
The Ohio EPA confirmed that public comments against its proposed statewide data center wastewater permit exceeded 7,000. 
Last Tuesday the agency announced it had scrapped the general permit drafted to help data centers release wastewater into Ohio’s lakes, rivers, and streams with heavily reduced review and analysis by the state. 
“After carefully reviewing the significant volume of public comments received on the draft National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) general permit for data centers, Ohio EPA has decided not to move forward with finalizing the general permit.” 
Would that have happened without 7,000 voices raised in opposition? 
If not for the public outcry would the Ohio EPA have handed Big Tech everything it wanted — a quick, one-size-fits-all permitting process that cut meaningful agency review, on-site scrutiny of data center wastewater discharges, dropped notice and comment opportunities for local communities? 
Ohio already provides massive sales tax exemptions for data centers (costing the state nearly $1.6 billion in 2025) and the state environmental agency was advancing an industry-friendly plan. 
In January, Ohio EPA director John Logue admitted the decision to propose a general permit (as opposed to individual, case-by-case authorization) was motivated in part by President Trump’s call to expedite the process for approving data centers. 
Getting an environmental permit to satisfy clean water requirements took too long. 
But as developers raced to build a wave of “hyperscale” data centers around Ohio — which hosts more than any other Great Lakes state at over 200-and-counting — controversy grew over wastewater generated by some of those facilities winding up in Lake Erie and its tributaries. 
The expedited permit proposal could have wrapped up the process in a month compared to as many as six for an on-site specific permit. 
Incredible as it sounds, the now defunct agency plan would have allowed all data centers, (regardless of size, location, or type) to discharge untreated waste and storm water directly into local waterways under certain conditions not subject to individual inspection. 
A single statewide blanket permit would cover an entire industry. 
When the Ohio EPA informed Ohioans that such a deal was in the works at the end of 2025, one phrase from the proposed change ignited alarm. 
“It has been determined that a lowering of water quality of various waters of the state associated with granting coverage under this permit is necessary to accommodate important social and economic development in the state of Ohio.” 
In other words, indulging the fast-track agenda of the artificial intelligence industry —  valued at hundreds of billions in direct market size with multi-trillion-dollar infrastructure spending and record-breaking personal wealth creation — is worth the price of polluting some Ohio lakes and streams?? 
The broadly ambiguous language in the agency’s drafted proposal underscored that tradeoff to Big Tech. 
It acknowledged a “decline in water quality” as an acceptable business proposition as long as data center wastewater isn’t “discharged within 500 yards upstream from a public water supply intake” or dumped “in a lake other than Lake Erie, or groundwater supplies” or “exhibits the reasonable potential” to break Ohio’s minimum water quality standards. 
All wording a major tech or AI company lawyer could drive a bus through without breaking a sweat. 
One provision of the streamlined permit did exhort data centers to “evaluate potential prevention methods and install the latest pollution prevention technology if it is economically feasible.” Another revision to exploit.
The overwhelming takeaway from incensed Ohioans was that the state was giving AI data centers a pass on polluting surface water in Ohio with weakened safeguards for local communities. 
The Ohio EPA appeared to sanction the necessary release of unknown contaminants from cooling-component water and other runoff from data centers into natural waterways to get operations up and running faster. 
An accommodation to AI barons regardless of the cost to Ohioans stuck with polluted water. 
Data centers consume massive amounts of water to cool servers and prevent overheating of equipment. 
Discharge from those water-cooling methods can contain hazardous forever chemicals (PFAS) — toxic compounds that break down slowly in nature and in the human body and are linked to serious health risks. 
While most data center wastewater in Ohio goes to municipal systems (treatment plants and sanitary sewers) instead of being dumped directly into lakes and streams, the Ohio EPA was prepared to approve that option for some data centers without requiring chemical measurements from the water prior to discharge and with limited public input. 
But the agency shelved the idea, thanks to more than 7,000 Ohioans who objected. Loudly. Who says you can’t fight city hall?

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Faith leaders call on the next governor to go all in on clean energy
description: A multifaith group focused on the environment is calling on whoever sits in the governor’s office in 2027 to commit Wisconsin to a clean energy future. “More than 100 faith leaders from across the state have signed an open letter to the next governor declaring that the climate crisis is a spiritual crisis, and our […]
text:
Rev. Teresa Thomas-Boyd, a faith partnership consultant for the Walnut Way Conservation Corp. in Milwaukee, speaks at a news conference in Madison Tuesday calling on Wisconsin's next governor to commit to a clean energy future. Behind her to the left is Laura Lane, Wisconsin outreach director for Faith In Place. (Photo by Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)
A multifaith group focused on the environment is calling on whoever sits in the governor’s office in 2027 to commit Wisconsin to a clean energy future.
“More than 100 faith leaders from across the state have signed an open letter to the next governor declaring that the climate crisis is a spiritual crisis, and our next governor must lead us to a just transition to 100% renewable energy,” said Laura Lane, the Wisconsin outreach director for Faith In Place, at a Tuesday morning press conference outside the state Capitol.
“Clean energy is the solution for lowering energy bills, having cleaner air and water, and enjoying a livable planet,” Lane said. “All Wisconsinites deserve the dignity of a life where the basic conditions of health and joy can be met. And the next governor must lead us to that future.”
Faith In Place is made up of individuals as well as houses of worship in Illinois, Indiana and Wisconsin, organizing to improve environmental conditions in the Upper Midwest. Lane said it was founded 27 years ago and has helped spawn “green teams” dedicated to environmental issues in religious congregations in all three states.
“Although God created everything good, we have not been good in America to the beautiful creation,” said Rev. Teresa Thomas-Boyd, a faith partnership consultant for the Walnut Way Conservation Corp. in Milwaukee.
“We need to have cleaner energy and not only to reduce the cost of energy for Wisconsin, but also to mitigate the natural disasters that we experience each year,” Thomas-Boyd said. “So I urge the future governor of Wisconsin to move us to be good stewards.”
Rev. Kelly Asbrooth-Jackson, a Madison Unitarian Universalist minister, said Wisconsin is behind both Illinois and Minnesota in the transition to renewable energy.
“The need for an environment friendly to human beings and the need for each of us to make ends meet have been pitted against each other for a very long time now,” Asprooth-Jackson said. “It is time for us to let go of that story because it has kept us from practicing the values common to so many of our religions, including my own — to care for the precious gift of this planet that has been entrusted to us and to care for our neighbors with whom we share it.”
The effects of climate change have been most recently experienced in severe weather events, including historic flooding and destructive tornados in Wisconsin, as well as wildfires in Canada that sent smoke hundreds of miles, including to the Wisconsin skies.
“We were breathing the smoke with our most dangerous air quality ever recorded,” said Rev. Nick Uptall, a Lutheran pastor. “And we know that it’s getting worse.”
Climate change threatens the future of a longstanding tradition for the young people in his church, Uptall said — an annual canoe trip to the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness on the border of Minnesota and Canada. Worse, however, it has harmed people as well as animals and plants, “which my faith understands to be our siblings in God’s creation,” he said.
“Jesus called us to love our neighbors as ourselves,” Uptall said. The state’s next governor must “lead Wisconsin to a better future, turning us from the waste and destruction of dirty energy and instead caring for God’s creation.”
The harms from climate change “fall disproportionately on those who have the least resources,” said Rabbi Abby Phelps of Milwaukee. “Ending our reliance on fossil fuels is a practical necessity and it is also a religious obligation.”
“The Earth becomes ours to use only after we bless it,” Phelps said, citing an interpretation of scripture by rabbinical commentators. “To take without blessing is theft. To take with blessing is partnership.”
Committing to renewable, clean energy honors that spirit, she added: “What better way could there be to bring blessing into this world than by harnessing its power in a way that protects the Earth and its inhabitants?”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Arnold leaves transit post, Scott readies for ‘rodeo,’ Mitchell hangs a shingle, in political notes
description: Maryland Transit Administration head Holly Arnold steps down after five years, Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott returns to Martha's Vineyard for a fundraiser and former delegate and Hogan administration adviser Keiffer Mitchell returns as a lobbyist, in political notes.
text:
Maryland Transit Administration Administrator Holly Arnold testifies in this 2024 photo on $450 million in cost overruns and a 234-day delay for the Purple Line transit project in the Washington suburbs. (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)After five years running the agency that runs the state’s trains and buses, Holly Arnold is stepping down.
Arnold, a holdover from the Hogan administration, said her last day as Maryland Transit Administration administrator will be Sept. 1. A successor to run the agency that manages the state’s MARC trains, light rail, subway and bus systems is expected to be named shortly thereafter.
“Serving as MTA Administrator has been the highlight of my career and I am grateful for the opportunity to lead this agency over the last five years,” Arnold said in the statement. “While I will miss the amazing MTA team, I am excited for what the future holds and look forward to spending more time with my family.”
First appointed to the job in 2021 by then-Gov. Larry Hogan, Arnold was reappointed when Gov. Wes Moore took office. During her tenure, the final stretch of track of the planned 16-mile Purple Line light rail was laid recently and the Red Line in Baltimore, killed by Hogan, was revived under Moore. The Washington-area Purple Line is expected to begin service in winter 2027, while ground has yet to be broken on the Red Line, more than 20 years after it was first discussed.
“During her more than 13 years of service with MTA, Administrator Arnold has been a tireless champion for transit, advancing initiatives such as modernizing the light rail, implementing transformative upgrades to the metro subway system, building the Purple Line and infusing a can-do spirit in her work and support of our phenomenal transit employees,” Maryland Department of Transportation Secretary Katie Thomson said in a statement. “We wish her the best in her next chapter.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Moore said in a statement that, as administrator, Arnold “faced challenges head-on and worked tirelessly to improve service for all riders. Our residents, employers and families have seen the impact of her efforts first-hand, and we are grateful to Administrator Arnold for her diligent service to our state.”
After she leaves office, Arnold’s successor will be appointed by Thomson, with Moore’s approval, according to state law.
“I am proud of what we have accomplished together and am confident the employees and leadership team at MTA will continue to advance the critical projects that will move transit in Maryland forward,” Arnold said.
‘Getting ready for the rodeo’ at Martha’s Vineyard
Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott (D) is returning to Martha’s Vineyard to fundraise for his next reelection race, which won’t start in earnest until 2028.
Scott, who is currently serving his second term in City Hall, made his first fundraising stop at the Massachusetts vacation destination last year, joined by former Baltimore Mayor Stephanie Rawlings-Blake and other Maryland political figures, said Marvin James, a campaign adviser to Scott.
“The mayor has — especially with his appeal as president of the African American Mayors Association — national appeal. There’s been a strong desire for him to go back to the Vineyard,” James said Tuesday.
An online invitation for the Aug. 18 event advertises tickets between $250 and $2,500. Scott’s most recent campaign report, filed in January, showed he had more than $250,000 in the bank.
Officially, the event will focus on Scott’s 2028 reelection bid. But James noted that Scott, who cannot run for a fourth term, has an “open mind” about his political future and job openings that may arise in 2030, including the governor’s mansion, since Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) will not be able to run again.
“This is him getting ready for the rodeo,” James said. “The mayor wants to be ready.”
The vacation town is a popular campaign destination for notable Democrats, including former Vice President Kamala Harris (D) and Moore, who has campaigned there in the past, including in 2023.
Scott cannot run for mayor again in 2032 after city voters in 2022 approved a two-term limit, beginning in 2024, for mayor, comptroller and city council members. The measure, which passed with 71% of the vote, was financially backed by David Smith, the executive chairman of Sinclair Broadcast Group, which owns Baltimore television station Fox 45.
Scott has attracted national attention at times during his tenure leading Maryland’s largest city, including for the city’s rapidly declining homicide rate, and in national television appearances following the collapse of the Francis Scott Key Bridge.
Mitchell opens Annapolis shop
Keiffer J. Mitchell Jr., a former delegate, former Baltimore City Council member and former senior adviser for Gov. Larry Hogan, has a new line for his resume: head of an Annapolis office for Washington-based lobbying firm BGR Group.
Keiffer Mitchell is opening an Annnapolis office for D.C.-based lobbying firm BGR. (Photo courtesy BGR)
BGR announced Monday that Mitchell, currently a vice president of state and local advocacy for the firm, will open an Annapolis office, “strengthening its ability to serve clients before Maryland’s executive branch, General  Assembly, and local governments,” the firm said in a statement announcing the move. It will be the latest state capital office of the company, which also has offices in Atlanta, Phoenix, Nashville and Austin, Texas.
“Keiffer  Mitchell is one of Maryland’s most respected public servants and political professionals,” BGR Group President Erskine Wells said in the announcement. “He and his  family have a distinguished history of service in the state. His experience and credibility in Annapolis  and across the state will help BGR clients understand the issues, build durable relationships, and  achieve results.”
Mitchell’s grandfather, Clarence Mitchell Jr., was a prominent lobbyist for the NAACP and his great-uncle was Rep. Parren Mitchell. An uncle, Clarence M. Mitchell III, served in the General Assembly, as did Clarence M. Mitchell IV. Keiffer Mitchell served on the Baltimore City Council from 1995 to 2007, when he ran unsuccessfully for mayor. He served one term in the House of Delegates, from 2010 to 2014.
Mitchell, a Democrat, then became an adviser to Hogan, a Republican, serving variously as a senior adviser, chief legislative officer and, briefly, as acting chief of staff. He left the Hogan administration in 2022 and joined BGR.
“I am proud to lead BGR’s  expansion in Maryland at a moment when businesses are looking for sophisticated guidance there,”  Mitchell said in the statement from the firm.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: What if there were no trash to pick up?
description: Call it waste management, trash disposal or sanitary engineering, garbage removal is still one of those unpleasant but necessary services for maintaining public health and welfare. You can ignore the men and women who do most of the dirty work for us. But trash doesn’t disappear on its own. The armies of trash haulers who […]
text:
Call it waste management, trash disposal or sanitary engineering, garbage removal is still one of those unpleasant but necessary services for maintaining public health and welfare.
You can ignore the men and women who do most of the dirty work for us. But trash doesn’t disappear on its own. The armies of trash haulers who regularly empty our waste and recyclables bins into the hoppers of their massive trucks deserve some respect and gratitude.

Judy Benson 

Tired of being largely unrecognized, unappreciated and condescended to, Montreal trash hauler Simon Paré-Poupart put a spotlight on the hard work he’s been doing for 20 years in the new book Trash! A Garbageman’s Story. His insights are worth noting as the 10th annual #DontTrashLISound campaign gets underway along the Connecticut shoreline.
The campaign by Connecticut Sea Grant and Save the Sound consists of beach cleanups and public messaging about avoiding single-use plastics and reducing the flow of all debris into Long Island Sound. It begins Aug. 8 with a cleanup of Fort Trumbull State Park and the surrounding New London neighborhood —a fitting location given the fort’s role in the Revolutionary War and the nation’s 250th anniversary —and will end Sept. 19 (International Coastal Cleanup Day) with a cleanup on Long Wharf Drive in New Haven.
In his book, Paré-Poupart describes the rough comradery he shares with his co-workers, the daily hazards of injury by nails or glass, flies in the summer, ice in the winter and smells all year long that he has become immune to but carries with him after his workday is done. The physical tolls of the job are many.
Yet Paré-Poupart takes pride in his work as an expression of an ethic he wishes more people would espouse.
“I have the soul of a ragpicker,” he writes.
He regularly finds items in the trash to keep or sell. He considers himself a devotee of freeganism, which advocates rescuing, repairing or sharing cast-offs as an act of protest against consumerism. Two decades of close contact with the excessive waste output of capitalist culture have made him so. He doesn’t view our current throwaway habits as a fait accompli, though. We can and should do better. Folk singer Pete Seeger perhaps laid out the challenge best in the chorus to his 1969 song, “Garbage”:

Garbage (garbage, garbage, garbage) Garbage!
We’re filling up the sea with garbage (garbage…)
What will we do when there’s no place left
To put all the garbage? (garbage…)

I hope you will join us in volunteering at Fort Trumbull Aug. 8, or at another of the many cleanups during the #DontTrashLISound campaign. If you can’t make a cleanup, pick up litter in your own community. But let’s also think about what we can do to produce less trash and give some love to the Simon Paré-Pouparts of our neighborhoods.
To register for the Aug. 8 cleanup at Fort Trumbull State Park, 90 Walbach St., New London, or another cleanup, visit: www.savethesound.org/2026cleanups/. Trash buckets, gloves and grabbers will be provided.
Judy Benson is the communications coordinator at Connecticut Sea Grant, based at the Avery Point campus of the University of Connecticut in Groton.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT must no longer delay compassion at the end of life
description: The role of government should not be to prescribe one universally acceptable way to die.
text:
No one wants to think about how life ends.
We celebrate medical breakthroughs that help us live longer and healthier lives, but we rarely talk about what happens when medicine reaches its limits. For thousands of Connecticut families every year, that conversation eventually becomes unavoidable.
Terminal illness has a way of stripping away certainty. It can rob people of their independence, their comfort, and, in many cases, the ability to make even the simplest decisions for themselves. Hospice and palliative care provide invaluable support and relieve suffering for many patients. Yet despite remarkable advances in end-of-life care, there remain some people whose physical suffering cannot be adequately relieved and whose final wish is simply to have control over their own dying.
For those individuals, Connecticut should finally enact a medical aid in dying law.
This issue has been debated at the State Capitol for years. Bills have been introduced repeatedly, received heartfelt testimony from patients, families, physicians, and advocates, and then quietly faded without becoming law. Meanwhile, Connecticut residents facing terminal illnesses continue to have fewer end-of-life options than people living in a growing number of other states.
This conversation is often misunderstood.
Medical aid in dying is not euthanasia. Under proposals considered in Connecticut and laws enacted elsewhere, the patient — not the physician — must make the request and self-administer the prescribed medication. Eligibility is limited to mentally capable adults diagnosed with a terminal illness and an expected prognosis of six months or less. Multiple safeguards are built into these laws to ensure decisions are voluntary and informed.
Perhaps more importantly, no one is compelled to participate.
Patients who oppose medical aid in dying because of religious, moral, or personal beliefs would never be required to choose it. Physicians who object would not be obligated to prescribe it. Healthcare systems could establish policies consistent with their values.
The law simply recognizes that people facing the end of life do not all share the same beliefs – or the same experience of suffering.
For many of us, personal autonomy is a guiding principle throughout healthcare. We have the legal right to refuse chemotherapy, decline surgery, or discontinue life-sustaining treatment, even when those decisions may hasten death. We honor advance directives because we believe competent adults should decide what kind of medical care they receive.
Why should that principle disappear when someone is dying from an incurable illness?
Reasonable people can disagree on this issue. Some believe that life’s natural course should never be intentionally shortened, regardless of the circumstances. Those convictions deserve respect. They are deeply held and often rooted in faith or philosophy.
But in a diverse society, one person’s beliefs should not determine another person’s most intimate medical decisions.
Compassion does not require agreement. It requires recognizing that suffering is deeply personal.
For one patient, dignity may mean pursuing every possible treatment until the very end. For another, dignity may mean spending precious final weeks at home with family instead of enduring prolonged physical decline that offers no hope of recovery. Neither choice diminishes the value of life.
Too often, discussions about medical aid in dying become dominated by hypothetical fears rather than the real experiences of terminally ill patients. The overwhelming majority of people will never request this option. Even among those who qualify in states where it is legal, many never take the medication. For some, simply knowing the option exists provides peace of mind during an otherwise frightening time.
That peace has value.
Medical aid in dying is not about choosing death over life. It is about choosing how to live the final chapter of life when death is already approaching and medicine can no longer change the outcome.
Connecticut has long been a leader in patient-centered healthcare. Our state has embraced advance directives, hospice care, and palliative medicine because we recognize that caring for patients means honoring both their medical needs and their personal values. Medical aid in dying is a natural extension of that philosophy.
The role of government should not be to prescribe one universally acceptable way to die. It should be to establish thoughtful safeguards while respecting the deeply personal decisions that belong to patients, their loved ones, and their healthcare providers.
Every legislative session that passes without action means more Connecticut families endure heartbreaking circumstances without access to an option available elsewhere. The debate has been thorough. The testimony has been heard. The need has not disappeared simply because the legislation has stalled.
None of us can prevent death. What we can do is ensure that when cure is no longer possible, compassion remains.
Connecticut lawmakers should finally pass a carefully crafted medical aid in dying law — not because every resident will choose it, but because every terminally ill resident deserves the dignity of having that choice.
Erin Mahoney lives in Avon.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Candidates for CT’s 1st Congressional District clash in fiery debate
description: U.S. Rep. John Larson, Luke Bronin, Jillian Gilchrest and Ruth Fortune faced off in a debate more about the political moment than policy.
text:
In a debate focused heavily on the unprecedented political moment rather than policy, U.S. Rep. John Larson defended his nearly three decades in Congress as his three challengers sought to make the case for new leadership amid some fiery exchanges. 
Tuesday night’s hour-long, taped debate hosted by WTNH News 8 swung between attacks on Larson and on former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, the two well-financed candidates in the race who have been dominating the airwaves in the final weeks before the Aug. 11 primary.
The first half of the debate focused on “one of the central questions of this election, which is whether there should be a new face of the 1st District,” as the moderators put it. Larson and his challengers fielded questions about the dynamics of the first primary in 28 years for the Hartford-based seat, which also put Larson’s tenure under a microscope.
But Bronin, the party-endorsed candidate, also took regular blows from Larson, West Hartford Rep. Jillian Gilchrest and Hartford Board of Education member Ruth Fortune.
The four candidates had appeared once previously at an NBC Connecticut televised forum in early July. But this was the first time they took part in a debate where they could directly respond to one another’s claims and criticisms.

U.S. Rep. John Larson, D-1st District, addresses former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin as state Rep. Jillian Gilchrest, D-West Hartford, and Hartford Board of Education member Ruth Fortune look on at a Democratic 1st Congressional District Primary debate in New Haven on Wednesday, July 28, 2026. Credit: WTNH NEWS 8

From the outset, Larson’s three opponents sought to make the case that someone new should represent Connecticut’s 1st District in Congress and, more broadly, vented their frustration with the Democratic Party for standing up, or not, to President Donald Trump.
Larson, who wouldn’t say whether he was running for his last term, said his main focus is ultimately on Trump. He has sought to push back against criticism that he and other Democrats in Congress aren’t doing enough to take on the administration. He noted the articles of impeachment he filed against Trump over his handling of the war in Iran.
“As I’ve said, many times, this seat will be open soon enough, but we’re in the middle of a crisis,” Larson said. “My quarrel is not with any of these candidates on the stage. My quarrel is with Donald Trump, and that’s who I’m going to continue to take on.”
But he and the other candidates sparred on various issues and over how Democrats can take on the Trump administration over the course of the hour-long debate.
At times, it got personal.
Bronin criticized Larson for not being able to move the needle on his signature bill, the “Social Security 2100 Act,” over the past decade since he introduced it. He noted that the bill didn’t advance even when Democrats controlled all of Congress and the White House.

U.S. Rep. John Larson, D-1st District, former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin and Hartford Board of Education member Ruth Fortune at a Democratic 1st Congressional District Primary debate in New Haven on Wednesday, July 28, 2026. Credit: WTNH NEWS 8

The former mayor also highlighted a bill that Larson voted against that raised Social Security benefits for tens of thousands of public service retirees and their families in Connecticut. Larson explained that he didn’t support the bill because it wasn’t paid for, but that his own legislation sought to repeal those provisions by having higher earners pay more.
“Well, first and foremost, Luke, I didn’t hear you saying anything about that when we were delivering billions to your community, that you needed the bailout from the governor, when you needed the bailout from the General Assembly and from the United States Congress,” Larson countered.
Bronin pushed back on Larson’s claim that his Social Security bill will be a top priority in the first 100 days of the next Congress if Democrats win back the House. 
“I think to say that it’s going to become law in the first 100 days of the next Congress when Donald Trump is in the White House, I think is not being honest with voters,” Bronin argued.
Bronin’s own record came under scrutiny at various points. He defended his time as mayor of Hartford at a time when the city was on the verge of bankruptcy. But his opponents argued that came at the cost of unions.
“We made some difficult decisions for our city,” Bronin said, adding that unions contributed in a major way. “We were able to get a city stable for the first time in a long time.”

State Rep. Jillian Gilchrest, D-West Hartford, speaks as U.S. Rep. John Larson, D-1st District, and party-endorsed Democrat Luke Bronin look on at a Democratic 1st Congressional District Primary debate in New Haven on Wednesday, July 28, 2026. Credit: WTNH NEWS 8

When asked to grade Bronin’s time as mayor, Bronin’s opponents gave him a smattering of average scores. Fortune gave him some grace and a “B,” saying “he did the best he could at the time.” Gilchrest, who gave Bronin a “C,” noted that the job is mayor is different than that of a member of Congress, though she took a shot at Bronin, saying he’s “really good at politics.”
Larson argued that he knows the building trades would have given Bronin an “F.” Larson has made his support from labor unions a centerpiece of his campaign, with dozens of endorsements. Bronin highlighted the endorsements he has from some local affiliates, such as public employees and firefighters.
Larson’s own personal assessment of Bronin as mayor? “C-minus.”
That dug up another quick back-and-forth between the two. Bronin reminded Larson that at the end of Bronin’s second term in 2023, Larson called him the “best mayor in the country.”
“I appreciated the partnership we had, and throughout this campaign, I’ve been respectful, because I do respect you, and I respect your service,” Bronin said. “But I’m proud of the work that we did in Hartford through some of the city’s toughest times, from bankruptcy through a global pandemic.”
But that brought up a raw moment from Larson, and he echoed Gilchrest’s earlier retort that Bronin is a savvy politician.
“You’re good at politics, but you can’t keep your word. And when you look somebody in the eye and you make a commitment to them, and you shake their hand, and you tell them you’re with him, and when you donate to their campaign, that’s not keeping your word,” Larson pressed. “And you’re entitled to do whatever you want, and I was proud to work with you, and I was proud when I called you the best mayor as well, because of all the help that we were able to collaborate and bring together. But it wasn’t just you … and especially in Congress, your words do matter.”
While they trained their fire on Larson and the need for change throughout the course of the debate, Gilchrest and Fortune sought to make the case that Bronin is largely indistinguishable from the 14-term congressman.

Hartford Board of Education member Ruth Fortune, right, speaks while state Rep. Jillian Gilchrest, D-West Hartford, U.S. Rep. John Larson, D-1st District, and former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin look on at a Democratic 1st Congressional District Primary debate in New Haven on Wednesday, July 28, 2026. Credit: WTNH NEWS 8

“They are two sides of the same establishment coin,” Fortune said. “Congressman Larson has been protected by the Democratic establishment for 28 years, and now Luke is their endorsed candidate.”
Gilchrest was critical both of the lack of action on Social Security in Congress as well as how she envisions Bronin handling the issue. 
“I don’t trust that Luke Bronin is going to be the champion of Social Security when he is bought by the billionaire class, who stand to make millions off of privatizing Social Security and who would never want to see their wages taxed at a higher rate,” she said.
Bronin pushed back that he’s introduced tax proposals when he first launched his campaign for Congress that would close loopholes in the tax codes and “make wealthiest Americans and corporations pay more.”
The moderators also asked Bronin why he’s challenging Larson for a seat in Congress when he’s previously had interest in running for governor of Connecticut.
“What changed is that Donald Trump won reelection for a second time, and then we saw a Democratic Party struggle to bring enough energy and clarity to that fight in this moment,” Bronin said. “And I think we would be a stronger Democratic Party if more of our leadership recognized that part of leadership is knowing when it’s time to pass the torch.”
Fortune, who is also an estate attorney, made a similar point about running for the seat now versus waiting another two years.
“Congressman Larson likes to say the seat will open up soon enough,” Fortune said. “The idea of waiting your turn is why we’re in this mess in the first place. Congress does not have an experience deficit. Congress has a perspective deficit. Congress has a courage deficit.”

Party-endorsed Democrat Luke Bronin speaks as state Rep. Jillian Gilchrest, D-West Hartford, U.S. Rep. John Larson, D-1st District, and Hartford Board of Education member Ruth Fortune look on at a Democratic 1st Congressional District Primary debate in New Haven on Wednesday, July 28, 2026. Credit: WTNH NEWS 8

They were all asked whether they’d support term limits for members of Congress. Bronin and Fortune said they support term limits. Larson said elections every two years essentially serve as them.
While she’s open to such restrictions, Gilchrest argued those things don’t matter unless there’s campaign finance reform.
“I’m open to a mandatory retirement age, and I’m also open to term limits, but both of those things don’t work if you don’t get money out of politics, because the same special interests are going to be buying the candidates who are elected,” Gilchrest said.
Fundraising has been one of the biggest sticking points in the race and played out again at Tuesday’s debate. And Larson and Bronin have been the two biggest beneficiaries of money, while they continue to spar over where it comes from. Gilchrest and Fortune are much farther behind.
Larson has taken aim at Bronin for getting a large portion of his individual donations from billionaires and other executives connected to the private equity and tech industries. (Larson has also received some similar donations from billionaires.) Meanwhile, Bronin has criticized the congressman for getting half of his total fundraising from political action committees, including corporate and union PACs.
Bronin argued there’s “a world of difference” between a corporation making contributions and “and an actual human being who’s making a decision to support a candidate for a number of reasons.”
Gilchrest argued that “both men have crossed the line” on where they get their money from but took on Bronin specifically for trying to make a distinction between the types of money.
“We’ve all heard the phrase ‘Thou doth protest too much,'” Gilchrest said, noting Bronin’s own fundraising from CEOs of corporations, hedge funds and AI data centers. “What do these folks think they’re getting with a Luke Bronin?”
“These two men haven’t raised money in this race,” she continued. “They’ve been bought by the billionaire class and by corporations.”
Larson said he agreed with Gilchrest’s assessment, saying the House had previously voted on campaign finance reform multiple times while Democrats were in power but the Senate didn’t take it up.

State Rep. Jillian Gilchrest, D-West Hartford, U.S. Rep. John Larson, D-1st District, former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin and Hartford Board of Education member Ruth Fortune at a Democratic 1st Congressional District Primary debate in New Haven on Wednesday, July 28, 2026. Credit: WTNH NEWS 8

The four candidates have little daylight between them on major issues, including immigration enforcement, health care and efforts to rein in Trump on the war in Iran.
But they sought to make some policy distinctions, particularly when asked by one of the moderators if they could name two instances when they would have voted differently than Larson.
Both Fortune and Gilchrest named the same votes, saying they wouldn’t have supported a House resolution that honored the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk or voted against a recent amendment that would have cut off more U.S. aid to Israel.
When he voted against that amendment to a federal spending bill, Larson had argued that it would have exacerbated issues such as blocked aid to Palestinian refugees and put “a two-state solution further out of reach.”
Bronin also criticized Larson’s vote on the Kirk resolution but took aim at the congressman’s vote in 2024 against the Social Security Fairness Act, a bipartisan bill signed into law by President Joe Biden that raised Social Security benefits for tens of thousands of people in Connecticut.
It eliminated a pair of provisions — the Windfall Elimination Provision and the Government Pension Offset — that reduced payments to certain beneficiaries as well as spouses and surviving family members who also collected a pension from jobs that were not covered by Social Security. They can include teachers, police officers, firefighters and government employees.
Larson was one of a few Democrats to oppose it because the law did not include an offset similar to that in his own Social Security reform bill, which would have temporarily removed those provisions. His own bill, “Social Security 2100 Act,” would have funded the repeal of WEP and GPO through raising the income cap on taxable earnings for Social Security as well as provide an across-the-board hike in Social Security benefits by 2%.
When asked about whether he regrets any votes, Larson said there’s “probably a lot of votes over a 20-year period” but didn’t name any specifics. “An important thing with voting is lead with your heart first.”
There were also small contrasts among the four when it came to the Middle East conflict and whether the U.S. should keep providing funding to Israel.
Both Gilchrest and Fortune called Israel’s war in Gaza a “genocide” and said they don’t support the U.S. sending additional aid. Gilchrest said she also wanted to see the military’s overall budget reduced.
Bronin toed the line more on the issue, saying he’s against taxpayers’ money going toward funding offensive military aid. He said he supports “defenses for civilians that protect civilian life against rockets and missiles and drones” as well as more humanitarian aid for Gaza.
Larson argued that Trump himself needs to enforce his deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu “so that there is no need to send extra weapons to Israel.” He defended his recent vote to ensure Israel gets aid from U.S. as well as humanitarian aid for the Palestinians.
The debate ended with a quick lightning round with some eyebrow-raising questions. But it was the question about “who is one current Republican you admire” that appeared to stump the congressman.
Larson labored over the question, saying, “It’s a very small group of people to pick from.” It seemed like he was going to mention a member on the House Ways and Means Committee he’s a part of, but the moderators ultimately moved on without an answer.
Fortune said “Honestly, none,” while Gilchrest and Bronin named Republicans they worked with in their separate roles.
On whom they support in the Democratic primary for governor, Fortune and Gilchrest said they support state Rep. Josh Elliott, while Larson and Bronin back Gov. Ned Lamont for a third term — though Bronin wasn’t direct at first when he answered, saying he will support the “endorsed Democratic slate.” Lamont won the party’s endorsement at the nominating convention, as did Bronin in a separate convention.
In a question about age unrelated to this particular campaign, the hosts noted that U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., will be up for reelection in 2028 at the age of 82. Larson’s three challengers ultimately answered affirmatively that Blumenthal’s current term should be his last.
Much like Larson’s own defense for seeking another term to Congress, he replied: “It’s up to him.”

description: Marcye Scott, the daughter of the late Congressman David Scott, fell short of winning a special election to finish her father’s term in office and will face former Gwinnett County School Board chair Everton Blair in a runoff next month.  The Associated Press made the call at around 8:45 p.m. Tuesday. As of late Tuesday […]
text:
Everton Blair and Marcye Scott advanced to a runoff in the special election in Georgia's 13th Congressional District. Photo credit: Ross Williams and Jill Nolin/Georgia RecorderMarcye Scott, the daughter of the late Congressman David Scott, fell short of winning a special election to finish her father’s term in office and will face former Gwinnett County School Board chair Everton Blair in a runoff next month. 
The Associated Press made the call at around 8:45 p.m. Tuesday. As of late Tuesday night, Scott led with 46% of the vote, according to unofficial results from the Georgia Secretary of State’s Office. Blair came in second with about 37% of the vote. 
The two Democrats will face off on Aug. 25 and that winner will serve a few months before the next term begins in January. State Rep. Jasmine Clark, who did not run in the special election, won the May primary and is expected to easily beat her Republican opponent in the safe Democratic seat in November and represent the district for a full term starting next year.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Blair, who placed third in the May primary for a full term, touted his experience in elected office and as the only candidate in the special election runoff who lives in the district and said he is ready to serve the district immediately. He said that he had “not seen anything but a continuation of what has been” from Scott, and that as a progressive, he’ll continue to fight against the current administration and work to lower living costs in the district.
“I’m the only Democrat that has been in the community representing us and serving this district in the capacities that have been most significant for everyday people,” Blair said.
Scott could not be reached for a comment Tuesday night. In a social media post, she thanked her supporters but said “the work isn’t finished.”
“I am incredibly grateful to everyone who believed in this campaign and helped us reach this moment. From our volunteers and supporters to every voter who put their trust in me — thank you,” Scott wrote.
In a previous interview, Scott said she entered the race with a focus on providing stability for the district’s constituents, saying that she would focus on ensuring that funding for earmarked projects that her late father requested reaches the district. Despite not living within its boundaries, she said that she’s known the district since it was created in 2002 when she first campaigned alongside her father, and that she already has established relationships with local leaders.
Scott’s father died in April after serving in Congress for more than two decades and left the seat unexpectedly vacant after he had qualified in early March to serve another term. 
The day before the special election, Scott said in a heartfelt social media post that running for her father’s seat “has been one of the most meaningful — and emotional — journeys of [her] life,” pointing to stories constituents recalled of her father on the campaign trail.
“I never imagined walking this path without my Daddy physically by my side. I missed my father’s guidance, his wisdom, and the quiet confidence he always gave me,” she said. “But everywhere I traveled across Georgia’s 13th Congressional District, I was reminded that I was not walking alone.”

title: Idaho Democrat David Roth ends campaign for US Senate seat held by Risch
description: Idaho Democrat David Roth announced Tuesday he is ending his campaign for U.S. Senate.  The candidate had faced pressure from some prominent Democrats to drop out and rally behind independent candidate Todd Achilles. However, Roth had previously told the Idaho Capital Sun he had no intention of supporting Achilles.  Roth won his primary contest in […]
text:
From left, incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, Democrat David Roth, and independent Todd Achilles.Idaho Democrat David Roth announced Tuesday he is ending his campaign for U.S. Senate. 
The candidate had faced pressure from some prominent Democrats to drop out and rally behind independent candidate Todd Achilles. However, Roth had previously told the Idaho Capital Sun he had no intention of supporting Achilles. 
Roth won his primary contest in May and was slated to face incumbent Idaho Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, independents Achilles and Natalie Fleming, and Libertarian Matt Loesby in the November general election. 
“I have concluded that I can make the greatest difference by focusing my time and energy on helping Democrats win up and down the ballot and in communities across Idaho,” Roth said in an emailed statement Tuesday.
His statement did not include a mention of Achilles or any other candidate in the race. Roth could not be reached for comment.
Roth, 44, is an Idaho Falls resident and a consultant. He previously ran for the state Legislature in 2020, and for federal elected positions in 2022 and 2024. In 2022, he became the first openly gay candidate in Idaho to win a primary contest for a federal position, he has said. 
“I hope this campaign showed LGBTQ+ Idahoans, especially young people, that they belong in our politics, their voices matter, and no office should ever feel beyond their reach,” he said in his statement.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Roth faced pressure to rally around Achilles, but did not endorse the independent

In June, former Idaho Democratic U.S. Rep. Larry LaRocco wrote opinion pieces in local newspapers, including the Idaho Statesman and Lewiston Tribune, calling for Roth to drop out and rally behind Achilles. LaRocco argued Achilles had a better chance to defeat the longtime incumbent. 
On July 8, Ada County Democrats sent a letter to Roth also encouraging him to drop out, the Spokesman-Review reported.  
Achilles told the Sun in a July 7 interview, “I think if David really wants to make change, there’s an opportunity to to work with us or work with others to to make that change. I think just being a name on a ballot isn’t good for Idaho.” 
However, Roth told the Idaho Capital Sun in a July 8 interview, that he disagreed with the reasoning behind the calls to rally around Achilles in an attempt to defeat Risch. 
“Prior to the filing deadline, there was discussion about whether or not we should just all rally behind the independent,” Roth said, “but the reality is, I met with Todd, and we talked about it, and we’re just too far away on issues that I think are absolutely critical to moving our country forward, and so we decided to run the primary.” 
Roth said he wanted to push forward progressive ideas, such a single-payer health care system and more substantial government housing investments. He said his stances on these issues were too different from Achilles, who generally has taken a more moderate approach. 
Roth’s campaign this year has raised about $8,600, according to Federal Election Commission data as of Tuesday. The Achilles campaign has raised more than $692,000, and Risch’s warchest has surpassed $3 million. 
“The campaign may be ending, but the work continues,” Roth said in his statement. “I remain committed to strengthening our party and electing leaders who will fight for Idaho families.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota governor wins Republican nomination to seek his own term after succeeding Noem
description: South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden won the Republican Party’s nomination for governor Tuesday in a runoff election, earning the chance to seek his own four years in office after filling out the remainder of former Gov. Kristi Noem’s last term. The Associated Press called the race at 8:08 p.m. Central with Rhoden receiving about 70% […]
text:
South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden attends the Sept. 9, 2025, grand opening of High Plains Processing in Mitchell. (Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden won the Republican Party’s nomination for governor Tuesday in a runoff election, earning the chance to seek his own four years in office after filling out the remainder of former Gov. Kristi Noem’s last term.
The Associated Press called the race at 8:08 p.m. Central with Rhoden receiving about 70% of the votes in partial returns, and Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden receiving about 30%. 
Doeden and Rhoden made it into the runoff by finishing first and second in a four-way June 2 primary election. Nobody in that race reached 35%, which triggered the first use of a 1985 state law requiring a runoff when no candidate meets that threshold in a statewide primary.


A turnout percentage for the runoff was not yet available, but advance voting numbers were roughly equal to the primary, which ended with 43% turnout among Republicans. Only registered Republicans were allowed to vote in the runoff.
Rhoden will face Democratic nominee Dan Ahlers, a former state legislator, in the Nov. 3 general election. The last time South Dakota elected a Democratic governor was 52 years ago in 1974.
Gov. Kristi Noem kickstarted the Republican primary race when she resigned in January 2025 to accept a job in President Donald Trump’s administration. Rhoden was Noem’s lieutenant governor and was automatically promoted to serve the last two years of her second term.
U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, R-South Dakota, entered the race as the presumptive frontrunner and led in several early polls. He had the most campaign money at his disposal and the highest statewide profile due to his four terms in the U.S. House, his previous service on the state Public Utilities Commission, and his 20-plus years of involvement in politics.
On primary election night, Doeden — an Aberdeen businessman who had never previously sought elected office — stunned the political establishment by finishing first at 31%, followed by Rhoden at 25%, Johnson at 23% and state House Speaker Jon Hansen at 21%. Johnson and Hansen not only failed to make the runoff but will leave office when their respective terms in the U.S. and state House end in January.
From the June 2 primary through the July 13 registration deadline for Tuesday’s runoff, the number of registered Republicans in the state grew by more than 7,300. One of those new Republicans was Alfred Slaathaug, of rural Brandon, who said in a polling-place interview that he had switched his registration from the Democratic Party.
“I changed my party just to vote for Rhoden,” Slaathaug said. “I don’t trust Doeden at all.”
 Doeden ran on shifting anti-property tax pledges

Doeden spent at least $4 million of his own money in the race, according to campaign finance reports. The 51-year-old built his fortune by owning vehicle dealerships and diversifying into other businesses and real estate. He has also described himself as an investor in bitcoin, a type of digital money secured with encryption technology.
Doeden tried to position himself early in the campaign as the most pro-Trump candidate, often mentioning Trump in advertisements and appearances — although not as much in recent months as Trump’s national approval rating fell below 40%. 

Republican candidate for governor Toby Doeden gives a speech to a room full of supporters in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, on June 2, 2026. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)

Doeden also ran on an anti-property tax platform, pledging at times to eliminate property taxes, at other times to phase them out, and saying earlier this month that his pledge applied only to homeowners. 
Homeowner property taxes rose sharply in parts of South Dakota as homebuyers flocked to the state and drove up prices during and immediately after the COVID-19 pandemic, when Noem invited people to relocate for the state’s freedom from mask mandates, business restrictions and other pandemic precautions.
South Dakotans paid more than $1.8 billion in property taxes last year, including $815 million by homeowners, but none of that money goes to state government, which is primarily funded by sales tax revenue. Property taxes go to schools, counties, cities and other local governments. 
Searchlight asked Doeden in a May podcast interview how he would replace lost property tax revenue for local governments.
“Once the economy starts growing, and it will; once I start collecting external revenue, which we will; and once I cut all the fat and pork out of our state budget, you are going to see, very quickly, within a matter of a couple years, a significant amount of annual budget surpluses,” Doeden said. “And yes, I will use that money to target the phase-out of things like property tax.”
A Sioux Falls voter, Mandy Berkhof, said Tuesday at her polling place that she voted for Doeden in the primary and the runoff.
“I just feel like he is going to bring a lot to South Dakota communities, things that we need and want, a little bit more than the other person,” Berkhof said.
 Rhoden criticized Doeden, touted own record

Rhoden said eliminating local property tax revenue would require the state to replace it, and he said that would blow a $1.8 billion hole in the state budget. The Rhoden campaign launched a “Reckless Toby Doeden” website featuring those assertions during the runoff campaign.
Those criticisms resonated with 55-year-old Scott Isburg, who said Tuesday at his polling place in Pierre that he voted for Rhoden in the primary and the runoff. Isburg said he trusted Rhoden to “run government in a way that’ll actually work.”
“I was a little bit concerned with some of the potential policies from Toby, if they would work or not,” Isburg said.
SD runoff voters talk decision-making, party switching, ‘the lesser of two evils’

Rhoden also aired advertisements during the runoff campaign about Doeden’s lack of past involvement in Republican politics, including an audio recording of Doeden saying “I think I may have even voted for Barack Obama.” Doeden has since denied voting for Obama.
Aside from those criticisms of his opponent, Rhoden ran on his record from nearly 18 months as governor, which has included working with legislators to sign several major bills into law.
Those include laws capturing revenue from sales tax increases to reduce homeowner property taxes, a law banning the use of a legal procedure known as eminent domain to gain land access for carbon capture pipelines, and a law funding construction of a $650 million replacement for the oldest parts of the state’s 145-year-old penitentiary.
“Good policy makes good politics,” Rhoden said while launching his campaign in November.
Sioux Falls voter Susan DeSautel said Tuesday at her polling place that Rhoden’s experience was an important factor in her support for him.
“I know there are a lot of people who like Doeden. I think they want somebody totally from left field, who’s not a politician,” DeSautel said. “And I understand that, but you’ve got to have some experience as a politician. We need that in a governor.”
Before Rhoden served as lieutenant governor and governor, he was a rancher, custom welder and legislator. He lives on a ranch near Union Center in the western part of the state.
If he wins in November, the 67-year-old Rhoden could potentially choose to run again four years later for what would amount to a third term. The state constitution includes term limits, saying “no person shall be elected to more than two consecutive terms as governor,” but Rhoden is serving his current stint as governor through the line of succession rather than direct election to the job.
South Dakota Searchlight’s John Hult, Joshua Haiar, Makenzie Huber and Meghan O’Brien contributed to this report.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Social workers eye compact to erase licensing hurdles
authors: Katie Castellani | State House News Service
description: SOCIAL WORKERS IN and outside of Massachusetts could see clients across state lines more easily under a policy senators embedded within the chamber’s economic development package. The Senate adopted a […]
text:
SOCIAL WORKERS IN and outside of Massachusetts could see clients across state lines more easily under a policy senators embedded within the chamber’s economic development package.
The Senate adopted a Sen. Robyn Kennedy amendment to the policy-heavy $575 million economic development bill (S 3178, as amended) that would pave the way for Massachusetts to join a multistate social worker licensure compact.
“It is critical that we support the social work workforce in our state to give them all the tools they need to operate here while also ensuring clients are protected and can continue care with providers they trust,” Kennedy said on the Senate floor.  
The proposal is meant to improve an individual’s access to care when cross state lines. Qualified social workers would also face fewer financial and administrative burdens associated with acquiring licenses to practice in other states. Social workers with a multistate compact license would be able to practice in other jurisdictions that are part of the compact. And the multistate license goes both ways: those in other states that are part of the compact could treat patients who relocated to Massachusetts.
Currently, social workers have to apply for an additional license in the state where their client has relocated to in order to continue seeing them. It’s often an expensive and lengthy process, which Kennedy said puts vulnerable clients at risk of losing continual access to care they need, particularly those who move out of state for college, or patients from other states undergoing medical treatments in Massachusetts. Members of the military, and their family, who frequently move can also benefit from the uninterrupted access to care the compact intends to support.
“That continuity of care is just really what’s at the core of this to be able to say ‘you can continue, you know, if you’re having a an episode or if you’re having, you experience a stressor and you want to be able to have a conversation with your clinician, you should be able to do that,'” Kennedy told the News Service.
Kennedy said 30 other states, including the other New England states, have joined the compact.
The amendment’s language is similar to legislation Kennedy and Rep. James O’Day filed (S 252 / H 380). Kennedy’s bill has been pending in the Senate Ways and Means Committee since November. The Joint Committee on Consumer Protection and Professional Licensure advanced a redrafted version (H 5272) of O’Day’s bill that has been in the House Ways and Means Committee since March. 
The Massachusetts Chapter of the National Association of Social Workers, which has more than 6,000 members, supports the Bay State joining the compact. During a September committee hearing on the legislation Rebekah Gewirtz, the group’s executive director, said the organization has heard from “so many” members who want Massachusetts to join the compact.
Gewirtz said that Massachusetts joining the compact can help fill in gaps in access to care created by shortage of behavioral health workers.
“There’s a real recognition across the field, across [National Association of Social Workers], across social workers at large that this is a problem when people can’t gain access or maintain access to the people who are helping them and supporting them in their lives,” Gewirtz told the News Service. 
Social workers can offer almost identical one-on-one counseling as a psychologist, Gerwirtz said. Social workers usually focus more on factors in a client’s broader environment like housing and financial challenges that may contribute to them seeking care. Meanwhile, psychologists hone in on someone’s clinical mental health diagnosis. Still, not all social workers focus on therapy as some also connect people with community resources they may need. 
Senators also adopted an amendment from Sen. Cindy Creem allowing Massachusetts to enter a psychology interjurisdictional compact, which also seeks to provide patients with consistent access to care and address similar issues as the social worker compact. An adopted Sen. Sal DiDomenico amendment would include Massachusetts in the physical therapy interstate licensure compact. 
If enacted, social worker compact licenses won’t be available right away. Kennedy said a commission made up of representatives from other states that have adopted the compact is still meeting to finalize the compact’s terms and is expected to do so in the coming months.
Massachusetts joined the nurse licensure compact under the Legislature’s 2024 economic development bill. Activating that compact in Massachusetts has been stalled in the face of delays of getting required criminal background checks because of backlogs at the Federal Bureau of Investigations, according to a July 20 newsletter from the Massachusetts Health and Hospital Association. The association and the Organization of Nurse Leaders – New England wrote a letter to the Bay State’s congressional delegation asking them to back legislation that would streamline the federal criminal background check process.
A provision enacting the social worker licensure compact was included in the Committee on Economic Development and Emerging Technologies’ version of the economic development bill. The Joint Committee on Ways and Means cut the language from its redraft of the bill. Representatives did not include an amendment from O’Day enabling Massachusetts to join the compact in the House’s economic development bill (H 5576).
The policy is in play as both chambers’ economic development packages are destined for a conference committee where negotiators are tasked with finding common ground on the policies and spending senators and representatives have proposed.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC Senate approves controversial elections bill along party lines
description: The NC Senate moved swiftly to pass two elections bills Tuesday that would alter many aspects of voting from registration to ballot counting.  Republicans said the changes would enhance election security and improve election administration.  House Bill 834 focused mostly on ballot counting and voters supplying missing signatures. It passed the Senate unanimo[...]
text:
Voters trickle into the Durham County Main Library to cast their primary ballots on the first day of early voting on Feb. 12, 2026. (Photo: Brandon Kingdollar/NC Newsline)The NC Senate moved swiftly to pass two elections bills Tuesday that would alter many aspects of voting from registration to ballot counting. 
Republicans said the changes would enhance election security and improve election administration. 
House Bill 834 focused mostly on ballot counting and voters supplying missing signatures. It passed the Senate unanimously. 
Most of the debate and controversy centered on House Bill 958.  It was approved in a 28-13 party-line vote with Republicans supporting it and Democrats opposed. 
Among the controversial provisions in House Bill 958 are: 

Reducing early voting periods during primaries, primary runoffs and special elections from 17 days to 10 days.
Requiring state Auditor Dave Boliek to conduct post-election audits of county election systems. 
Using federal databases and information from other states to identify people who have died but remain on the voter rolls. 

As the vote was taken a few opponents sitting in the Senate gallery began to chant, “The people united will never be defeated.” The group was removed from the gallery.
The Senate votes on the bills came after leaders fast-tracked them through two committees on Tuesday. 
Sen. Warren Daniel, R-Burke, told the Senate Rules Committee the bills are “intended to aid in elections administration, as well as continue our efforts to secure and ensure election integrity in our elections.”
During the floor debate, Sen. Joyce Waddell, D-Mecklenburg, called the controversial bill “a power grab.” 
“This bill is protecting the people who are already in charge, and that shouldn’t be,” she said.
To counter Democrats’ arguments that Republicans have passed law after law to hinder voting, Sen. Benton Sawrey, R-Johnson, said the percentage of eligible voters who turn out for elections has increased since Republicans took control of the legislature. One of his comparisons was the 2002 midterm election turnout versus turnout in the 2022 midterm. 
“People have confidence to go vote when they know the election process works,” Sawrey said.
NC House passes its controversial elections bill with only GOP votes

Republicans passed a controversial law in 2024 that gave Republican North Carolina Auditor Boliek the power to appoint members of the state Board of Elections, taking that power away from Democratic Governor-elect Josh Stein. Boliek also appoints all county board of elections chairs. 
Sen. Val Applewhite, D-Cumberland, said voters didn’t elect Boliek to run elections. State and local elections boards already conduct audits. 
“Why is the bill voting to double down on top of the power he’s already been given?” she asked. “Why is he being given the power to walk into our county boards after every election and check their work?”
Warren said the audits will provide for continuous improvement. 
Sen. Jay Chaudhuri, D-Wake, argued that unreliable federal databases should not be used to flag dead voters. Instead, he said, the state should join ERIC, the Electronic Registration Information Center, an organization some states use to keep their voter rolls up to date.
Critics of an NC elections bill sit in the Senate gallery with Vote No signs on July 28, 2026. Some began chanting and were removed from the gallery as senators voted. (Photo: Claire Michal/NC Newsline)
None of the changes Senate Democrats proposed won approval from majority Republicans. They voted to sideline nearly a dozen Democratic amendments, including one that would allow the state to join ERIC and another requiring voters flagged as dead by  federal databases to be notified before they’re removed from the rolls. Sen. Mujtaba Mohammed, D-Mecklenburg, said eligible voters could be removed due to confusion over similar names, a known issue with the federal SAVE database.
Members of the public told the Senate Rules Committee bills are aimed at problems that don’t exist. They said the measure feeds into a false idea that elections are not secure and that large numbers of noncitizens or voters posing as people who have died are casting ballots. 
“What problems are these things supposed to fix?” asked Durham resident Karen Ziegler of the advocacy group Democracy Out Loud. “I am having less trust in you with each passing day.”
Bob Rodrigues of Wake County, a member of Democracy Out Loud, told the committee that truncating early voting will harm voters who work long shifts, travel, or work more than one job. 
“That seven days matters,” he said. 
Both bills must go back to the House for votes, potentially as soon as next week.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Judge won’t order state to implement expanded access to KidCare
description: A state judge has refused to order Florida health care officials to implement a 2023 law that would allow as many as 68,000 uninsured children to access subsidized health insurance coverage through the Florida KidCare program. Circuit Court Judge Joshua Hawkes in Tallahassee, appointed by Gov. Ron DeSantis, wrote in a four-page ruling that those […]
text:
Gov. Ron DeSantis signed into law a 2023 bill championed by legislative Republicans that expand access to the Florida KidCare program but has refused to implement the law. (Photo by Johner Images/Getty Images)A state judge has refused to order Florida health care officials to implement a 2023 law that would allow as many as 68,000 uninsured children to access subsidized health insurance coverage through the Florida KidCare program.
Circuit Court Judge Joshua Hawkes in Tallahassee, appointed by Gov. Ron DeSantis, wrote in a four-page ruling that those suing the state must first pursue their claim through a state administrative court.
This ruling is yet another setback to efforts to expand health care coverage to children, initially promoted by Republican legislative leaders, including Republican gubernatorial hopeful and former House Speaker Paul Renner, to make the state more affordable for working families.
The lawsuit was filed earlier this year against Florida Healthy Kids and the Agency for Health Care Administration by three Florida families with the help of Florida Health Justice and the National Health Law Program.
In addition to requiring those suing to first go through state administrative court, Hawkes said the lawsuit fell short of other legal requirements.
“While Petitioners may regard that decision as unfair, the Court does not find that they are without remedy, although the Legislature could have barred a remedy if it chose to. Instead, Petitioners simply do not have a cause of action in this Court regarding their coverage decisions,” Hawkes wrote, adding that state administrative court orders and agency final orders can be appealed to a state appellate court.
Florida Health Justice did not immediately respond to Florida Phoenix’s request for comment.
Hawkes in his decision agreed with the state that the Florida Healthy Kids Corp., whose board administers the Florida KidCare program along with the state, could not be sued for “failure to make health services available to any person.”
The ruling followed a court hearing Hawkes held on the case last week. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Florida KidCare is the state’s version of the federal Children’s Health Insurance Program, or CHIP. It’s an optional Medicaid expansion program for children aged 5-18 whose families earn too much to qualify for the traditional Medicaid program.
Unlike traditional Medicaid, which is free for enrollees, Florida KidCare enrollees who qualify for a subsidized plan are required to pay small monthly premiums; according to the website, it’s $15 or $20 a month per household. They also make co-payments for services.
Families lose access to the subsidized health insurance plan once their income exceeds 200% of the federal poverty level, or $54,640 for a three-person household. 
The 2023 law ostensibly allows a family of three to earn up to $81,960, or 300% of the federal poverty level, and continue to qualify for the children’s health insurance coverage.
Florida Health Justice failed to convince Hawkes the state was obligated to provide the coverage because the federal government had approved a Medicaid waiver submitted by the state to expand the program. 
That approval came Dec. 2, 2024, after the federal government passed a law requiring children participating in Medicaid and the state Children’s Health Insurance Program to remain enrolled in the programs for a year. The law was implemented through a rule finalized in 2025.
The state has filed three lawsuits in federal court over the continuous eligibility requirement.
It filed a different lawsuit in February that it subsequently withdrew.
‘Conversations with CMS’
AHCA Deputy Secretary for Medicaid Brian Meyer in April told members of a joint legislative spending panel that he was having “conversations with CMS about this, so we are actively trying to get to an agreeable place between both parties so we can move this program.”
CMS is the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
Meyer was getting pushback from Republican and Democratic members of the Joint Legislative Budget Commission who were pressing him about the DeSantis administration’s positions on children’s health insurance.
The administration has blamed the federal government for the failure to expand Florida KidCare and it has ignored the continuous coverage requirement, dropping children from the Florida KidCare program whose families didn’t pay premiums.
At one point, the state had removed in one year more than 43,000 children from the program whose family had not paid premiums. More than 17,000 of them were never re-enrolled.
State report: More than 43K children dropped from program for nonpayment

DeSantis administration gets pushback for its child health policies

The state has filed at least three challenges over the requirement, one of which, filed in Pensacola federal court, still is being litigated.

name: Washington State Standard
title: More than 40 WA legislators make bipartisan plea for developmental disabilities program
description: A bipartisan group of nearly four dozen Washington lawmakers is urging the state to maintain a program considered vital among parents of children with developmental disabilities.  The Parent to Parent program is threatened as the state faces another year of budget woes. Its future isn’t guaranteed past August, while Washington’s Department of Social and Heal[...]
text:
The dome at the Washington state Capitol. (Photo by Bill Lucia/Washington State Standard)A bipartisan group of nearly four dozen Washington lawmakers is urging the state to maintain a program considered vital among parents of children with developmental disabilities. 
The Parent to Parent program is threatened as the state faces another year of budget woes. Its future isn’t guaranteed past August, while Washington’s Department of Social and Health services assesses if it should be cut. 
In their Monday letter to Gov. Bob Ferguson and Department of Social and Health Services Secretary Angela Ramirez, the 44 lawmakers from the state House and Senate acknowledged the state’s fiscal challenges.
“However, we believe the Parent to Parent program represents exactly the kind of investment government should protect,” they wrote.
Spokespeople for Ferguson and Ramirez didn’t immediately provide comment.
Stacy Dym, executive director of The Arc of Washington State, said Tuesday the letter is a “clear indication of the widespread impact that Parent to Parent has.” Dym’s organization advocates for people with developmental disabilities, and oversees the statewide program under a contract with the Department of Social and Health Services.
Dym hopes Ferguson and Ramirez “will take note of this outpouring of support and reconsider how they prioritize limited state funding for our most vulnerable residents.”
Parent to Parent offers support for families of children with autism and other developmental disabilities. It pairs newer parents with more experienced ones to help guide them through the complicated system of resources. 
Families attest that the experience of raising a child with a developmental disability can be isolating, but this program provided them with much-needed community. It serves families in all of the state’s 39 counties, and gets tens of thousands of requests for help each year.
Parent to Parent costs $900,000 a year, and received funding in the current budget.  Advocates are shocked the program could suddenly be on the chopping block.

“Our goal is to meet the challenge of the moment in a way that sustainably protects core services and ensures that Washington has a solid financial foundation for the long-term,” spokesperson Jessica Nelson said in an email.
They argue the program’s low cost helps avert more costly interventions and improve outcomes. 
“Programs like Parent to Parent help families become stronger advocates for their children while reducing unnecessary frustration and helping connect them with the services they need,” the legislators wrote.
Ferguson has urged state agencies to look for spending cuts as Washington faces yet another potentially multibillion-dollar shortfall. He has specifically cited programs created or expanded after 2019 as possible targets for reductions. Parent to Parent wouldn’t seem to fit that description. 
State departments will make their funding requests to the governor in September ahead of his rollout of a two-year budget proposal in December. Lawmakers will consider his blueprint as they craft the state’s spending plan.
Advocates are frustrated at the prospect of the Parent to Parent program being cut outside of the legislative process, with no chance to provide public input.
