“Long-term care workers are critical in addressing the health needs of Washingtonians, especially as the number of people in need of long-term services and support grows due to age demographics and prevalence of disability,” the trio wrote. “We look forward to implementing the recommendations in this report and working together on improving credentialing processes.”
The auditor’s office has been reporting on this issue every couple years, consistently finding persistent challenges in the certification process, especially in testing.
“It sounds as if we have not made significant progress there,” Rep. Gerry Pollet, D-Seattle, said in a recent hearing on the audit.



Workforce shortage
In a symbol of the workforce shortage, one-third of Medicaid clients used 75% or less of their authorized long-term care in Washington’s 2024 fiscal year. Medicaid, the insurance program for low-income residents, is the largest payment source for long-term care. Other states’ aide shortages are far worse than Washington’s.
But it has still left employers here to resort to contracting with temporary staffing agencies, which is more expensive. By 2050, the state expects the number of Washingtonians needing long-term care paid for by Medicaid will increase 55%, while workers would go up 17%. Aging baby boomers are driving the projected increasing demand.
When aides aren’t available, people are either forced to go without care or stay in nursing homes, which are more expensive and face their own bed shortages.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: We’ve made progress against Big Tobacco, and we can do the same with the latest batch of bad air
description: My grandfather always told me, “I don’t want to go by the lungs.” Those were his words for telling me he feared dying due to lung failure.  I spent so much time at the hospital during his treatment and recovery from a near fatal aortic aneurysm that my parents say I learned to walk there. […]
text:
A hot hazy day in Minneapolis, July 15, 2026. Wildfire smoke has moved south from fires in northeastern Minnesota. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)My grandfather always told me, “I don’t want to go by the lungs.” Those were his words for telling me he feared dying due to lung failure. 
I spent so much time at the hospital during his treatment and recovery from a near fatal aortic aneurysm that my parents say I learned to walk there.
His aneurysm was not a fluke. My grandfather, the oldest of 11 in a poor Irish family, started smoking at the age of 7 to take the edge off his hunger. He smoked for decades.
He eventually did go by the lungs, 16 years after his aneurysm. 
The year he died, 2008, was also the year the Minnesota Pollution Control Agency began issuing air quality alerts.
Twelve years later, I had a baby. In December 2024, I knelt at my child’s bedside as air whistled through his throat, watching the skin tighten around his ribs. I held him as he coughed, barking, unable to stop.
It took two visits to Children’s Hospital before his breathing issues became manageable, and I still carefully monitor triggers that could induce wheezing, like wildfire smoke. I don’t want my child to go by the lungs.
Many Minnesotans have recently experienced the worst air quality on record, and Minnesota held the status of having the worst air quality in the world. Without change, we will continue to experience poor air quality due to wildfire smoke that’s linked to the hotter, drier summers that turn forests into kindling. 
Cleaner energy mandates, lawsuits against the oil companies and financial investments in new technologies are critical tools for mitigating climate change. Those stopping progress — like refusing to provide federal permits for wind farm projects — are delaying this shift, driving up hospital admission rates and costing lives. 
We can’t let frustration mutate into despair that prevents us from taking the actions we can. We can still use a hammer when our nail gun is missing and continue building structures while we save up for a new nail gun.
Tobacco companies were once seen as invincible, too: Cigarette smoking rates among American adults dropped from 43% to 12% between 1965 and 2022. That change didn’t happen all at once. Public policy shifted gradually with lawsuits, higher taxes and restrictions on smoking in public buildings, while the culture also changed — one conversation, one business decision, one peer interaction at a time.
We face the same daunting policy and cultural challenge when it comes to climate change. 
Here’s another lesson from the tobacco wars as we assemble the coalition needed to make progress on climate change: Hope and kindness and empathy are harder emotions to wield than shame and despair, but they are far more effective. The American Lung Association reflects this in their advice for helping someone quit smoking. In their words: “No nagging, scolding or preaching — that just doesn’t work.” 
With this approach, the smoker can admit that they have a harmful, addictive habit they want to change and find self-respect in each hour they live without the habit. These actions compound, and eventually someone discovers that they haven’t smoked in a year, and one of their friends is quitting too.
Similarly, we must accept the grim reality of climate change and choose to honor each small action we take to address it. 
We did something about the scourge of tobacco, and we can do something about the once-inconceivable event of wildfire smoke rolling in every summer. 
Quitting smoking doesn’t undo lung damage. But it might mean that your grandchild grows up in a household free of secondhand smoke.

name: Missouri Independent
title: After juvenile violence, accountability and rehabilitation must work together
description: Recent high-profile cases involving juveniles have reignited a difficult conversation in our region about youth crime, accountability and public safety. Victims do not suffer less because the person who caused the harm was 16. Families deserve to have that harm recognized, and communities have every right to expect protection. At the same time, a 16-year-old[...]
text:
(Darrin Klimek/Getty Images).Recent high-profile cases involving juveniles have reignited a difficult conversation in our region about youth crime, accountability and public safety.
Victims do not suffer less because the person who caused the harm was 16. Families deserve to have that harm recognized, and communities have every right to expect protection. At the same time, a 16-year-old does not become fully developed because the charge is serious.
Two things can be true at the same time.
Too often, our response is framed as an either-or choice: accountability or rehabilitation, public safety or the needs of the young person. That is not how the problem works. These concepts are not mutually exclusive.
Understanding why a young person committed an offense is not the same as excusing it. It is how we determine what has to change. Two young people may face the same charge but arrive in court through very different paths. One may be following peers. Another may be dealing with untreated trauma, substance use, anger, fear or an escalating pattern of violence. Those differences do not erase responsibility. They help us decide what response is most likely to prevent another person from being harmed.
Young people may know an action is wrong while still lacking the mature judgment, emotional regulation and resistance to peer pressure that adults are more likely to possess. Those capacities continue developing into early adulthood. The law may assign adulthood on an 18th birthday. Human development does not.
That matters for emerging adults between 18 and 25. They are old enough to receive the full weight of adult punishment, yet many are still developing in ways that affect decision-making and self-control. Treating them exactly like older adults may give us a clear legal line, but it does not guarantee safer communities.
Some young people will require secure confinement. Public safety may demand it. But confinement cannot simply be a place where time passes. If we are serious about what happens when they return, those settings must provide individualized assessment, treatment, education, family engagement, employment preparation and meaningful reentry planning. That requires trained staff, stable funding and programs designed for this population. Research on emerging-adult programs points to the need for a broader continuum of care, not a courtroom acting alone.
Most young people prosecuted in adult court will eventually come home. They will live in our neighborhoods, work beside us and raise families in our communities. The condition in which they return is part of public safety.
Parents of victims want assurance that another family will not endure what theirs has. Parents of accused young people want to believe their child can become more than the worst thing they have done. Those hopes are not incompatible.
Accountability should require young people to face the harm they caused. It should also place them in systems capable of reducing the likelihood that they will cause that harm again.
That is not softness. It is what serious, lasting public safety requires.

name: Nevada Current
title: Trump administration demands hospitals share emergency room records
authors: Amanda Seitz/KFF Health News, Maia Rosenfeld/KFF Health News, Darius Tahir/KFF Health News
description: A tiny federal agency tasked with protecting the public from injuries caused by lawn mowers and coffeemakers is demanding that some of the nation’s biggest health systems turn over detailed, personally identifiable medical records of all patients who seek help at their emergency rooms. The Consumer Product Safety Commission, responsible for tracking and issu[...]
text:
Hospital lawyers and other industry experts have questioned the Consumer Product Safety Commission’s authority to collect, its ability to safeguard such a swath of sensitive information, and whether it has followed the legal process to overhaul its surveillance system. (Photo: Getty Images)A tiny federal agency tasked with protecting the public from injuries caused by lawn mowers and coffeemakers is demanding that some of the nation’s biggest health systems turn over detailed, personally identifiable medical records of all patients who seek help at their emergency rooms.
The Consumer Product Safety Commission, responsible for tracking and issuing recalls of dangerous products sold in the U.S., began discreetly pressuring hospital executives this year to share personally identifiable health data with a private contractor. But hospital lawyers and other industry experts have questioned the agency’s authority to collect, its ability to safeguard such a swath of sensitive information, and whether it has followed the legal process to overhaul its surveillance system.
After KFF Health News asked the CPSC about the new system, the agency announced the program on July 21. Left unmentioned, however, is the alarm it has raised among hospital executives, as well as the nature and extent of the agency’s data demands.
In a stark departure from its product-focused mission, the agency’s goal is to obtain millions of Americans’ medical records from emergency room visits for most injuries, from a broken bone to a childhood vaccine reaction or even a suicide attempt, according to documents and emails obtained by KFF Health News, as well as interviews with five people involved or familiar with the discussions.
A CPSC official also insisted in the emails that the institutions provide all ER patients’ identifiable information — such as names, addresses, diagnoses, and other personal details — to the contractor, Konza Health, for analysis. In correspondence with hospital executives, Konza representatives described participation as “mandatory” or “required.”

As a condition of viewing the correspondence, KFF Health News agreed not to republish some of the emails it obtained.
The CPSC wants at least 100 hospitals to start sending detailed medical records by the end of this year, according to an internal memo.
“The whole thing is troubling,” said Sharona Hoffman, a professor of health law at Case Western Reserve University who noted that giving a private entity access to a sweeping collection of data will introduce risks to patient privacy. “If this company really is collecting identifiable information, that is worrisome for patients.”
The new project was launched amid upheaval at the traditionally independent agency, which is without a governing board since President Donald Trump fired the CPSC’s three Democratic board members. Nearly 1 in 5 career staffers left the CPSC in the first 16 months of the new administration, according to a KFF Health News analysis of federal workforce data.
The initiative also comes as the Trump administration has sought unprecedented access to millions of Americans’ medical records, with the Office of Personnel Management requesting federal workers’ sensitive health information and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. using a private organization to collect more medical records for his studies on vaccines and autism.
Steve Roney, CPSC spokesperson, said in an emailed statement on July 10 that the CPSC is “modernizing” its surveillance system. Asked whether the CPSC will file complaints against hospitals that do not participate, he said only that while the previous system “operated as a voluntary program, the ability of hospitals to opt out limited the sample size and usefulness of the data.”
Roney also acknowledged that the agency had not yet notified the public, as “required by law.”
Federal law requires the agency to provide notice and a public comment period before requesting information from 10 or more entities, a step it has not taken despite plans for 100 hospitals to join the surveillance system. KFF Health News independently confirmed with over a dozen hospitals that they had been approached.
Federal public health authorities cannot legally mandate that private health data be reported. But CPSC officials have suggested publicly and privately that if hospitals decline to share data with the new surveillance system, they could be subject to strict penalties from a data-sharing regulation known as “information blocking.”
Yet some hospital executives say they are reluctant to share patients’ sensitive data because they’re concerned about a different violation — that of federal privacy law.
AI Takes Over
Dozens of ERs across the country already participate in the CPSC’s voluntary National Electronic Injury Surveillance System, or NEISS, through which trained hospital workers report injuries involving consumer products, almost always stripped of patients’ identifiable information. The system helps the CPSC identify products, such as baby loungers, toys, and household appliances, with a pattern of injuring consumers.
The new injury surveillance program goes much further.
At a toy industry trade event in February, acting CPSC Chairman Peter Feldman said the agency is “investing in AI-enabled workflows that improve the quality and quantity of injury surveillance data, while also building up digital infrastructure to handle a massive new volume of electronic health records.”
Konza Health, a Kansas-based organization that runs the state’s health data exchange, will automatically pull and analyze medical records of all patient visits from ERs nationwide. Konza won a five-year contract worth up to $15.9 million with the CPSC last fall.
In email correspondence with hospital technology officials, Konza Health President and CEO Laura McCrary also has described ERs’ participation as “required,” stipulating that they share patients’ records with identifying information.
McCrary told KFF Health News by email that the company is not using AI to process the records it receives, saying instead that Konza will use “advanced analytic parsing and filtering capabilities.” Roney, the CPSC spokesperson, did not answer questions about the use of AI.
For years, agency officials have discussed moving away from human contractors and automating NEISS to save time and money.
But without workers on-site, hospital staffers may no longer receive training to determine what clinical information is important to include for the CPSC. In short, the changes could dilute the quality of the product safety data the agency collects.
“They want to suck in as much data as possible, but I’m not sure how thoughtful they’re being about what is collected and what is actually needed by the agency,” said former CPSC chair Alexander Hoehn-Saric, one of the Democratic appointees Trump fired last year.

Wanted: Injuries From Vaccines and Stingrays
The CPSC’s new data collection appears to contradict its own 214-page operating manual, which instructs hospitals not to include identifiable information “such as names, birthdates, or addresses” when reporting cases.
The agency is supposed to receive patients’ identifying information only when needed for follow-up investigations, which happens in fewer than 1% of reported cases, according to the manual.
The CPSC has also historically limited the records it collects to minimize privacy violations in case of a data breach.
The risk is not hypothetical: From 2017 to 2019, the agency improperly released personal health information of around 30,000 people, a disclosure that a top Republican at the time called “concerning.”
Konza, however, will receive even more sensitive information on many more people. McCrary said in a statement that Konza will remove patients’ names, addresses, and medical information “not needed by CPSC” before sharing records with the agency.
Leaving a private organization to collect sensitive information introduces risks, including that it could be stolen or used for business purposes, said Hoffman, the Case Western professor.
“Very often, they will use information for marketing because now they’re going to know what conditions people have,” she said.
Roney said that its contract with Konza, which has not been made public, prohibits the organization from selling or marketing the data it collects.
The CPSC’s manual also identifies types of ER visits that should not be reported to the CPSC, which has jurisdiction over only certain consumer products. Excluded injuries are those caused by food, illegal drugs, medical devices, alcohol, or plants, as well as injuries that did not involve consumer products — such as a cut from a rock or broken bones from a fall on the ground — and suicide attempts by adults.
But in a contract offered to one hospital and reviewed by KFF Health News, Konza set no such limits on the information it would gather from ER records and said it would hold on to patient health information for at least 30 days.

In an email sent to hospital technology officials, McCrary wrote that Konza would provide the CPSC with records when a patient is treated in the ER for any of more than 10,000 conditions. The expansive list of diagnostic codes Konza provided in the email includes injuries that do not involve consumer products.
Child injuries resulting from “poisoning by” vaccines or contact with stingrays, neither of which is regulated by the CPSC, are included in the list.
A limited number of hospitals once shared deidentified data on all injuries — regardless of product involvement — through the NEISS using the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s injury-tracking program. But the CDC halted that data collection, after funding and staffing were cut last year, and has not restarted it.
Pressure on Hospitals
CPSC Chief Data Officer Elizabeth Puchek, who joined the agency late last year after engineering U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ data system, has told hospitals in emails that they must seek an exemption from the program if they decline to share patients’ emergency room records with Konza.

The CPSC’s targeted outreach has included some of the nation’s largest urban and rural health systems, as well as small, publicly owned hospitals.
Staff members at Mary Greeley Medical Center in Ames, Iowa, said that Konza and federal officials told them their participation in the new program was mandatory. The hospital, which has long participated in NEISS, signed a new contract in April to share its ER records with Konza.
Yet the hospital is reevaluating its participation after being notified that the funds it received to participate in NEISS were “no longer available,” spokesperson Steve Sullivan said.
Several hospital executives, lawyers, and others have raised doubts about the CPSC’s claimed authority.
Harborview Medical Center spokesperson Susan Gregg said the Seattle hospital’s emergency room has “voluntarily submitted de-identified data for many years, but we are not obligated to report this information.”
In Boston, Mass General Brigham has declined to participate in the new program, with spokesperson Kelly Mitchell saying that “to protect patient privacy, we are unable to provide these medical records.”
Henry Ford Health in Detroit; St. Luke’s in Boise, Idaho; and Sanford Health based in Sioux Falls, South Dakota — which together handle over a million ER visits a year — are among the health systems that have been approached but not yet entered into an agreement with Konza, according to representatives. Several of the nation’s busiest hospital systems targeted for the program — including the Mayo Clinic in Minnesota, Yale New Haven Hospital in Connecticut, Nationwide Children’s Hospital and the Cleveland Clinic in Ohio, and Baylor Scott & White Health in Texas — declined to answer questions about whether they’re participating.
Hoehn-Saric, the agency’s former chairman, said he was surprised that the CPSC would insist that hospitals provide identifiable records from all emergency room visits.
“This idea that they can simply demand patient information from a hospital and that the hospital would provide it — I really don’t understand the basis for that,” he said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Still no report: Lawmakers question why firm hasn’t provided review of prison health care
description: After reports and allegations of lack of health care for inmates in Mississippi, lawmakers passed a law calling for a review of the prison system's medical services contract.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
In December of 2025 Kristen Windham, director of policy for Gov. Tate Reeves, emailed a state lawmaker with a “report” on the status of a long-awaited review of Mississippi’s prison health care system. 
The document that Windham called a report was a letter that barely stretched beyond a page. And her update was that the monitoring report lawmakers were expecting still did not exist. 
That came as a surprise to lawmakers who passed a law that said they are due a review of the medical services contract from the corrections department on Dec. 15 of each fiscal year. The state recently approved paying the law firm Butler Snow $700,000 for monitoring prison health care, despite no report being delivered yet. 
The urgent interest in the review stems from the alleged denial of health care in state prisons. 
Mississippi Today has documented potentially thousands of people living with hepatitis C going without treatment, amputations following delayed care and trouble getting cancer screenings. Such findings, as well as handwritten letters sent to lawmakers by prisoners seeking care and panicked messages from their family members, drew bipartisan condemnation in the state House and numerous hearings at the Capitol.  
“They have decided to treat 50 inmates a year with Hepatitis C when there are thousands,” House Corrections Chairwoman Becky Currie, a Republican from Brookhaven, said in a recent interview with Mississippi Today. “They provide care when the Hepatitis C patients are so far gone that they need a liver transplant or die.” 
In her email to Currie, Windham cited a lengthy process, one that involved developing a “monitoring program” and “auditing tools” – neither of which had been put in place five years after VitalCore Health Strategies became the medical contractor for Mississippi’s prisons. The Kansas-based company was initially awarded four no-bid emergency contracts, raking in hundreds of millions of dollars in the process, before securing a three-year contract. 
“As you are no doubt aware, developing a medical monitoring program and audit tools tailored to ensure both contract compliance and to evaluate the quality of healthcare takes months to develop,” Windham wrote in the December email. “When development of the audit tools and the initial site visits are completed, MDOC will be able to estimate when the first monitoring report will be completed.”
Seven months later, the Mississippi State Personnel Board on July 16 approved paying the law firm to monitor Mississippi’s prison healthcare system. But several lawmakers granted access to the report under state law told Mississippi Today they still have not seen it, and it’s unclear what progress has been made toward its production. 
“I have not received anything,” Currie said. “If we had used the money that we are paying Butler Snow to tell us what we already know, we could have cured so many people suffering in prison.”
The state law that said lawmakers are due a report from MDOC on Dec. 15 of each fiscal year passed in May of 2025. But Dec. 15 came and went later that year without lawmakers receiving a monitoring report. Windham’s email, obtained by Mississippi Today, shows what the governor’s administration has been telling lawmakers about the process for monitoring Mississippi’s troubled prison healthcare system, a process that has largely unfolded out of public view.
House Public Health Chairman Sam Creekmore, a Republican, and Senate Public Health Chairman Hob Bryan, a Democrat, also told Mississippi Today they had not yet seen any report. Under state law, both of the chairman are owed a copy of the report. They said the last formal update they received was in a December 2025 letter – previously obtained and reported on by Mississippi Today – from Corrections Commissioner Burl Cain, who said a private attorney will manage a team “experienced in correctional healthcare management” to conduct contract oversight. 
That attorney, Bill Lunsford of Butler Snow, the politically connected law firm contracted to monitor Mississippi’s prison health care contract, did not respond to a list of questions. Spokespeople for the Mississippi Department of Corrections also did not respond to messages with similar questions.  
Mississippi Today filed a public request asking for all monitoring reports submitted by Butler Snow on health care available to the state’s incarcerated population. In May, MDOC said the agency does not possess any such documents. 
The genesis of the still-awaited prison health care audit dates back to May of 2025, when the Legislature passed a bill instructing the corrections department to deliver a report on the contractor’s performance. The department hired Butler Snow, a Mississippi-based law firm that has defended prison systems and private prison health contractors in civil rights lawsuits alleging health care failures in several states. 
The 2025 legislation mandating the report on prison health care said MDOC shall provide a report of the monitoring and review of the medical services contract to the chairmen of Senate and House Appropriations, Corrections, and Public Health committees and to the Legislative Budget Office.
Currie had tried to give the Mississippi State Department of Health the authority to monitor prison health care. But her push was defeated, in part due to opposition from Gov. Reeves, who wanted to award monitoring authority to a private firm, according to Currie. 
In MDOC’s search for a medical contractor in 2023, it wrote that the agency “does not employ any licensed personnel responsible with oversight of its contracted healthcare provider,” but said it planned to reestablish a medical compliance office within three to six months of executing the contract. 
At that time, VitalCore had served as the agency’s medical contractor since 2020 after being awarded four no-bid emergency contracts worth $324 million for the services. Combined with its current role, VitalCore has been awarded over $600 million in state contracts.
In the months leading up to the 2026 legislative session, Currie developed a sweeping legislative package of reforms aimed at improving the quality of care in Mississippi prisons and introducing more oversight of the prison medical contract.
Currie wanted to use the report lawmakers had been promised to fine-tune the legislation and build consensus in the Senate, where all her reforms had failed the prior year. So in December of 2025, weeks before lawmakers were set to return to Jackson, Currie began asking for updates.
“I am asking for the audit that the Governor insisted on doing by hiring a firm for over $700,000 dollars to audit Vitalcore,” Currie wrote. “I would like to get it tomorrow before the Christmas Holiday and give me time to study it before the session.”
Windham replied that the contract “provided a six-month implementation period before monitoring activities would commence.”
“Over the next several months, the auditing/monitoring tools will be developed, and the monitoring team of experts will conduct initial site visits of MDOC facilities and begin utilizing the tools,” Windham added. 
Windham did not respond to a list of questions about the site visits, the monitoring tools and the status of the report. 
Without the report in hand, Currie still proceeded with advancing her reforms through the House. But the legislation was ultimately doomed again in the state Senate. 
Corrections Committee Vice Chairwoman Lydia Chassaniol, a Republican from Winona, refused to advance the bills out of committee. Chassaniol had been running the committee while Corrections Chairman Juan Barnett, a Democrat from Heidelberg, was out with an illness. Chassaniol claimed she was honoring Barnett’s wishes. 
“The Health Department was going to do it for free,” Currie said of the long-awaited report. “Now we are charging the taxpayers all this money for a report that supports the inadequate care.”
Mississippi Today reporter Gwen Dilworth contributed to this report

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Here’s why we should pay attention to the Oklahoma State Chamber’s annual survey
description: These days it feels increasingly easy to ignore survey results given the bombardment of people attempting to survey everything from most popular video games to most livable cities. But I find myself hopeful that Oklahomans will pay attention to the 2026 findings of the State Chamber’s annual  Oklahoma Business Roundtable survey. While it’s designed to […]
text:
State Chamber President and CEO Chad Warmington speaks at the State of Business Forum, focusing on education initiatives, on Nov. 17, 2025, at the National Cowboy & Western Heritage Museum in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)These days it feels increasingly easy to ignore survey results given the bombardment of people attempting to survey everything from most popular video games to most livable cities.
But I find myself hopeful that Oklahomans will pay attention to the 2026 findings of the State Chamber’s annual  Oklahoma Business Roundtable survey.
While it’s designed to serve as “a guide for growth to the legislators who shape the state’s economic and business development initiatives,” this year’s report is aptly named  “Oklahoma Has Momentum, But Execution Matters.”
This year’s survey of Oklahoma’s business leaders highlights the growing need for conversations between business leaders, educators and researchers. And, it lays out a roadmap for how those could set the stage for “win-win” solutions for both economic growth and provide meaningful learning to prepare students for the 21st century.
The survey found that 64% of the participants “believe Oklahoma is moving in the right direction relative to the national economy, and that 81% of businesses plan to hire in the coming year.”
Most leaders said they “do not see taxes as their top barrier to growth,” and nearly 60% said the state “should invest surplus funds in public priorities rather than return the money through tax cuts.”
Moreover, workforce development and education are the top concerns, with 74% of those surveyed identifying those as one of the top two most important issues facing Oklahoma business growth.
Mark Funke, president of the Business Roundtable, said that “business leaders in the state clearly see education as the foremost issue.”
He said that 89% of respondents “agreed the state should prioritize funding for education outcomes, particularly in elementary reading and math.”
Getting into the details, 91.5% of survey participants agree  that Oklahoma’s CareerTech system does a good job preparing students for the workforce, and 76.8% say that universities do a good job preparing students for the workforce.
But not surprisingly, a huge majority find that high schools are falling short in preparing students for the workforce.
Thankfully, they identify childcare as a critical need, writing that “Childcare Is No Longer a Side Issue. It Is a Workforce Issue.”
I hope they also understand that early education is more than a side issue for K-12 education, and that schools cannot be turned around without first investing in efforts that expand access to early childhood education along with mental and physical health services.
When I read the entire survey results, as opposed to the headlines about reading instruction theories, I’m reminded of my experiences in the inner circle of the MAPS for Kids project, which saved the Oklahoma City schools from financial collapse.
I was told from day one that our coalition needed to be completely apolitical and base our recommendations on high-quality education research and listening to the community.
One of the first lessons to be learned from scholarly research is that the key factor for teaching students to read is background information, which comes from reading books and from studying history, science, arts, music, and critical thinking.
It’s most definitely not test prep, teaching to a test or basing the measure of a student’s solely on a high-stakes standardized test.
I expect today’s business people, who are also parents, would support research-based solutions.
Also, I expect that we could agree that we need to come together and think through the rapidly expanding benefits and harms of artificial intelligence.
If we can build better conversations between business people and educators, I believe we could build on that foundation.
When unveiling the survey, Funke said that nearly half of those surveyed said “workforce recruitment and retention is their greatest obstacle to increased profitability and growth.”
Access to high-quality schools at all levels would improve those recruitment and retention rates.
And, a major key to getting there is to create public schools that prepare for success in the 21st century. 
That requires schools that teach critical thinking and learning how to learn. 
It requires mentorship. 
It requires schools that bring kids out into diverse communities and brings a full range of adults into schools. 
It requires shared cultures that enhance both an Oklahoma workforce environment that attracts and retains innovators and public schools that provide holistic, thoughtful, and innovative learning environments.

title: Idahoans who are ‘medically frail’ are exempt from Medicaid work requirements. How do you prove it?
description: Starting next year, Idahoans on Medicaid expansion will need to prove they’re working to keep accessing the health insurance public assistance program. That’s only if they don’t meet one of several carveouts, like going to school, or being a caregiver for young kids or people with disabilities.  State officials think most of the roughly 85,000 […]
text:
Advocates for Idaho Medicaid and people with disabilities rally against proposed federal Medicaid cuts in front of the Idaho State Capitol on Thursday, March 20, 2025. (Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)Starting next year, Idahoans on Medicaid expansion will need to prove they’re working to keep accessing the health insurance public assistance program.
That’s only if they don’t meet one of several carveouts, like going to school, or being a caregiver for young kids or people with disabilities. 
State officials think most of the roughly 85,000 people on Medicaid expansion are already meeting the new rules. But if Idahoans want to tap one broad exception, meant for people with disabilities, they might need a doctor’s note, according to a top official at the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare, which runs Medicaid. 
“The department will review any medical documentation submitted, but the most straightforward documentation will be a note from their health care provider,” Idaho Medicaid Administrator Sasha O’Connell said in a statement. “This would only be needed if we don’t already have evidence of medical frailty in our claims system for existing members.”
Some advocates in Idaho say that will add another hurdle to a process that they say is already filled with administrative burden.
Randy Johnson is Idaho’s government relations director for the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network. (Courtesy of the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network)
“If somebody is diagnosed with cancer, it’s already a full-time job in itself,” American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network’s Idaho Government Relations Director Randy Johnson said in an interview. “You’re trying to navigate your treatment, you’re trying to get your life tasks, and then just simply trying to get out of bed or brushing your teeth. And so the ability to have your insurance being taken away by another set of bureaucracy that’s put in front of people — it’s terrifying.”
As states rush to change Medicaid enrollment systems to comply with new work requirements in President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the Trump administration narrowed its interpretation of one exception for the new rules: For people who are “medically frail.”
In June, about six months before most states needed to roll out the work requirements, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services published guidance clarifying that to qualify for the “medically frail” designation, a person must have a significant health condition and be significantly impaired in their ability to work, Stateline reported. Then 25 states — all led by Democrats — sued, arguing that the narrowed definition may cut out many sick and disabled people from the program.
In Idaho, a Republican-led state, state health officials have been developing their own policy for the exemption that leans on a mix of medical claims and requiring medical documentation from patients.

 The feds let states ease patients into providing medical proof. Idaho isn’t taking it.

The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare isn’t going to give patients a one-year grace-period that the feds allowed — in which patients can simply claim the exemption without providing proof, O’Connell said.
Idaho Medicaid Deputy Director Sasha O’Connell presents to the Legislature’s Medicaid Review Panel in Rexburg on Dec. 15, 2025. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)
“We plan to accept attestations the first time someone is subject to the new Medicaid rules for Medicaid, and will require medical documentation if we do not see in our claims system that the person had a corresponding doctor’s visit, hospital stay, or other interaction supporting that they have a condition that makes it difficult for them to meet the new rules,” she said.
But after then, state health officials will rely on a mix of medical claims data and notes from healthcare providers.
Health and Welfare couldn’t immediately provide estimates for how many people on Medicaid expansion could be subject to the exemption. But O’Connell suggested the number would likely be small, since the “vast majority of people with disabilities who rely on Medicaid” qualify for traditional Medicaid, not Medicaid expansion, which is the only population affected by the work requirements.
On an initial review, she said Health and Welfare found that “the vast majority” of people on Medicaid expansion were already “meeting the new requirements.” The agency found that 68,400 Idahoans on Medicaid expansion met the new work requirements, out of the roughly 83,000 on the program at the time of the review, she said.

Medicaid work requirements and other changes in the “Big Beautiful Bill” could kick 20,000 to 34,000 Idahoans off Medicaid expansion by 2028, according to an analysis by the Urban Institute and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. That’s lower than what some other researchers estimate.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming GOP’s decision to endorse primary candidates faced healthy internal opposition
description:
When confronted by party members opposed to picking winners and losers instead of letting voters decide, leaders ducked the issue, writes columnist Kerry Drake.
The post Wyoming GOP’s decision to endorse primary candidates faced healthy internal opposition appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
I’m going to do something that’s very uncharacteristic for me: be positive about what happened at a Wyoming Republican Party leadership committee meeting last week.
It could be painful, but here goes.

Opinion

The panel has long leaned to the far right, and a meeting to decide who the GOP would endorse in the Aug. 18 primary was no exception. But I was encouraged by how much internal opposition surfaced to the idea of party leaders endorsing candidates in the first place. 
Members of the party’s central committee who disagreed could have stayed silent and, for the sake of party unity, continued to let the public think the GOP is actually united. It is not, and nothing proves that louder or clearer than what some conscientious members said in their dissents.
In the top three races, the committee endorsed Rep. Harriet Hageman for U.S. Senate, Secretary of State Chuck Gray for the U.S. House, and Brent Bien for governor. It marked the first time in decades that the party chose not to remain neutral in a primary.
I believe the party weighing in to sway an intraparty election is against Wyoming law, and I think state Republican Party Chairman Bryan Miller knows that full well. He’s hoping to win a federal lawsuit, and in doing so overturn the state’s ban on using party resources to help individual primary candidates. In other words, he wants to overturn the common-sense law that bars parties from hand picking their favorite — and most obedient — candidates instead of letting voters decide for themselves.
“I don’t think it’s a good idea to be endorsing candidates at all,” said Hot Springs County GOP State Committeeman Phil Scheel. He voiced his dissent when the panel of about 50 voting members were deciding who to endorse for the U.S. Senate.
If the party values what its members think, Scheel’s comments should have prompted debate on the controversial issue. But state Republican Party Vice Chair Bob Ferguson foreclosed the discussion by ruling Scheel’s comment out of order.
I understand Ferguson’s position: A majority of delegates voted to establish a process for vetting and endorsing candidates at its April state convention. Shutting down any opposition to that move may be within the leadership’s rights, but it’s simply not smart politics.
If already engaged party members who’ve shown up at the meeting to vote on endorsements want to address their belief that the party is making a big mistake, why not let them? Not allowing the committee’s minority to state the obvious — that the party isn’t speaking in one voice on this issue — will only further antagonize supporters of candidates who didn’t make the grade.
Several Republicans have told me they’re troubled by the fact that how much money candidates have donated to the party is one of the factors used to determine who gets endorsed. 
Strangely, even when a member of the committee agreed that it should endorse Gray but questioned his policies on election issues, that attempted conversation was also shut down by Ferguson, who ruled it wasn’t germane.
“I’m endorsing him, all I’m saying is that a lot of things Chuck has said about voter integrity and getting rid of voter dropboxes is not true,” said Mitch Benson, a state committeeman from Fremont County.
Miller stopped everything when he said the debate had reached the three-minute time limit. But there was no “debate,” the clock ran out over a disagreement about whether Benson could fully state his position or be muted.
Not allowing Benson to discuss Gray’s record in office was hypocritical. Earlier, when Scheel questioned the endorsement process before the vote to endorse Hageman, Ferguson said the committee should be focusing on Hageman’s record. So why is an opinion about Gray’s competency in his current job not germane?
Niobrara County GOP Chair Janae Miller saw an opportunity to publicly oppose the endorsement process without being ruled out of order for saying it out loud.
“Niobrara County constituents have been vocal in their opposition to endorse any candidate no matter their excellent or poor performance,” she wrote in the Zoom meeting’s chat. “They want the voters to decide at the polls.”
The endorsement votes for the three major candidates demonstrate that a significant portion of the members agree with Janae Miller.
If you combine the “no” votes each candidate received with the abstentions, here are the results: Hageman, 32-19; Gray, 33-18; Bien, 34-17. While each won their endorsement by about two-to-one, that’s a much closer vote than most observers expected.
If the party wants its endorsements to have any credibility with voters, it shouldn’t effectively say it doesn’t care what members think if they don’t agree. Why should people stick around and participate if all it’s going to do is rubber-stamp what its leaders have already decided? 
Bryan Miller told the committee last week that he believes the state law, which prohibits the party from spending any money directly or indirectly to promote any candidate, is unconstitutional. He said the party will not give any of its endorsed candidates any money before the primary.
Endorsements have been interpreted to also be banned, a position Miller noted is challenged in the lawsuit.
But there is definitely a connection to the two issues. The party has to spend money to conduct the type of vetting process it has created. It would also be expensive to print and distribute a voter’s guide explaining how the party rates candidates, which Miller has advocated. Spending money for these purposes is definitely an indirect benefit to endorsed candidates.
The party is spending money to finance its expensive lawsuit to challenge state law. It certainly has the right to do that, but people who disagree with that decision also contribute money and time to the party. Why does their voice keep getting muzzled?
If the leadership truly cares about protecting its First Amendment rights, which is one of the prime reasons stated for the lawsuit, the idea that it won’t even let people broach a sensitive subject runs totally counter to its legal argument.
The best thing opponents of party endorsements like Scheel did was convince the committee to not pass an extremely dumb motion to officially oppose the gubernatorial candidacy of state Sen. Eric Barlow, R-Gillette, a traditional, mainstream, Wyoming conservative whose unwillingness to kowtow to party leadership contrasts sharply with his radical opponents Bien and Superintendent of Public Instruction Megan Degenfelder.
An anti-Barlow position by the party would have been the only one directly opposing a candidate. Republican leaders should be glad that one was shot down, if they recognize that their new endorsement policy has further polarized a party that was already split into MAGA and old-school conservative factions. 
I doubt that the GOP’s endorsement of Bien will have much of an impact on the contest. But if the party decided to officially start attacking Barlow, he would have had a field day slamming it for going to extremes instead of letting the process that’s worked well for 50 years prevail: Let the voters decide.
The post Wyoming GOP’s decision to endorse primary candidates faced healthy internal opposition appeared first on WyoFile .

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Trump administration demands hospitals share emergency room records
authors: Amanda Seitz, KFF Health News, Darius Tahir, KFF Health News, Maia Rosenfeld, KFF Health News
description: A tiny federal agency tasked with protecting the public from injuries caused by lawnmowers and coffeemakers is demanding that some of the nation’s biggest health systems turn over detailed, personally identifiable medical records of all patients who seek help at their emergency rooms. The Consumer Product Safety Commission, responsible for tracking and issui[...]
text:
Hospital lawyers and other industry experts have questioned the Consumer Product Safety Commission’s authority to collect, its ability to safeguard such a swath of sensitive information, and whether it has followed the legal process to overhaul its surveillance system. (Photo: Getty Images) A tiny federal agency tasked with protecting the public from injuries caused by lawnmowers and coffeemakers is demanding that some of the nation’s biggest health systems turn over detailed, personally identifiable medical records of all patients who seek help at their emergency rooms.
The Consumer Product Safety Commission, responsible for tracking and issuing recalls of dangerous products sold in the U.S., began discreetly pressuring hospital executives this year to share personally identifiable health data with a private contractor. But hospital lawyers and other industry experts have questioned the agency’s authority to collect, its ability to safeguard such a swath of sensitive information, and whether it has followed the legal process to overhaul its surveillance system.
After KFF Health News asked the CPSC about the new system, the agency announced the program on July 21. Left unmentioned, however, is the alarm it has raised among hospital executives, as well as the nature and extent of the agency’s data demands.
In a stark departure from its product-focused mission, the agency’s goal is to obtain millions of Americans’ medical records from emergency room visits for most injuries, from a broken bone to a childhood vaccine reaction or even a suicide attempt, according to documents and emails obtained by KFF Health News, as well as interviews with five people involved or familiar with the discussions.
A CPSC official also insisted in the emails that the institutions provide all ER patients’ identifiable information — such as names, addresses, diagnoses, and other personal details — to the contractor, Konza Health, for analysis. In correspondence with hospital executives, Konza representatives described participation as “mandatory” or “required.”
As a condition of viewing the correspondence, KFF Health News agreed not to republish some of the emails it obtained.
The CPSC wants at least 100 hospitals to start sending detailed medical records by the end of this year, according to an internal memo.
“The whole thing is troubling,” said Sharona Hoffman, a professor of health law at Case Western Reserve University who noted that giving a private entity access to a sweeping collection of data will introduce risks to patient privacy. “If this company really is collecting identifiable information, that is worrisome for patients.”
The new project was launched amid upheaval at the traditionally independent agency, which is without a governing board since President Donald Trump fired the CPSC’s three Democratic board members. Nearly 1 in 5 career staffers left the CPSC in the first 16 months of the new administration, according to a KFF Health News analysis of federal workforce data.
The initiative also comes as the Trump administration has sought unprecedented access to millions of Americans’ medical records, with the Office of Personnel Management requesting federal workers’ sensitive health information and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. using a private organization to collect more medical records for his studies on vaccines and autism.
Steve Roney, CPSC spokesperson, said in an emailed statement on July 10 that the CPSC is “modernizing” its surveillance system. Asked whether the CPSC will file complaints against hospitals that do not participate, he said only that while the previous system “operated as a voluntary program, the ability of hospitals to opt out limited the sample size and usefulness of the data.”
Roney also acknowledged that the agency had not yet notified the public, as “required by law.”
Federal law requires the agency to provide notice and a public comment period before requesting information from 10 or more entities, a step it has not taken despite plans for 100 hospitals to join the surveillance system. KFF Health News independently confirmed with over a dozen hospitals that they had been approached.
Federal public health authorities cannot legally mandate that private health data be reported. But CPSC officials have suggested publicly and privately that if hospitals decline to share data with the new surveillance system, they could be subject to strict penalties from a data-sharing regulation known as “information blocking.”
Yet some hospital executives say they are reluctant to share patients’ sensitive data because they’re concerned about a different violation — that of federal privacy law.
AI Takes Over
Dozens of ERs across the country already participate in the CPSC’s voluntary National Electronic Injury Surveillance System, or NEISS, through which trained hospital workers report injuries involving consumer products, almost always stripped of patients’ identifiable information. The system helps the CPSC identify products, such as baby loungers, toys, and household appliances, with a pattern of injuring consumers.
The new injury surveillance program goes much further.
At a toy industry trade event in February, acting CPSC Chairman Peter Feldman said the agency is “investing in AI-enabled workflows that improve the quality and quantity of injury surveillance data, while also building up digital infrastructure to handle a massive new volume of electronic health records.”
Konza Health, a Kansas-based organization that runs the state’s health data exchange, will automatically pull and analyze medical records of all patient visits from ERs nationwide. Konza won a five-year contract worth up to $15.9 million with the CPSC last fall.
In email correspondence with hospital technology officials, Konza Health President and CEO Laura McCrary also has described ERs’ participation as “required,” stipulating that they share patients’ records with identifying information.
McCrary told KFF Health News by email that the company is not using AI to process the records it receives, saying instead that Konza will use “advanced analytic parsing and filtering capabilities.” Roney, the CPSC spokesperson, did not answer questions about the use of AI.
For years, agency officials have discussed moving away from human contractors and automating NEISS to save time and money.
But without workers on-site, hospital staffers may no longer receive training to determine what clinical information is important to include for the CPSC. In short, the changes could dilute the quality of the product safety data the agency collects.
“They want to suck in as much data as possible, but I’m not sure how thoughtful they’re being about what is collected and what is actually needed by the agency,” said former CPSC chair Alexander Hoehn-Saric, one of the Democratic appointees Trump fired last year.

Wanted: Injuries From Vaccines and Stingrays
The CPSC’s new data collection appears to contradict its own 214-page operating manual, which instructs hospitals not to include identifiable information “such as names, birthdates, or addresses” when reporting cases.
The agency is supposed to receive patients’ identifying information only when needed for follow-up investigations, which happens in fewer than 1% of reported cases, according to the manual.
The CPSC has also historically limited the records it collects to minimize privacy violations in case of a data breach.
The risk is not hypothetical: From 2017 to 2019, the agency improperly released personal health information of around 30,000 people, a disclosure that a top Republican at the time called “concerning.”
Konza, however, will receive even more sensitive information on many more people. McCrary said in a statement that Konza will remove patients’ names, addresses, and medical information “not needed by CPSC” before sharing records with the agency.
Leaving a private organization to collect sensitive information introduces risks, including that it could be stolen or used for business purposes, said Hoffman, the Case Western professor.
“Very often, they will use information for marketing because now they’re going to know what conditions people have,” she said.
Roney said that its contract with Konza, which has not been made public, prohibits the organization from selling or marketing the data it collects.
The CPSC’s manual also identifies types of ER visits that should not be reported to the CPSC, which has jurisdiction over only certain consumer products. Excluded injuries are those caused by food, illegal drugs, medical devices, alcohol, or plants, as well as injuries that did not involve consumer products — such as a cut from a rock or broken bones from a fall on the ground — and suicide attempts by adults.
But in a contract offered to one hospital and reviewed by KFF Health News, Konza set no such limits on the information it would gather from ER records and said it would hold on to patient health information for at least 30 days.
In an email sent to hospital technology officials, McCrary wrote that Konza would provide the CPSC with records when a patient is treated in the ER for any of more than 10,000 conditions. The expansive list of diagnostic codes Konza provided in the email includes injuries that do not involve consumer products.
Child injuries resulting from “poisoning by” vaccines or contact with stingrays, neither of which is regulated by the CPSC, are included in the list.
A limited number of hospitals once shared deidentified data on all injuries — regardless of product involvement — through the NEISS using the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s injury-tracking program. But the CDC halted that data collection, after funding and staffing were cut last year, and has not restarted it.
Pressure on Hospitals
CPSC Chief Data Officer Elizabeth Puchek, who joined the agency late last year after engineering U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ data system, has told hospitals in emails that they must seek an exemption from the program if they decline to share patients’ emergency room records with Konza.
The CPSC’s targeted outreach has included some of the nation’s largest urban and rural health systems, as well as small, publicly owned hospitals.
Staff members at Mary Greeley Medical Center in Ames, Iowa, said that Konza and federal officials told them their participation in the new program was mandatory. The hospital, which has long participated in NEISS, signed a new contract in April to share its ER records with Konza.
Yet the hospital is reevaluating its participation after being notified that the funds it received to participate in NEISS were “no longer available,” spokesperson Steve Sullivan said.
Several hospital executives, lawyers, and others have raised doubts about the CPSC’s claimed authority.
Harborview Medical Center spokesperson Susan Gregg said the Seattle hospital’s emergency room has “voluntarily submitted de-identified data for many years, but we are not obligated to report this information.”
In Boston, Mass General Brigham has declined to participate in the new program, with spokesperson Kelly Mitchell saying that “to protect patient privacy, we are unable to provide these medical records.”
Henry Ford Health in Detroit; St. Luke’s in Boise, Idaho; and Sanford Health based in Sioux Falls, South Dakota — which together handle over a million ER visits a year — are among the health systems that have been approached but not yet entered into an agreement with Konza, according to representatives. Several of the nation’s busiest hospital systems targeted for the program — including the Mayo Clinic in Minnesota, Yale New Haven Hospital in Connecticut, Nationwide Children’s Hospital and the Cleveland Clinic in Ohio, and Baylor Scott & White Health in Texas — declined to answer questions about whether they’re participating.
Hoehn-Saric, the agency’s former chairman, said he was surprised that the CPSC would insist that hospitals provide identifiable records from all emergency room visits.
“This idea that they can simply demand patient information from a hospital and that the hospital would provide it — I really don’t understand the basis for that,” he said.

title: Agency providing legal help to immigrant kids forced to shut doors amid Trump administration cuts
description: Hundreds of immigrant children in Tennessee will soon lose access to their attorneys as a result of the Trump administration’s decision to withhold legal grant payments and end long-time contracts. Mid-South Immigration Advocates serves about 400 children — ranging from infants to teens — who entered the U.S. without a parent or legal guardian and […]
text:
About 800 low-income immigrant children will lose legal representation in Tennessee as the Trump administration withholds funding from a West Tennessee organization. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Hundreds of immigrant children in Tennessee will soon lose access to their attorneys as a result of the Trump administration’s decision to withhold legal grant payments and end long-time contracts.
Mid-South Immigration Advocates serves about 400 children — ranging from infants to teens — who entered the U.S. without a parent or legal guardian and remain in Tennessee in federal custody or with family or sponsors. 
On Friday, it announced it is closing its doors in Nashville and Memphis, a decision with “dire consequences” for immigrant children, said Sally Joyner, legal director. Joyner said the organization’s closure will also strip legal representation for hundreds of adult clients it assists every year.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Children without attorneys must appear before immigration judges on their own, placing them at heightened risk for deportation, Joyner noted. Without legal representation, fewer than 1% of immigrant children are granted relief to remain in the United State in immigration courts, according to the Acacia Center for Justice, an umbrella organization for 100 nonprofit organizations nationwide that provide immigrant children with legal aid.
Joyner called it a “another level of disaster” with “dire consequences” for the children the nonprofit organization has been assisting with immigration legal assistance. 
The nonprofit is among scores of legal services organizations across the country that have struggled since the early months of the second Trump administration to receive longtime federal grants under existing contracts to provide legal representation to immigrant kids.
In March 2025, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services tried to permanently end the funding. A legal challenge to the funding decision put those funding cuts on hold, for now.
Then, in November, the administration implemented a new policy requiring that recipients of the grant funding begin turning over personal information about the children as a condition of receiving payments.
Joyner said legal organizations like hers cannot ethically share the privileged legal information and refused to provide confidential information about their young clients. As a result, Mid-South Immigration Advocates hasn’t been reimbursed $500,000 in federal funding for the legal assistance it has provided since November.
Joyner said her organization, with few exceptions, has been unable to accept new clients since early 2025. Fundraising has not bridged the funding gap and the agency has already tapped existing reserves, she said.
“We have diligently fulfilled our obligations by using reserve funding, and we have sought foundation funding to fill the gap,” the organization said in a message to clients and supporters. “But we are running out of resources, and therefore we are running out of time”
In total, the U.S. Health and Human Services agency has withheld more than $65 million in reimbursements to more than 100 agencies nationwide that it contracts with to provide immigrant children with legal representation, according to the Acacia Center for Justice.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Federal judge allows state to use lethal injection to execute Jeffery Lee
description: A federal district judge Wednesday denied an Alabama death row inmate’s request to stop the state from executing him by lethal injection after he successfully halted his nitrogen gas execution. In a 16-page opinion, U.S. District Judge Emily Marks rejected Jeffrey Lee’s argument that a 2018 settlement with the state prevented it from using lethal […]
text:
A jury convicted Jeffery Lee, 50, of the 1998 murders of Jimmy Ellis and Elaine Thompson during a pawn shop robbery. A federal judge last week denied a motion from Lee's attorneys to prevent his execution by lethal injection. (Alabama Department of Corrections)A federal district judge Wednesday denied an Alabama death row inmate’s request to stop the state from executing him by lethal injection after he successfully halted his nitrogen gas execution.
In a 16-page opinion, U.S. District Judge Emily Marks rejected Jeffrey Lee’s argument that a 2018 settlement with the state prevented it from using lethal injection on him, writing that her June injunction against the state’s use of nitrogen gas executions was “narrowly tailored” to address its use and that the ruling would not “further delay” his execution.
“Considering the totality of the circumstances, including the circumstances of the dismissal of Lee’s lethal injection challenge, equity does not demand that the court prohibit the state from executing Lee by lethal injection, the state’s default execution method and one which it is presently able to use,” Marks wrote.
A message was sent to Lee’s legal team on Monday seeking comment.
Lee was sentenced to death in 2000 for the 1998 murder of Jimmy Ellis and Elaine Thompson during a robbery of an Orrville pawn shop. In June, a federal appeals court ruled that executing Lee by nitrogen gas would cause “air hunger” that violated Lee’s Eighth Amendment protections against cruel and unusual punishment. Marks, who initially ruled against Lee, entered an injunction against the state using nitrogen gas, which the U.S. Supreme Court allowed to stand.
The Alabama Attorney General’s Office next moved to execute Lee by lethal injection. In a July 7 filing, Lee’s attorneys argued the state could not execute him by the method due to a 2018 agreement between Lee and the state. Lee dropped a lawsuit against Alabama’s lethal injection protocol after agreeing to be executed by nitrogen gas, while the state agreed not to execute him by nitrogen gas.
Lee’s legal team argued the state was bound by the terms of the dismissed case. His legal team also said executing Lee by lethal injection violates state law because it could only be used only if nitrogen gas was declared unconstitutional.
Nitrogen gas, as a general method of execution, remains viable in the state. Marks’ earlier ruling only prohibits the specific nitrogen gas procedure that Alabama planned to use.
The Alabama Attorney General’s Office said in a filing last week that lethal injection is allowed by the U.S. Constitution and that Alabama can use the method because Marks only permanently enjoined the nitrogen gas protocol.
Marks agreed, writing that “the change in the state’s position is attributable to a change in essential facts.”
“To be sure, Lee successfully established that the ADOC’s nitrogen hypoxia protocol is facially unconstitutional, and a permanent injunction prohibiting his execution using the unconstitutional protocol was and remains appropriate,” Marks wrote. “But balancing all of the equities, including the state’s and the victims’ interests in the enforcement of Lee’s sentence, the broader, modified injunction Lee now seeks is not warranted.”
Marks also wrote that Alabama gets to decide what is legal for the state.
“To that end, ‘federal courts do not have the authority to compel state actors to comply with state law,’” Marks said in her ruling. “This rule applies equally to a request for a declaration that state officials’ conduct violates state law.”
Gov. Kay Ivey had not set a new execution date for Lee as of Monday afternoon.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Plans for North Dakota nickel processing unclear as company also evaluates Michigan site
description: This is the second in a two-part series about North Dakota projects that would process Minnesota mining materials. Read about a pig iron processing plant proposed near Minot here. A ceremony last year celebrated a key step in converting a former North Dakota coal mine into a processing site for nickel mined in Minnesota. But […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Julie Fedorchak, left, speaks with Talon Metals president Mike Kicis, center, and Jessica Johnson, Talon's vice president for external affairs, on May 28, 2025, in Beulah, N.D., where Talon signed an agreement to process nickel at the Westmoreland coal mine. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)  This is the second in a two-part series about North Dakota projects that would process Minnesota mining materials. Read about a pig iron processing plant proposed near Minot here.
A ceremony last year celebrated a key step in converting a former North Dakota coal mine into a processing site for nickel mined in Minnesota.
But now the future of the project looks less clear, with a feasibility study also examining whether to send the nickel by rail to Michigan.
At an event last May, Westmoreland Mining signed an agreement to let Talon Metals use parts of an old coal mine in Beulah to transform ore into concentrate. 
Joined by multinational mining company Rio Tinto, Talon Metals proposes to target a high-grade nickel reserve 2,000 feet underground at a site near Tamarack, Minnesota. Nickel is mostly used for batteries and stainless steel, often coming from foreign markets. 
Support for the project is rooted in a national push to keep critical minerals on U.S. soil and out of “adversarial” countries. In 2023, the Department of Defense awarded Talon Metals $20.6 million for nickel exploration. 
North Dakota’s governor and congressional delegation joined for the signing ceremony for the project that would be the first of its kind in the country.   
North Dakota coal mine to become processing site for Minnesota nickel

One year after the Beulah signing, however, major details about the project remain out of public view — like who will use the material, where it will be processed and how much the entire operation will cost. 
It was signaled in the May 2025 agreement the processing site would be in North Dakota. 
However, according to the company’s external affairs manager, Jess Johnson, Talon Metals might instead use its existing Eagle Mine and Humboldt Mill site in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula for processing. 
“We are evaluating both options for ore to either go to North Dakota or go to the already operating mill in Michigan,” she said. “It could be both.” 
North Dakota regulators have not received applications for the project.
A Talon Metals press release from July 9 refers to both a Beulah processing facility and Michigan ore processing facility.  
If the company opts for North Dakota, it would need to employ approximately 150 people for operations. Whereas in Michigan, it would use the existing 450-person workforce, Johnson said. But railing the ore through northern Wisconsin to Michigan will likely cost more than railing it directly to North Dakota. 
After recent talks with Talon Metals, Beulah Economic Development Director Granville “Beaver” Brinkman is under the impression the company still plans on coming to North Dakota.
“The state has a lot to offer a company like Talon Metals. I hope they don’t go somewhere else,” he said, citing jobs and tax revenue as some major pluses of bringing the industry to small-town Beulah. 
According to Westmoreland Mining External Affairs Director and Counsel Jon Heroux, Talon Metals isn’t bound to the land; it merely has an option to use it for the processing facility. 
The decision is expected to come this fall as part of an overall feasibility study. 
Other information will be folded into that study, according to Johnson. 
The company held onto a $115 million Department of Energy grant amid a flurry of cuts made at the federal level, and entered an informal deal with Tesla. 
According to public filings from 2024, the project would involve supplying the electric vehicle maker with 75,000 metric tons, or 165 million pounds, of processed nickel once operations begin. 
Talon Metals vowed to use “commercially reasonable efforts” to begin production on or before Jan. 1, 2026. That hasn’t happened, but the agreement allows for both Talon Metals and Tesla to decide whether to move forward with the deal by the end of the year. 
Talon Metals has also been in early talks with Fargo-based defense technology company Packet Digital. 
As it stands, the 18-month construction of the mine in Minnesota would begin in late 2028 or early 2029; earliest production from a processing facility could begin in 2030, according to Johnson.
That timeline largely hinges on the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources environmental impact study, which includes a public comment period that runs through Sept. 12. Additional permitting will follow depending on the results of the report.
Neither the North Department of Environmental Quality nor the Department of Water Resources has received any applications for the Beulah site. Deputy Director Karl Rockeman said earlier this month the department has had preliminary discussions with the company, but hasn’t heard from it in around a year. 
Minnesota opposition
Paula Maccabee, executive director and attorney for Water Legacy, said she has never seen a project of such magnitude have so many details that are unavailable. Water Legacy is an environmental advocacy group based in Minnesota. 
Maccabee has been holding onto documentation released to the public since plans for the nickel mine in Minnesota were announced, and has noticed that the initial environmental-forward plans outlined in the outset of the project are absent in recent communications.
Johnson confirmed those plans — from using electric vehicles on site to experimenting with carbon sequestration — are being evaluated in the feasibility study. 
Proposed North Dakota pig iron plant to turn Minnesota mine waste into steel, a first for US 

For some, the stagnance allows for more time to stop the project altogether.  
On the Minnesota side, communities surrounding the site are scared of its potential impact on local ecosystems, said Kelly Applegate, natural resources commissioner for the Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe.  
Documents submitted to Minnesota regulators show the mine could use up to 50 million gallons of water yearly and occupy around 380 acres. 
Applegate said locals first learned about the project when it hit news headlines.
“Sadly, it’s a problem and a theme that happens within Indian Country,” he said of that timeline. “We become just a box on a checklist; they reach out and have a little conversation with us, and we bark back a little bit back and forth, and then they say ‘OK we’re done with the consultation.’ We want to be at the table at the beginning.”
The closest Band members live approximately 1.3 miles from the proposed mine site, which is tucked into wetlands, rivers, lakes and streams that surrounding people rely heavily on for sources of food and medicine.
Taking into account those concerns, Johnson said the company altered the mine design to be completely underground. 
“Trust is something that is built and earned over time. And I think we’re very aware of that and want to continue open communication and work to engage as best as we can,” Johnson said. 
Applegate said the community is concerned about the risks of transporting raw materials. 
“When you’re railing it across all of these wetlands, train derailments happen, there’s the risk. Those sealed rail cars aren’t impervious to water and if they spill over and go into wetlands and whatnot, there could be some significant damage done,” Applegate said. 
The biggest concerns are tied to tailings, the toxic byproducts leftover after processing ore, which have historically destroyed ecosystems and polluted drinking water.
Though, because the project hasn’t seen movement in North Dakota since last May, it hasn’t been as much of a hotbed topic in comparison to Minnesota, according to Scott Skokos, executive director of the Dakota Resource Council. 
He said the council is generally against waste coming from out of state to North Dakota for processing or permanent disposal. 
“A lot of the locals we’re getting calls from keep asking ‘Why does Minnesota keep sending its waste to North Dakota?’” Skokos said. 
Water Over Nickel, the Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe, the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy, Dakota Resource Council, Friends of the Mississippi River and Water Legacy are groups leading the multi-state campaign against the proposed operation. 
Anyone is able to participate in the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources’ public comment period. More information can be found on its website.
