name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Democrat PSC candidates question attorney’s safety stance
description: Democratic candidates for North Dakota Public Service Commission say recent statements by a PSC attorney about pipeline safety point to larger problems in state government.  PSC attorney Zachary Pelham told a judge that the agency can’t consider public safety when evaluating the route of an interstate hazardous liquid pipeline in North Dakota.  John Pederson[...]
text:
From the left, Republican Public Service Commissioners Sheri Haugen-Hoffart and Jill Kringstad and Democratic-NPL candidates John Pederson and Scot Kelsh. (Photos courtesy of the PSC and the candidates)Democratic candidates for North Dakota Public Service Commission say recent statements by a PSC attorney about pipeline safety point to larger problems in state government. 
PSC attorney Zachary Pelham told a judge that the agency can’t consider public safety when evaluating the route of an interstate hazardous liquid pipeline in North Dakota. 
John Pederson and Scot Kelsh, Democrats who are challenging Republican incumbents for two positions on the PSC, took issue with those comments during a news conference in Fargo last week.
“The current Public Service Commission should publicly refute their staff attorney’s finding and make a determination that considerations of the public, both welfare and safety, will be the primary criterion when siting not only pipelines, but any infrastructure project that affects multiple stakeholders,” Pederson said Thursday. 
Safety not a factor in determining North Dakota pipeline routes, attorney says

Pederson of Mayville is running for the seat held by Sheri Haugen-Hoffart, a full six-year term. Kelsh of Fargo is running for the seat held by Jill Kringstad, a two-year term. 
The comments by Pelham came July 14 during a district court hearing on a lawsuit challenging a permit for the Summit Carbon Solutions pipeline. The commission approved the permit for the pipeline in November 2024, but the project has stalled.  
Pelham said pipeline safety was strictly a federal regulatory responsibility. The PSC considers public welfare, which Pelham said is different from safety. 
“The commission determines whether or not there is compliance with the regulatory and statutory requirements to provide a minimal adverse impact on the public welfare of the citizens of the state of North Dakota,” Pelham said. “It doesn’t say that there’s a guarantee of safety as to where the pipeline is at.”
John Pederson, left, and Scot Kelsh, Democratic candidates for Public Service Commission in North Dakota, speak July 23, 2026 in Fargo. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)
Pederson and Kelsh said Pelham’s arguments were off target. 
“The narrow legal arguments in district court that the Public Service Commission cannot consider safety are emblematic of a broader leadership problem at the commission,” Pederson said. 
Kelsh, a former legislator, added: “If the law, century code, is that ambiguous that the PSC cannot even consider public safety when siting a pipeline, then we’re going to need legislative changes in order to make that ambiguity go away.” 
Kringstad said in an interview that the PSC can and does consider what might be the safest route for a pipeline during the siting process.
“We consider general safety standards and look at, specifically from the locational side … maybe there’s other alternatives where we can enhance safety,” said Kringstad, who was not on the PSC when the Summit route was approved. 
Sheri Haugen-Hoffart speaks at Republican campaign event on May 29, 2026, in Fargo, North Dakota. At right is Jill Kringstad, who along with Haugen-Hoffart were running for seats on the Public Service Commission. Also pictured at Attorney General Drew Wrigley, left, and Secretary of State Michael Howe. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)
Haugen-Hoffart said in an interview that the federal Pipeline Hazardous Materials Safety Administration would have jurisdiction over safety for the interstate pipeline. She said the PSC docket reflects that. 
“I am comfortable that we consider safety when it comes to siting,” she added.
The original plans for the Summit pipeline would transport carbon dioxide captured at ethanol plants to a permanent underground storage site northwest of Bismarck. Legal hurdles and permitting delays have led Summit to target a storage site in Wyoming instead. 
The main trunk of the North Dakota route would run through Emmons and Burleigh counties, both of which are seeking to have Summit’s permit repealed. 
One argument from attorneys seeking that repeal is that an alternative southern route, keeping the pipeline farther away from Bismarck, didn’t receive enough consideration. 
Public safety was a topic that came up frequently during public hearings on the controversial Summit pipeline. Carbon dioxide in high concentrations can be deadly. 
Commission Chair Randy Christmann said the PSC has not put strict limits on what the public can discuss during a public hearing. 
“I think, on all topics, we have always tried to be pretty generous with people to let them air their thoughts with us,” Christmann said. 
He said Thursday he had not gone back to listen to Pelham’s comments but stood by the PSC process.
“As far as our siting, I think the courts will find that we are correct, and that PHMSA controls safety aspects of that,” Christmann said
South Central Judicial District Court Judge Jackson Lofgren questioned Pelham on what the PSC is able to consider when siting a pipeline, but did not rule on the permit appeal.  
PHMSA did not respond to emailed questions from the Monitor. 
Erin Sutherland, policy and program director for the Pipeline Safety Trust, said federal pipeline regulators generally leave siting authority up to the states. And states “absolutely” have a responsibility to consider public safety, she said. 
She said zoning laws, such as required setbacks from homes, and exercising siting authority don’t infringe on federal regulatory authority. 
Reach North Dakota Monitor deputy editor Jeff Beach at jbeach@northdakotamonitor.com

name: Colorado Newsline
title: How Colorado will celebrate its 150th birthday on Aug. 1
description: From an art market in downtown Denver to a pancake supper in Olathe, public events will be held all across the state this weekend to celebrate the 150th anniversary of Colorado statehood. A proclamation by President Ulysses S. Grant on Aug. 1, 1876, admitted Colorado as the 38th state in the union. Coming less than […]
text:
A historic 38-star American flag, featuring a star for Colorado, the 38th state. (Photo courtesy of History Colorado)From an art market in downtown Denver to a pancake supper in Olathe, public events will be held all across the state this weekend to celebrate the 150th anniversary of Colorado statehood.
Click the image to see Newsline’s special reporting project on 150 years of Colorado statehood.
A proclamation by President Ulysses S. Grant on Aug. 1, 1876, admitted Colorado as the 38th state in the union. Coming less than a month after the nation’s 100th birthday celebration, Grant’s proclamation ensured that Colorado would be known by the nickname that a Denver newspaper had first suggested a year earlier — the Centennial State.
Now, after the commemoration earlier this month of its semiquincentennial, marking the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, Colorado’s 150th birthday party — its sesquicentennial — will take center stage. The state’s America 250-Colorado 150 commission was established by the Legislature in 2022 to coordinate the celebration of the twin anniversaries, dubbed the “sesquisemiquincentennial.”
The commission approved 12 signature initiatives for 2026, including a documentary film series, a new historic marker program, a “digital passport” program to encourage travel and tourism around the state, and “A Portrait of Colorado at 150,” a collection of oral histories from at least 150 living Coloradans. Its website includes an expansive list of events commemorating Colorado’s 150th anniversary throughout the summer.
Colorado Day
Denver’s Civic Center Park will kick off this weekend’s events with a “Homegrown Colorado” night market on Friday. More than 90 Colorado-based vendors will showcase local food, beverages and other artisanal products at the event, which is free and open to the public.
On Colorado Day, Aug. 1, the main event in downtown Denver will be a Community Fest hosted by History Colorado in the Golden Triangle, just south of Civic Center Park and the state Capitol. The festival will begin with a free pancake breakfast at 9 a.m., followed by musical performances, a street festival and an art market.
The History Colorado Center, the Center for Colorado Women’s History and the Denver Art Museum will offer free admission throughout the festival. A museum exhibit, “38th Star: Colorado Becomes the Centennial State,” is currently on display at the History Colorado Center.
The Colorado Capitol building will be open for its own celebration on Colorado Day. Lt. Gov. Dianne Primavera and state lawmakers will be on hand for a schedule of events that includes a reenactment of Colorado’s 1876 statehood proclamation, a new art exhibit in the Capitol rotunda, the dedication of a commemorative tapestry and the ceremonial cutting of a 150th birthday cake.
The Governor’s Residence at Boettcher Mansion will also host two open house events between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. on Friday and Saturday. The Colorado State Archives, too, will host public tours of its collections on July 31.
Other events in the Denver area on Saturday include the Colorado Day BAZAAR at Commons Park, scheduled to begin at noon and featuring performances from Denver bands like Los Mocochetes and Brothers of Brass; the Mile High 150 Expo air show at 4 p.m. at Broomfield’s Rocky Mountain Metropolitan Airport; and the Mile Long Table, a food-focused event at the National Western Center beginning at 5 p.m.
A special 250-150 drone show will follow the Colorado Rockies game at Coors Field on Aug. 1, with the first 15,000 fans receiving a commemorative Colorado at 150 flag, while the Colorado Rapids will celebrate Colorado Night at Dick’s Sporting Goods Park with postgame fireworks.
14er climbs
Local events are also planned in communities across the state, from an ice cream social in Kiowa to a 150th Birthday Bash in Olathe. Events in Colorado Springs include a daytime celebration at the Colorado Springs Pioneers Museum and the United We Rock festival at Rock Ledge Ranch.
In partnership with the state’s Office of Outdoor Recreation Industry, select teams of climbers will ascend many of Colorado’s “14ers” on Saturday in another of the America 250-Colorado 150 commission’s signature initiatives. Applicants to participate in the commemorative climbs were selected through a public lottery.
A list of events across the state can be found on the America 250-Colorado 150 website.

title: South Dakota Republicans go to polls in historic runoff for governor nomination
description: Republican voters will select their nominee for governor today in South Dakota’s first statewide runoff election. Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. local time. The runoff is the only item on the ballot, and because the state Republican Party does not open its primaries to non-Republican voters, only registered Republicans are allowed […]
text:
South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden, left, and Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden are the candidates in today's runoff election for the Republican nomination for governor. (Photos by South Dakota Searchlight)Republican voters will select their nominee for governor today in South Dakota’s first statewide runoff election.
Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. local time. The runoff is the only item on the ballot, and because the state Republican Party does not open its primaries to non-Republican voters, only registered Republicans are allowed to vote. The registration deadline was July 13.


Voting info
Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. local time today.
The election is only open to Republican voters who registered by the July 13 deadline. Voters can use the state’s Voter Information Portal to check their registration status and find their polling place.
Identification is required to vote. Acceptable forms include a South Dakota driver’s license or non-driver ID card, a passport or other picture ID issued by the U.S. government, a tribal photo ID, or a current student photo ID issued by a South Dakota high school or college.


Gov. Larry Rhoden and Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden are the last Republican candidates standing after a four-way primary on June 2. Nobody reached the legal threshold to win that election — the first time that’s happened since lawmakers approved a state law in 1985 requiring a top-two runoff when nobody reaches 35% in primaries for governor, U.S. House and U.S. Senate. Previously when no candidate received 35%, delegates at state political party conventions chose the nominee.
Today’s winner will advance to the Nov. 3 general election to face the Democratic nominee for governor, former legislator Dan Ahlers.
Republican turnout for the primary election was 43%. Advance voting for the runoff has been underway since June 12 and was continuing Monday, with 24,502 ballots received by Monday morning. That’s about the same pace as the primary, when 26,125 Republicans voted early. There are nearly 330,000 registered Republican voters in the state.
The scramble for the Republican nomination started in January 2025 when then-Gov. Kristi Noem resigned to accept a job in President Donald Trump’s administration. Rhoden was Noem’s lieutenant governor and was automatically promoted to serve the last two years of her second term.
State House Speaker Jon Hansen became the first Republican to announce a candidacy for governor on April 24, 2025. Doeden, U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson and Rhoden entered the race in the ensuing months.
Johnson was the presumptive frontrunner and led in several early polls. He had the most campaign money at his disposal and the highest statewide profile due to his four terms in the U.S. House.
But on primary election night, Doeden surprised the political establishment by finishing first at 31%, followed by Rhoden at 25%, Johnson at 23% and Hansen at 21%.

title: Facing financial headwinds, rural Arkansas hospitals turn to partnerships
description: Arkansas’ largest state-funded healthcare institution recently partnered with two rural hospitals in an effort to improve care, a move that health leaders say could provide a model for providers facing financial strain. It’s one way hospitals statewide and nationwide are adapting to an increasingly difficult healthcare landscape that has forced hospitals to[...]
text:
The UAMS medical sciences campus on Markham Street in Little Rock. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas’ largest state-funded healthcare institution recently partnered with two rural hospitals in an effort to improve care, a move that health leaders say could provide a model for providers facing financial strain.
It’s one way hospitals statewide and nationwide are adapting to an increasingly difficult healthcare landscape that has forced hospitals to cut services or close entirely. There were 40 hospital mergers and acquisitions nationwide in the first half of 2026, one of the highest numbers in the same time span so far this decade.
The University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences will co-manage the Mena Regional Health System in western Arkansas and the Helena Hospital in the Delta. Administrators of both smaller hospitals said they’re optimistic that partnering with UAMS will enhance their ability to provide high-quality care.
“For the future, having some strong, solid partners that you can build some service lines or brand recognition with is going to become important,” Mena hospital CEO Paul Ervin said.
Within the past month and a half, Baptist Health acquired the Magnolia Regional Medical Center, acquired the South Arkansas Regional Hospital in El Dorado and transferred Baptist Health family clinics in four River Valley cities to the Springdale-based Community Clinic healthcare system.
“It’s been great for hospitals to maintain independence, but I just don’t see how that’s going to be a good model going forward,” Helena Hospital interim CEO Rex Jones said.
Low reimbursement rates force Arkansas hospitals to scale back services

 Hospitals face low reimbursement, rising costs

Arkansas hospitals receive among the nation’s lowest reimbursement rates from both private and government-run insurers, but labor, equipment and administrative costs have increased. Additionally, one parent company of multiple Arkansas health insurance plans will stop participating in the state’s Medicaid expansion next year.
Fewer payment sources strains the system because with more self-paying patients, “self-pay often means no pay,” UAMS Chancellor C. Lowry Barnes said.
Some hospitals have changed their number of beds or primary forms of patient care in order to get more federal Medicare and Medicaid funding. The Helena Hospital is classified as a rural emergency hospital, meaning it reduced inpatient services in exchange for more federal funds.
In November 2024, the Mena Regional Health System became a critical access hospital to get more federal funds for inpatient treatment of Medicare recipients. The Magnolia Regional Medical Center became a critical access hospital a year later.
Both facilities are located at least 35 miles from other hospitals, have no more than 25 acute care beds and provide 24/7 emergency care. As of January, there are nearly 1,400 critical access hospitals nationwide.
Critical access status was good for the Mena hospital financially, but partnering with UAMS gives it a new set of resources, including a radiology technician training program and a family medicine rotation, Ervin said.
 Changes follow string of labor units closing in state

When asked for comment on Community Clinic’s acquisition of Baptist Health’s family clinics in Alma, Van Buren, Greenwood and Fort Smith, a Baptist spokesperson deferred to its June 30 announcement.
“Together, we are working toward a seamless transition that ensures patients continue to receive the trusted, compassionate primary care they know close to home while advancing our shared commitment to improving the health and well-being of the communities we serve,” Brandi Stewart, interim president and chief nursing officer of the Baptist Health Western Region, said in the release.
Community Clinic CEO Judd Semingson said in the release that the organization is committed to “listening first, showing up consistently and earning trust over time” in the River Valley.

Drive time to Arkansas hospitals for labor and delivery getting longer, report shows


Between April and June, Baptist’s Fort Smith hospital cut 150 jobs, shuttered several outpatient clinics and stopped providing a range of inpatient services, including oncology and pulmonary care, Talk Business & Politics reported.
The cuts came after Baptist Health-Fort Smith became Arkansas’ eighth hospital since 2020 to close its labor and delivery unit. The closures mean rural Arkansans face increasingly long drives to delivering hospitals, according to the Arkansas Center for Health Improvement.
Baptist’s footprint in western Arkansas has shrunk as its footprint in south Arkansas has grown. One of south Arkansas’ largest hospitals and one of the region’s few with a labor and delivery unit is the newly rebranded Baptist Health Medical Center-El Dorado.
The specifics of the new resources available to Baptist Health Medical Center-Magnolia are still to be determined, president and CEO William Giles said, but overall he is “surprised and thankful that Baptist came in and saved the hospital.”
 Rural areas’ health needs

Fort Smith’s Mercy Hospital still delivers babies, but the closure of the maternity ward at Baptist Health-Fort Smith made the one in Mena even more important to western and southwestern Arkansas, a region lacking in maternal health resources, Ervin said.
Partnering with UAMS makes it easier for the Mena Regional Health System to care for high-risk pregnancies, Ervin said, thanks to UAMS’ perinatology and maternal-fetal medicine specialties.
Access to other specialty care such as cardiology and neurology will reduce the Mena hospital’s need to transfer patients to hospitals in larger cities, Ervin said, because they can determine someone’s need for a hospital stay via telehealth consultations with UAMS professionals.
“Many times [with] the patients that we do transfer out to another community, they get there and the specialists take a look at them and say, ‘Well, you know what? You’re fine. There’s really nothing serious. You can take care of this at home,’” Ervin said.
In Helena, Jones said “one of our bigger threats” to the healthcare landscape is that some local physicians are nearing retirement. He and Giles both said they hope mergers can help recruit new physicians.
Rural Health Transformation program won’t make up for federal budget cuts, experts agree

“A lot of people have an idea, especially as a physician, ‘Perhaps I can’t make it in a rural area, or I don’t know if I really want to practice in a rural area,’ and so they don’t want to give it a try,” Jones said. 
But, Jones said, rural medicine “can be extremely attractive, economically and just personally.”
Improving rural healthcare in any way possible is especially important in the face of federal Medicaid cuts, Ervin said. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 slashes rural Medicaid spending by $15.5 billion annually over the next decade. The new law also imposes work requirements that are expected to cut thousands from Medicaid expansion.
Ervin said rural hospitals should prepare for an influx of debt-burdened, low-income patients in the coming years.
“Hopefully between now and then, there’s going to be some things done to try to shore up the shortfalls and keep people covered,” he said.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Candidates bank on endorsements as primary draws near
description: Political endorsements and independent spending are ramping up as congressional candidates wrangle for votes in the closing days of the Aug. 6 primary. U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles of Culleoka is depending on the backing of President Donald Trump, U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson and the House Freedom Caucus to carry him to another term in […]
text:
Tennessee congressional and gubernatorial candidates are benefitting from big name endorsements, including, clockwise from left, state Rep. Justin Pearson, Sen. London Lamar, U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn and U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles. (Photos:  John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Political endorsements and independent spending are ramping up as congressional candidates wrangle for votes in the closing days of the Aug. 6 primary.
U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles of Culleoka is depending on the backing of President Donald Trump, U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson and the House Freedom Caucus to carry him to another term in the redrawn 5th Congressional District where he faces former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher. Trump is hosting a tele-town hall with Ogles on Tuesday, the same type of event he held for now-U.S. Rep. Matt Van Epps days before November’s special election.
In the waning days of the election, Hatcher is drawing the support of former Gov. Bill Haslam, former Georgia Gov. Sonny Perdue and former U.S. Rep. Zach Wamp.
He also netted the backing of state Sen. John Stevens, three firefighters associations and a political action committee called Invest in Tomorrow Coalition. The PAC is planning to spend heavily over the next week on TV ads backing Hatcher and attacking Ogles, according to a report.
Ogles, who also received the endorsement of Republican Sens. Bill Hagerty and Marsha Blackburn, a gubernatorial candidate, has spent more than $617,000 since early 2025 but had only $57,600 in his account at the mid-July reporting deadline, according to Federal Election Commission reports. Hatcher raised nearly $720,000 since last August and had $104,800 in his federal account, the latest report shows, while also benefiting from the outside spending, which is attacking Ogles over questions about his resume and an investigation into his campaign finances.
Former governor steps in
Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder landed the endorsement of former Tennessee Gov. Phil Bredesen in the Democratic primary for the 5th Congressional District seat.
“I admire the way he has handled himself as mayor — focused on results, not theatrics,” Bredesen, a two-term governor and two-term Nashville mayor, said in a release.
Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder (Photo: J. Holly McCall/Tennessee Lookout)
Former U.S. Rep. John Tanner, outgoing U.S. Rep. Steve Cohen, the Congressional Black Caucus PAC and his father-in-law, Ripley Mayor Craig Fitzhugh, one-time leader of the House Democratic Caucus.
Molder is running against Yolanda Cooper-Sutton, DeVante Hill, Rachel Hurley and Carrie Ann Iacomini but will see his toughest opposition in either Hatcher or Ogles in the general election to be decided in November.
Democrats tout support
In the Democratic primary for the 9th Congressional District seat, state Rep. Justin Pearson received the endorsement of the Service Employees International Union and the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees while raising $2.2 million.
Pearson is going up against Democratic state Sen. London Lamar, who received the support of Cohen, who has represented Memphis in the Tennessee Legislature and Congress since 1983. She also landed the backing of Memphis Mayor Paul Young.
Pearson also netted the endorsement of U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who said the Tennessee candidate would stand up to “the rich and power-hungry elites,” as well as Massachusetts U.S. Sen. Ed Markey, U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio Cortez and multiple members of the state Senate and state House.
More Trump backing
Republican state Sen. Brent Taylor of Shelby County received the endorsement of Trump as he goes head-to-head with state Rep. Todd Warner in the 9th Congressional District primary.
Blackburn, Hagerty, U.S. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Tennessee congressional delegation members, U.S. Reps. Matt Van Epps, Diana Harshbarger and Chuck Fleischmann, and Tennessee Lt. Gov. Randy McNally are supporting Taylor as well. 
President Donald Trump endorsed state Sen. Brent Taylor, a Memphis Republican, in the latter’s race for the 9th Congressional District. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Warner, who keeps a life-sized cutout of Trump in his state office, drew the support of Republican state Rep. Jody Barrett of Dickson County. Both state lawmakers opposed Gov. Bill Lee’s private-school voucher program but couldn’t stop its passage.
On the gubernatorial front
Blackburn and U.S. Rep. John Rose are both hoping for the endorsement of Trump, which is usually considered a path to victory. But the president has declined to issue an official endorsement of either candidate.
Instead, Blackburn has gotten the endorsement of U.S. Reps. Tim Burchett, Van Epps and Fleischmann, in addition to Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, who is her  treasurer and could be the frontrunner for her Senate seat if she wins the governorship.
Rose netted the endorsement of former U.S. Rep. Diane Black of Gallatin, also an ex-member of the state House, who ran for governor in 2018.
State Rep. Monty Fritts received the backing of Barrett.

title: Fifty for 150: Colorado State Fair incorporated in Pueblo in 1886
description: The Southern Colorado Agricultural and Industrial Association, after holding multiple fairs in Pueblo County since the 1870s, incorporated as the State Fair Association on Nov. 17, 1886. That established Pueblo as the host of Colorado’s annual state fair, now entering its 140th year of the tradition. Previous official state agricultural and industrial fairs[...]
text:
Leonard Stroud trick rides on a horse at the Colorado State Fair rodeo in Pueblo in this undated photograph from between 1910 and 1930. The State Fair Association officially incorporated in Pueblo in 1886. (Courtesy of Denver Public Library Special Collections, Z-693)The Southern Colorado Agricultural and Industrial Association, after holding multiple fairs in Pueblo County since the 1870s, incorporated as the State Fair Association on Nov. 17, 1886. That established Pueblo as the host of Colorado’s annual state fair, now entering its 140th year of the tradition.
 


This story is part of Colorado at 150. Each Fifty for 150 story focuses on an event that helped define Colorado over 150 years of statehood. Newsline is publishing one Fifty for 150 story every weekday in reverse chronological order until the sesquicentennial, Aug. 1, when the final of 50 stories, about the declaration of statehood, will appear.



Previous official state agricultural and industrial fairs took place near Denver, but there was general dissatisfaction with the events and the agricultural displays. A lot of Colorado’s cultivated land at the time was along the South Platte and Arkansas Rivers and their tributaries, making southern Colorado a prime location for a permanent state fair.
The fair purchased 50 acres of land near what is now Mineral Palace Park in Pueblo and held the first fair the next year. Horse races were especially popular in the early years of the fair.
“The state fair opens today, and every citizen should make it his special duty to visit it and induce others to do so,” said an Oct. 4, 1887, article in The Pueblo Daily Chieftain. “Everything is in excellent shape at the fairgrounds for the reception of visitors, and those who go will see many things that they never dreamed were to be seen in Pueblo.”
Many local businesses decided to close on the Thursday of that first fair so their employees could attend “and contribute not only to their own personal pleasure, but to the success of an undertaking in which we should all feel a pride.”
In 1890, the fair sold its original location and bought a new site west of Lake Minnequa. The association then moved to the current Colorado State Fairgrounds on Beulah Avenue in 1900 and built a new half-mile racetrack, grandstand, exhibition hall and stables. Attendance at the new site boomed to nearly 16,000 people.
The SFA deeded that land to the state in 1917, and the Legislature created a commission to run the fair.
During World War I in 1917, the fairgrounds served as a training base for the Colorado Army National Guard. New Deal-era funding helped the construction of new buildings, including the Palace of Agriculture, and other infrastructure at the fairgrounds. Fiesta Day, dedicated to Pueblo’s Hispanic culture, was introduced in 1966 and now includes a parade and pageant.
Today, the fairgrounds span over 100 acres and the event, a point of pride for Pueblo, lasts 11 days. It includes concerts, rodeos, agricultural and livestock exhibits, fine art competitions and a carnival. In 2025, about 430,000 people attended the fair, down from a recent peak of over 509,000 in 2023.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Kentucky’s nurses want effective leadership from their governing board
description: Across Kentucky, a troubling pattern is emerging. Whether in healthcare, education, or non-profit organizations, board decisions are increasingly being questioned — not simply because difficult decisions are being made, but because stakeholders are asking how those decisions are being made. Recent events involving boards governing Fayette County Public Schoo[...]
text:
The Kentucky Nurses Association needs to answer members questions, two advocates say. (Getty Images)Across Kentucky, a troubling pattern is emerging. Whether in healthcare, education, or non-profit organizations, board decisions are increasingly being questioned — not simply because difficult decisions are being made, but because stakeholders are asking how those decisions are being made.
Recent events involving boards governing Fayette County Public Schools, the University of Kentucky, and the Kentucky Hospital Association, demonstrate a broader trend: the public is demanding greater transparency, stronger governance, and meaningful accountability from those entrusted with leadership.
However, one major nonprofit board remains largely silent about a decision impacting more than 93,000 Kentucky nurses. Six months after the departure of Delanor Manson — a nationally acclaimed nurse executive who served as the organization’s CEO — the Kentucky Nurses Association (KNA) Board of Directors have failed to provide a transparent, public accounting of the departure decision. This prolonged silence fuels uncertainty and erodes confidence in leadership.
Credit: Kentucky Nurses Association.
Nurses are taught that silence is not a virtue when patient safety is at stake. The landmark Silence Kills research reinforced a core professional value: speaking up is an ethical responsibility. That same principle should extend beyond the bedside and into the boardroom. Board leaders cannot expect transparency from frontline nurses while exempting themselves from the same accountability. Six months of limited communication regarding significant leadership decisions does not strengthen confidence in governance — it weakens it.
While each situation is unique, there are common issues facing board governance in Kentucky that are strikingly similar to KNA board leadership, including:

Oversight vs. overreach: Boards must govern strictly at the policy level rather than micromanaging daily operations.
Transparent communication: Stakeholders expect leadership choices to be explained openly while balancing essential legal boundaries.
Due process: Abrupt executive departures spark valid concerns about whether established evaluation and disciplinary policies were followed.
Fiduciary duty: Directors owe a legal duty of care, loyalty, and obedience to keep decisions aligned with the core mission.
Absolute independence: Boards must resist external pressures from political figures, lobbyists, or donors, protecting objective deliberation from outside agendas.

Nurse leaders are increasingly asking the question whether boards are receiving sufficient education and mentoring. Individuals often join boards because they are respected leaders in their professions, but expertise in medicine, nursing, education, business, or law does not automatically translate into expertise in board governance. The success of an organization depends on board leaders who embrace mentorship and recognize the value of the wisdom from previous leaders. Their historical perspective, institutional knowledge, and lived experience provide invaluable insights that inform sound decision-making, strengthen governance, and support the organization’s long-term success.
The larger concern is not simply the performance of Kentucky’s nonprofit boards. It is the growing expectation that boards uphold their fiduciary responsibilities with unwavering fidelity to the missions they serve – and the public’s diminishing tolerance when they do not.
Non-profit and member-based organizations, such as the Kentucky Nurses Association, perform vital work that strengthens our communities. Their success depends on boards that embrace transparency, respect due process, and recognize that their ultimate responsibility is not to themselves, but to the mission and the members they have been entrusted to serve.
Equally important is the independence of board decision-making. Directors have a fiduciary obligation to exercise independent judgment that places the organization’s mission and the interests of its members above external pressures. Whether those pressures come from special interest groups, political leaders, lobbyists, influential donors, business partners, or other outside stakeholders, board members must remain steadfast in their duty of loyalty to the organization they were elected or appointed to serve. 
Decisions influenced by outside agendas rather than objective deliberation undermine public confidence, create the appearance of conflicts of interest, and erode the trust that is essential to effective governance.  Trust is built through transparency. And transparency begins with boards that understand accountability is not something to be feared—it is the very essence of good governance and strong organizations.
Kentucky nurses who are members of professional nursing organizations have every right to expect that board decisions are made with integrity and based on facts, sound judgment, ethical principles, and the organization’s governing documents including member approved policies, procedures, and bylaws — not on political influence or the preferences of those with the loudest voices or greatest access. 
The time for silence has passed. Trust is restored not by silence, but by truth, accountability, and transparency. Adopt strategies such as our Safeguarding Association Fiduciary Excellence (SAFE) efforts  and attend board meetings and demand the answers all stakeholders deserve.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: What Colorado loses with the politics of performance
description: I fell in love with politics because I believed democracy was built through relationships. At 16, I knocked on doors because I believed ordinary people could shape their communities. At 18, I became a Democratic National Convention delegate because I believed democracy depended on participation. I saw politics not as a path to branding, but […]
text:
(Getty Images)I fell in love with politics because I believed democracy was built through relationships.
At 16, I knocked on doors because I believed ordinary people could shape their communities. At 18, I became a Democratic National Convention delegate because I believed democracy depended on participation. I saw politics not as a path to branding, but as a responsibility to listen, organize and serve.
Today, after nearly a decade of organizing and working around Colorado politics, I find myself asking: When did politics become more about performance than public service?
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Disagreement is not the problem. Democracy requires debate, competing ideas, and contested elections. What concerns me is that our political culture increasingly rewards visibility over substance.
Social media has transformed campaigns into branding exercises. Candidates are judged by how effectively they communicate online rather than the depth of their work. Outrage spreads faster than nuance. Somewhere along the way, we began mistaking being loud for being effective.
But a digital presence is not inherently a problem. Leaders like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani demonstrate that communication strategies can coexist with grassroots organizing and policy advocacy. The lesson is not to abandon communication, but to ensure visibility is matched by substance.
A viral post can start a conversation, but it cannot replace listening to constituents, building coalitions, negotiating, and delivering results.
When I first became involved in Colorado politics, success was measured by relationships and results — not visibility. We disagreed, but we still knocked on doors and made phone calls because lasting change required trust.
Those moments rarely go viral. But they are the foundation of democracy.



A viral post can start a conversation, but it cannot replace listening to constituents, building coalitions, negotiating, and delivering results.



Today, too often, politics feels driven by internet battles, ideological purity tests, and public call-outs. People are judged by whether they use the “right” language or belong to the “right” group rather than whether they can solve problems.
This year’s Colorado primaries reminded me how important trust is. Across races involving candidates with different backgrounds and priorities, I found myself asking: Before we divide volunteers, donors and communities into competing camps, have we done enough to build relationships with one another first?
Competition is healthy in democracy. Primaries give voters choices and strengthen accountability. But competition should not replace collaboration.
How often do candidates with similar values sit down over coffee before launching campaigns? How often do we ask whether communities would be better served by building coalitions rather than brands?
These questions are not about any one candidate or election. They are about the political culture we are creating.
Before every election, voters should ask: What are we actually rewarding? Experience? Character? Integrity? Policy knowledge? The ability to build coalitions? Or are we simply rewarding whoever dominates our social media feeds?
There are important questions and legitimate debates surrounding organizations and candidates, but instead of finding answers, people are often met with vitriol from voices chasing online attention rather than solutions. If someone’s goal is to “win” an argument instead of approaching the conversation with the intention of understanding or persuading they distort the very candidate or cause they claim to represent. 
In an era of algorithms, AI summaries, and social media feeds, it has become harder to distinguish reporting from commentary and evidence from opinion. Verifying information requires time, and time is limited in today’s world.
That reality should not make us less willing to engage. It should make us more willing to seek context, ask questions, and approach difficult conversations with humility.
Despite everything, I haven’t lost faith in democracy — I’ve lost faith in a political culture that rewards internet warriors over bridge-builders, performative victories over practical solutions, and outrage over organizing and service.
Colorado deserves a culture where leadership is measured not by followers or viral moments, but by humility, integrity, trust and the work of serving communities.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Brown water, dust and loud noises: Louisa homeowner sues Amazon over data center construction
description: From the driveway of his Louisa home and business, Austin Newsome sees dozens of dump trucks barrel down Route 33 most days, hauling dirt and other debris. The road is stained rusty red from the soil displaced by the construction of Amazon’s latest data center campus in the county.  One day, Newsom said, his neighbor […]
text:
Austin Newsom explains how construction of a new Amazon data center campus across the street from his home has disrupted his life, July 2026. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)From the driveway of his Louisa home and business, Austin Newsome sees dozens of dump trucks barrel down Route 33 most days, hauling dirt and other debris. The road is stained rusty red from the soil displaced by the construction of Amazon’s latest data center campus in the county. 
One day, Newsom said, his neighbor across the street up and left. 
“I was like, oh no, he’s picked up and gone. And then I looked up who owned the property, and it was Amazon,” Newsom said in the garage of Central VA Marine, the business he co-owns and runs near his home.
Newsom’s home rests on the border of the Northeast Creek technology overlay district, a portion of the county zoned to attract specific businesses, including data centers. 
It is the site of Amazon’s second data center campus in the county, with plans for this project detailing ten buildings, three substations, stormwater structures, logistic and administrative buildings and associated infrastructures. Construction is slated to be completed in 2031.
A truck hauling materials barrels down Route 33 in Louisa from the site of an under-construction Amazon data center campus. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)
When the project started  in March 2025, Newsom reported to county officials several disturbances —  loud noises, trucks kicking up big clouds of dust — and his tap water turned a muddy brown color. 
The water discoloration persisted off and on for months as the data center buildout continued. 
“(My well has) made it through four major droughts we’ve had since the ’50s and never had an issue with it,” Newsom said. “I’ve lived here for 11-12 years. Never had an issue with it ever until they started doing things over there.”
Newsom and his spouse also experienced loud sounds emitting from the construction site in the late hours of the night. They said light pollution from the site floods their children’s bedroom. 
One of his chief concerns is that dust from the project is covering the roadway. Amazon responded by deploying street sweepers and spraying water to keep the dust down. But Newsom said it isn’t enough.
“They got this truck out there that just pretty much just dumps water on the road. The roads are covered with mud, Newsom said. “Now all the mud just washes into my driveway.” 
In August 2025, Newsom filed a lawsuit against the company seeking relief from the negative impacts the construction levied on his home and boat detailing and repair business. 
In the private nuisance suit, Newsom alleged that vibrations from the construction are cracking the foundation of his house. The project is devaluing his home, disrupting natural drainage and impacting his mental health, Newsom said in the filing.
Newsom operates his business in a workshop near his home. He said in his filing that his customers, who are often towing boats, have had many “near accidents” with the trucks.
The closest school is just one mile away from the construction site. A Louisa Public Schools representative said the trucks have not yet posed any issues. 
Amazon is already constructing another data center in the county near the Lake Anna Power Station within the county and was planning for a third project but withdrew it in July 2025 due to public backlash.
 Many problems, few solutions

Newsom has aired his complaints to county leaders and Amazon many times. He said he was met with promises that the issues would be looked into, but they remain unresolved
Board of Supervisors Chair Duane Adams said he had been in contact with Newsom and his wife multiple times about their concerns and worked to help get some of them addressed.
“I’ve treated Mr. and Mrs. Newsom as I do with all my constituents. I try to be very responsive and help address issues that may be impacting them and help mitigate the circumstances,” Adams said.
When work began to build the data center, it pushed Newsom to start building his family a new home. 
He has put his current home up for sale, but he said there haven’t been any bites because when potential buyers find out what’s under construction across the street, they lose interest.
A sign advertises a home for sale n Louisa County across the street from Amazon data center construction site. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)
 Transmission line presents another obstacle

Another challenge is that the preliminary route options for the high-voltage Valley Link transmission line could run through Newsom’s property. The line will feed power to energy-intensive data centers in Northern Virginia, and may force Newsom to tear down the workshop that houses his business.  
Map of potential Valley Link transmission routes through Louisa County. (Valley Link Transmission)
“So I’m getting out of here, but I’m just going to be stuck with this property,” Newsom said. “(I’m) going to be stuck with two mortgages.”
The final preferred route has not been selected for the 115-mile 765 kilovolt transmission line that will stretch from Lynchburg to Culpeper County. 
What’s ahead
Newsom’s lawsuit continues playing out in court, with a preliminary hearing set in the case for Aug. 19, according to U.S. District Court for the Western District of Virginia (Charlottesville) records. 
Amazon tried to persuade the court to throw out the nuisance claim lawsuit, arguing in its court filing that “the brown water, noise, diminished air quality, and light pollution, are each insubstantial and thus require dismissal of the entire nuisance claim.”
U.S. District Judge Jasmine H. Yoon allowed the nuisance claim to move forward, but dismissed Newsom’s claim of injunctive relief, stating it could still be done as part of the nuisance claim but not as a separate claim. 
The Louisa man’s story has captured the attention of prominent environmental advocate and paralegal Erin Brockovich, who led a successful lawsuit against a major oil and gas company for groundwater contamination in 1993. 
Brockovich’s latest campaign raises awareness about the environmental impacts of data centers nationwide. Brockovich has posted multiple videos on her social media with Newsom, describing his experiences and walking through his lawsuit. 
Newsom said he plans to keep pushing back against the disturbances created by the forthcoming data center campus. 
“You know, one person can make a difference,” Newsom said. “So if one person like myself can get as far as I have and make the differences that I have with everything, everybody else can, too.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Does extreme heat cause train derailments? A Virginia railroad expert weighs in.
description: After a freight train derailed in Richmond earlier this month, questions have emerged about what caused the crash and whether the extreme heat played a role. Excluding the July train accident in Richmond, Virginia has recorded four derailments, all at speeds under 9 mph, since January, Federal Railroad Administration data shows. The incidents reflect the […]
text:
CSX Transportation is working to repair the damage near the intersection of Dock and 20th Streets in Richmond that contributed to three train cars derailing from a 200-car train and crashing into the Riverfront Canal on July 3, 2026. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)After a freight train derailed in Richmond earlier this month, questions have emerged about what caused the crash and whether the extreme heat played a role.
Excluding the July train accident in Richmond, Virginia has recorded four derailments, all at speeds under 9 mph, since January, Federal Railroad Administration data shows. The incidents reflect the broader challenge of preventing derailments, which can stem from track defects, equipment failures, human error, or adverse weather conditions.
J.B. Jones Chair of Mechanical Engineering at Virginia Tech and director of the Center for Vehicle Systems & Safety Mehdi Ahmadian is an expert in how extreme weather affects rail tracks, the role of steel in rail infrastructure and how rail operators respond to extreme weather events.
“I can tell you confidently that the railroads do an exceptional job of maintaining the general condition of the track,” Ahmadian said. “There are thousands of trains and rail cars that operate on this complex railroad network that we have around the country, and by and large, they will travel on those tracks safely and without any incidents.”
Ahmadian, also the founder of the Railroad Transportation Laboratory, designed to help improve rail and truck safety through research and to educate students who will enter the transportation industry and advance public safety, said the U.S. rail network is “extremely complex,” carrying mostly heavy freight and sharing passenger trains in some corridors.
With over 35 years in the industry, Ahmadian said he believes railroads do an exceptional job maintaining track conditions. High-profile derailments can distort public perception, he added.
Ahmadian said one misconception is that all derailments result from extreme heat.
 Impact to rail tracks in extreme weather

Regardless of the weather, Ahmadian said railroad tracks can be affected by both extreme heat and cold temperatures. This is one of the biggest challenges for railroad operators when moving passengers and cargo.
Even though train wheels look large, Ahmadian said the actual spot where each wheel touches the rail is only about the size of a quarter, roughly one-inch across.
Under extreme heat, Ahmadian said rail tracks can expand and buckle, resembling a large S-shaped curve. Even the slightest deviation in the track can cause a wheel to drop between the rail tracks, triggering derailment, with each railcar carrying thousands of pounds over eight wheels.
In extreme cold conditions, rail tracks can contract as tension increases, like tightening a guitar string, Ahmadian said. If the force exceeds the rail’s strength, it will break, creating a gap in the track and possible derailment.
Railroad tracks near Keokee, Va. (Sarah Vogelsong/Virginia Mercury)
 Steel remains the best ‘practical material’ for rail tracks

Since the 19th century, steel has been the preferred material for railroad tracks and Ahmadian said it’s still the best choice for rail construction and maintenance.
“There is no better practical material that we can use for the extreme demands of running heavy trains,” Ahmadian said.
Steel has evolved over 150 years and is now specifically engineered to withstand extreme mechanical loads from heavy trains and resist wear. 
Rail tracks can last between 20 and 40 years, depending on traffic volume and other conditions, Ahmadian said, which is amazing considering the continuous heavy loads, thermal cycling between heat and cold and constant environmental exposure.
Ahmadian said rail steel is a cost-effective engineering achievement that can’t be easily replaced.
 Rail operators’ response to extreme weather

Passenger rail operators regularly adjust travel schedules that can trigger train delays if weather conditions impact rail tracks. Ahmadian says this is common for maintaining safe travel for passengers.
On hot days, Ahmadian said operators may implement “slow orders,” which require trains to run at reduced speeds on affected segments of the rail track and help reduce the risk of a heat-weakened track causing a derailment.
Ahmadian said rail operators could also temporarily suspend traffic if conditions are deemed particularly risky, typically on the hottest parts of the day. He said services typically resume once conditions are considered safe.
Maintenance crews inspect tracks for cracks or breaks caused by cold-induced contraction on extremely cold days.
Crews also investigate rail tracks ahead of trains, often using pickup trucks fitted with rail wheels to move efficiently along the tracks. Ahmadian said these patrols monitor for lateral rail shifting,  signs of track panel shifting or potential buckling. They then recommend slow orders, repairs, or other interventions, if needed.

 Richmond derailment still under investigation

CSX is still working on repairing the damage near the intersection of Dock and 20th Streets in Richmond that contributed to three train cars derailing from a 200-car train into the Riverfront Canal on July 3. 
No injuries and no HAZMAT issues resulted from the accident. Crews continue to remove the grain from the three cars submerged in the canal. A spokesperson said the case is still under investigation.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: It’s time for Virginia lawmakers to expand protections for domestic violence victims
description: I am a Virginia attorney, and have lived here most of my life. I know the legal system here and understand the burden of proof. I believed that my knowledge of the law, and my ability to hire experienced counsel, would allow me to protect myself when I left an abusive marriage. I was wrong. […]
text:
Virginia should consider studying how other states have incorporated coercive control into their family law frameworks while preserving due process, guest columnist Maria Riegger writes. (Photo byI am a Virginia attorney, and have lived here most of my life. I know the legal system here and understand the burden of proof. I believed that my knowledge of the law, and my ability to hire experienced counsel, would allow me to protect myself when I left an abusive marriage.
I was wrong.
Access to justice is not simply about access to lawyers or financial resources. It is also about whether the law provides an effective remedy.
Virginia has made important progress in addressing domestic violence, but our legal system still struggles to provide relief when abuse consists primarily of coercive control rather than direct physical harm, leaving victims without timely or clearly applicable protection.
Virginia law recognizes some forms of nonphysical abuse, including stalking. But victims of abuse consisting primarily of coercive control often must fit their experiences into legal doctrines and evidentiary frameworks that were developed largely around violence, threats, and physical injury.
That gap can leave victims, most of them women, especially vulnerable during divorce.
Domestic violence experts define coercive control as a pattern of behavior intended to cause the victim to fear that violence will be used against them, or behavior that causes the victim to experience repeated trauma that has a significant effect on the victim’s daily activities.
Coercive control is about eroding the victim’s autonomy over time through gaslighting and manipulation. This type of psychological abuse is essentially a campaign to wear down the victim’s defenses so that the abuser can more easily control them.
Coercive controllers sometimes do end up being violent when victims decide to leave the relationship. 
In 2021, The Virginia Mercury reported that about 40% of intimate partner homicides take place while or after a relationship is ending. This is precisely the time when abusers face a loss of control over the victim.
Some abusers appear adept at engaging in conduct that terrifies and destabilizes a partner while remaining difficult to fit into existing legal categories.
Like most other victims leaving these psychologically abusive relationships, I asked my attorney how I could keep my husband, an alcoholic with access to firearms, away from me while the divorce was pending.
The answer: Not much, unless I could obtain a protective order.
Although courts can exclude an abusive spouse from the home through a protective order, the victim must first prove conduct fitting a statutory framework focused on violence, force, threats or bodily injury. A sustained pattern of domination and psychological abuse may not fit neatly within this analysis.
And if the victim leaves the marital home to escape the control, the spouse who physically leaves may also face allegations of desertion unless the evidence establishes legal justification or constructive desertion.
Virginia precedent allows extreme nonphysical mistreatment to constitute cruelty as a fault basis in exceptional cases, thereby allowing the victim to file for divorce immediately. However, proving emotional or mental cruelty generally requires evidence of a sustained course of conduct serious enough to threaten health or make continued cohabitation unsafe.
And even if the victim files for divorce based on cruelty immediately, getting a hearing takes months, maybe even a year, still leaving the victim vulnerable while living with the abuser.
It is easier to prove physical harm because there is clear evidence, such as bruises.
But how do we prove coercive control? How do we prove psychological harm?
One way is through documenting the patterns through written narratives, text messages, and even video, but compiling a record takes time that the victim may not have.
How can victims protect themselves, and their children, when Virginia law does not provide timely relief?
Virginia has taken meaningful steps to address domestic violence over the past several decades, such as making stalking a basis for a protective order. The next challenge is to ensure that our legal system can respond effectively to protect victims when abuse is psychological, coercive, and cumulative rather than immediately visible. 
Moreover, coercive control often unfolds gradually and privately. Professionals trained to evaluate discrete incidents may not immediately recognize a pattern of domination when the evidence arrives piecemeal over months or years.
Money alone will not solve this problem.
Creative lawyering can help document patterns and identify existing remedies, but lawyers cannot create protections the law does not provide.
Virginia should consider studying how other states have incorporated coercive control into their family law frameworks while preserving due process. 
Several, such as Massachusetts and New Jersey, have enacted legislation recognizing coercive control in family-law proceedings, offering examples to study as Virginia lawmakers consider whether existing remedies adequately address this form of abuse.
At the same time, judges, attorneys, guardians ad litem, therapists and professionals who work with families should receive additional education on identifying patterns of coercive abuse and understanding how those patterns may appear in litigation.
