title: Estimated cost of proposed eastern South Dakota water pipeline is at least $8.4 billion
description: SIOUX FALLS — One of several proposed pipeline systems to deliver Missouri River water in South Dakota could cost $8.4 billion to $10 billion, according to estimates shared Monday. Dakota Mainstem Regional Water System Executive Director Kurt Pfeifle was on a panel speaking to the Rotary Club of Downtown Sioux Falls. “That includes about a […]
text:
A map of water providers that would be served by the proposed Dakota Mainstem Regional Water System pipeline project. (Courtesy of Dakota Mainstem)SIOUX FALLS — One of several proposed pipeline systems to deliver Missouri River water in South Dakota could cost $8.4 billion to $10 billion, according to estimates shared Monday.
Dakota Mainstem Regional Water System Executive Director Kurt Pfeifle was on a panel speaking to the Rotary Club of Downtown Sioux Falls. 
“That includes about a 30% contingency, but right now, there’s just so many unknowns,” Pfeifle said, referring to a cost estimate buffer. 
The system’s proposed pipeline would serve nearly 60 water providers across much of eastern South Dakota and portions of three neighboring states, with a capacity of 195 million gallons per day.
South Dakotan tells Congress of ‘growing water security risk’ if pipeline project is delayed

Pfeifle said the organization recently completed an initial study to arrive at those numbers and is beginning a $4.2 million feasibility study expected to take about two and a half years. 
Pending federal legislation sponsored by South Dakota’s congressional delegation would provide funding to help with that study and two other studies for the proposed Western Dakota Regional Water System pipeline, which has an estimated projected cost of $4 billion, and a planned expansion of the Lewis & Clark Regional Water System in southeast South Dakota, which has an estimated project cost of $2.5 billion. 
Lewis & Clark Regional Water System Executive Director Troy Larson and Minnehaha Community Water Corporation Executive Director Scott Buss were also on the panel.
Construction began on the Lewis & Clark system in 2003 and is ongoing, although the constructed portion already serves 20 member cities and rural water systems. Completion of the three-state, 44-million-gallon-per-day “base system” is estimated to cost $825 million, with completion sometime in 2028. Federal funding covers 80% of the cost.
Larson said the planned expansion will increase capacity to 60 million gallons per day by 2030. But he said the system’s members already project they will need an additional 95 million gallons per day over the next 40 years.
“That’s 60 plus 95, not 60 and then get to 95,” Larson said.  
The projects are driven by industry and population growth.
Minnehaha Community Water is a member-owned utility that receives water from the Lewis & Clark pipeline and the Big Sioux River aquifer, and delivers it to 5,300 rural customers and seven cities. Buss said the system has approached its limits during recent summers — particularly during droughts — and has rejected some economic development opportunities because it could not guarantee it would be able to deliver enough water.

text:
A powerful tornado hit parts of Appleton and Menasha Monday. (Photo by Appleton Police Department)A tornado hit parts of Appleton and Menasha Monday afternoon, damaging homes and leaving thousands without power. 
The National Weather Service described the storm as “extremely dangerous” and issued a particularly dangerous situation tornado warning — the second-highest level warning — shortly after noon. The agency said that a cluster of thunderstorms moved southeast across the state and that preliminary surveys are being conducted in the Appleton area to assess the damage and strength of the tornado. 
The NWS also said that two-inch hail was reported across the area. 
More than 110,000 homes across the state were still without power as of 5:15 p.m., according to We Energies. 
“We are aware of severe damage in broad areas. We are asking the public to stay indoors, watch out for downed power lines, do not drive around road closures, and do not drive around the area unless absolutely necessary,” the Menasha Police Department posted on Facebook. 
Wisconsin has seen a higher than average number of tornadoes this year as shifting weather patterns caused by climate change push the country’s traditional “tornado alley” eastward. The state climatology office said that June 2026 was the state’s most active June for storms since at least 2008.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: How Alaskans can help native bees thrive
description: On a bright June morning in Soldotna, a homeowner steps into the yard with a cup of coffee and notices a bumblebee working its way across a patch of blooming chives. It’s a small moment, but one that reflects a larger truth: the choices Alaskans make in their gardens, on their land and in their […]
text:
A bee is seen pollinating a backyard chive flower in Alaska. (Photo by Timothy Bundy)On a bright June morning in Soldotna, a homeowner steps into the yard with a cup of coffee and notices a bumblebee working its way across a patch of blooming chives. It’s a small moment, but one that reflects a larger truth: the choices Alaskans make in their gardens, on their land and in their communities can have a meaningful impact on the state’s native bees.
Alaska is home to more than a hundred species of native bees, from familiar bumblebees to tiny solitary bees that nest in the ground or in hollow stems. These insects pollinate wildflowers, berry bushes and many of the plants that support wildlife and local food production. As Alaska’s climate changes and invasive species spread, the role of everyday Alaskans in supporting pollinators has never been more important.
Plant flowers that feed bees
One of the simplest and most effective ways to help native bees is to plant flowers that provide nectar and pollen throughout the growing season. Early‑blooming willows, mid‑summer fireweed and late‑season asters offer food when bees need it most. Even small patches of flowers in yards, community gardens or along driveways can make a difference.
Native plants are especially valuable because they adapt to Alaska’s climate and support the bees that evolved alongside them. But many common garden plants — such as chives, raspberries and sunflowers — also provide excellent forage.
Plant native flowers in clumps rather than scattering individual plants, because larger patches are easier for bees to find and allow them to gather food more efficiently.
Protect nesting habitat
Unlike honeybees, most native bees in Alaska do not live in hives. Many nest in the ground, while others use hollow stems, old rodent burrows or natural cavities in wood. Leaving parts of your yard slightly wild—with bare soil, dead stems or undisturbed corners—can provide nesting habitat for solitary bees.
Avoiding heavy mulch, landscape fabric or frequent tilling can also help ground‑nesting bees find places to raise their young.
Limit pesticide use
Pesticides can harm bees directly or reduce the availability of flowers they depend on. If you choose to use pesticides, apply them sparingly, follow label instructions carefully and avoid spraying when flowers are in bloom or when bees are active.
Many gardeners find that healthy soil, diverse plantings and natural predators reduce the need for chemical treatments.
Support local efforts to monitor bees
Community science programs, including the Alaska Bee Atlas, rely on volunteers to help document where bees live and how their populations are changing. Participating in these efforts — or simply sharing observations from your yard — helps scientists build a clearer picture of Alaska’s pollinators.
Even small contributions, such as photographing bees or planting a pollinator‑friendly garden, can support statewide conservation efforts.
Reduce the spread of invasive plants
Invasive species such as white sweetclover and bird vetch can outcompete native plants and alter the availability of food for bees. Learning to identify invasive plants, removing them when possible, and choosing non‑invasive garden species can help protect Alaska’s natural habitats.
Local Cooperative Extension offices and conservation districts offer resources to help homeowners manage invasive plants responsibly.
A shared responsibility
Supporting native bees does not require large tracts of land or specialized knowledge. It begins with simple choices — planting flowers, protecting nesting sites, reducing pesticide use and staying informed about changes in Alaska’s ecosystems.
On that June morning in Soldotna, the homeowner watches the bumblebee disappear into the chives and realizes that small actions can add up. Across Alaska, thousands of similar moments are helping create a landscape where native bees can thrive.
This is the fifth of a six commentary series about Alaska’s native bees.

text:
Former Boise State University quarterback Tony Hilde has been named executive director of Idaho Technical Career Academy virtual public charter school. (File photo by Getty Images)Tony Hilde
Former Boise State University quarterback Tony Hilde has been named executive director of Idaho Technical Career Academy virtual public charter school, officials with the school announced last week. 
Hilde has been with the school since 2025, when he was hired to serve as career technical education coordinator. Hilde succeeds former executive director Monti Pittman, who retired. 
During his time with Idaho Technical Career Academy, or ITCA, officials said Hilde has expanded the school’s career technical education offerings, added a veterinary technology course, added a cybersecurity pathway and rebranded the digital arts program.
Idaho Technical Career Academy is a tuition-free virtual public charter school affiliated with Stride Inc. and its brand K12, which provides software and digital curriculum materials 
“Tony’s depth of knowledge in CTE, combined with his real-world business experience, makes him an asset to ITCA students and staff.” Teri Cady, executive director at K12, said in a press release. “His work to expand and strengthen these programs reflects a commitment to making sure every ITCA student graduates with the skills and credentials employers are looking for.” 
Before joining Idaho Technical Career Academy, Hilde was a co-founder of Trosky EdTech, Trosky Ranch and was a business education teacher and department chair in the West Ada School District. He holds a teaching license in Idaho and Oregon. 
Hilde played quarterback on the 1994 Boise State University football team that played in the 1994 NCAA Division 1-AA championship game.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Board suspends license of chiropractor convicted of fraud, money laundering
description: State regulators have suspended the license of a Bettendorf chiropractor convicted of bank fraud and money laundering and accused of misuse of COVID-relief funds and the unlicensed practice of medicine. In July 2025, the Iowa Board of Chiropractic charged Jason Rannfeldt with practicing outside the scope of the profession, being convicted of an offense that[...]
text:
The Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing is responsible for overseeing Iowa's licensing boards. (Photo illustration via Getty Images; logo courtesy of the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing) State regulators have suspended the license of a Bettendorf chiropractor convicted of bank fraud and money laundering and accused of misuse of COVID-relief funds and the unlicensed practice of medicine.
In July 2025, the Iowa Board of Chiropractic charged Jason Rannfeldt with practicing outside the scope of the profession, being convicted of an offense that directly relates to the duties and responsibilities of the profession, and representing oneself as a chiropractor without an active license.
According to state records, those disciplinary charges were filed 14 months after Rannfeldt pleaded guilty to criminal charges of making false statements to a financial institution, bank fraud, money laundering and filing a false bankruptcy declaration.
The board also alleged Rannfeldt had continued to practice chiropractic even after his license lapsed in 2023, and that he had posted videos in which he described himself as a physician and discussed treatments for diabetes, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and thyroid dysfunction.
In order to resolve the disciplinary case, the board recently agreed to suspend Rannfeldt’s chiropractic license for one year and also agreed to “back date” that suspension to November 2025, meaning he’ll be eligible for reinstatement in four months.
Once the license is reinstated, it will be placed on probationary status for up to six years, with Rannfeldt’s billings and financial reports subject to outside review, the board ordered. Rannfeldt will also be required to complete 15 hours of educational training on ethics and professionalism.
Indicted on 20 separate charges
Federal court records show that in March 2023, Rannfeldt was accused by prosecutors of using his clinic, Rannfeldt Family Chiropractic, and several other businesses he owned, to secure financial assistance from the federal Paycheck Protection Program, an economic-assistance program that provided forgivable loans to small businesses to maintain payroll, rehire laid-off staff, and cover overhead costs during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Prosecutors alleged Rannfeldt falsified numerous PPP loan applications and routed the money to his personal bank account. He was also alleged to have falsified records to secure loans for a down payment on a new, $785,000 home.
Court records indicate many of the falsified loan applications were denied by bankers, resulting in what prosecutors called “attempted losses,” although some of the applications were approved.
According to the prosecutors, Rannfeldt’s scheme resulted in $115,000 in attempted losses to each of three separate financial institutions — Quad-Cities Bank & Trust, U.S. Bank and Northeast Bank — plus $465,692 in attempted losses to Cross River Bank. In addition, Cross River Bank sustained actual losses of $29,542, and Vibrant Credit Union sustained $262,333 in actual losses, prosecutors claimed.
After being indicted on 20 separate charges, Rannfeldt pleaded guilty to five charges, including bank fraud, money laundering and making false statements to a financial institution, and prosecutors dismissed the remaining 15 charges. Rannfeldt was then sentenced to three years in prison and ordered to pay $291,875 in restitution to the Small Business Administration.
Rannfeldt: ‘This is not me.’
During the criminal court proceedings, prosecutors alleged Rannfeldt had continued to file fraudulent documents even after entering a guilty plea in the case. They alleged Rannfeldt, as part of a residential lease application in November 2023, fraudulently presented his father-in law as a guarantor, included fraudulent earning statements in the application, and forged his father-in-law’s signature.
In arguing for a significant prison sentence, prosecutors cited what they called Rannfeldt’s “repeated and blatant fraud” against taxpayers and the government. “He lied and used falsified documents to get loans,” they told the court. “He lied and used falsified documents to get those loans forgiven. He lied and used falsified documents to get bankruptcy protection. And … he hasn’t stopped.”
At his sentencing in May 2024, Rannfeldt’s attorney informed the court that his client, while having pleaded guilty to misusing COVID-19 relief funds, was also suffering from the medical effects of “long COVID” — the condition in which those who contracted the virus suffer from a variety of long-term effects.
“He still has multiple physical problems, breathing problems, memory problems, muscle issues by way of cramping, headaches,” the attorney, Terence L. McAtee, told the court. “He also has multiple mental health issues.”
McAtee described Rannfeldt as a “beloved husband, father, successful chiropractor, church member, and pillar of the community.”
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Rannfeldt for comment, but at his sentencing in 2024, Rannfeldt apologized to the court for his conduct.
“This is not me,” he said at the time. “No matter what the reason, there is no excuse for this, to waste (the) taxpayer dollars wasted on this case. I’m honestly so embarrassed for what has happened. My family means a lot to me, and I’m going to spend the rest of my life trying to recover that.”

title: Iowa crops rated highly; some counties have access to disaster funding

Corn grown for grain in Iowa rated 80% good to excellent and […]
text:
Blooms visible on a soybean plant in mid July. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Iowa corn and soybean crops are generally in good to excellent condition, according to the latest report, even while parts of the state were hit with heavy rains that triggered disaster assistance from a federal agency for houses and businesses in certain counties.
Corn grown for grain in Iowa rated 80% good to excellent and soybean crop condition was rated 78% good to excellent in the latest crop progress and condition report from the U.S. Department of Agriculture. 
Corn silking reached 87% across the state for the July 20 through July 26 reporting period. This is 6 percentage points ahead of the 2025 crop and 7 percentage points ahead of the five-year average. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Twenty-eight percent of corn acres had corn in the dough stage during the reporting period, which was 4 percentage points behind last year, but 3 percentage points ahead of the five-year average. This was also an increase from the week prior, when just 8% of the crop had reached the dough stage. 
Soybeans blooming reached 80% which is 1 percentage point ahead of the year prior and 1 percentage point behind the five-year average. Nearly half, 48%, of soybeans were setting pods, which is slightly behind last year’s pace and 3 percentage points ahead of the five-year average. 
Oats rated 82% good to excellent and the harvest of the crop continues to be significantly ahead of the 2025 crop. With 67% of the crop harvested as of the reporting period, it was 20 percentage points ahead of harvest from the year prior. 
Soil moisture conditions were rated short for 27%  of topsoil and 28% of subsoil.
Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig said “many” areas of the state could “use a good rain.” 
“As I’ve traveled across Iowa in recent weeks, I’ve generally seen strong crop conditions, though wind, hail and pockets of both excessive rainfall and persistent dryness have created some variability,” Naig said in a statement. 
Naig noted the “stifling” temperatures and humidity toward the end of the week are forecast to “break” toward the middle of the coming week.
Despite the high temperatures at the end of the reporting period, State Climatologist Justin Glisan’s weekly weather report shows the statewide average temperature for the period, at 72.2 degrees Fahrenheit, was slightly below the climatological normal. 
While more of Iowa slid into moderate drought and abnormally dry conditions during the reporting period, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor, the statewide average precipitation was 0.99 inch, about one-tenth of an inch more than the normal. 
Glisan reported several severe weather events at the beginning of the reporting period. Storms on July 20 had strong wind gusts and “torrential downpours” in some areas and 2- to 3-inch-diameter hail and tornadoes in other parts of the state. 
Federal disaster loans available to eight Iowa counties 
The U.S. Small Business Association granted Gov. Kim Reynolds’ request to make low-income disaster loans available to homeowners, renters, businesses, and most nonprofit organizations in Boone, Dallas, Jasper, Madison, Marion, Polk, Story, and Warren counties that were affected by flooding and severe storms over the July Fourth weekend. 
Some of these areas received more than two months’ worth of rain in a period of several days. While the Small Business Association cannot provide loans for agricultural losses, it can offer homeowners up to $100,000 in low-interest loans to repair personal property, and loans of up to $2 million for businesses and nonprofits that sustained damage from the storms. 
Those interested in applying for the aid can reach out to their local Disaster Loan Outreach Center or apply online.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Two New Mexico House members officially retire, teeing up Democratic primary winners to replace them
description: State Reps. Susan Herrera (D-Embudo) and Joanne Ferrary  (D-Las Cruces) had previously announced they intended to retire, but their terms do not end until January. Both told Source NM on Monday that they decided to leave office early to give Democratic primary winners in their districts a chance to start early at the Roundhouse.
text:
Two longtime Democratic New Mexico state representatives, Joanne Ferrary and Susan Herrera, officially retired July 27, 2026, and named their preferred replacements to serve out the remaining months of their terms. (Ferrary photo by Danielle Prokop; courtesy photo of Herrera; file photo of state Legislature)Two Democrats in the New Mexico House of Representatives officially left office Monday, setting in motion a process to replace them that ultimately ends in the coming weeks at Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham’s desk. 
State Reps. Susan Herrera (D-Embudo) and Joanne Ferrary  (D-Las Cruces) had previously announced they intended to retire, but their terms do not end until January. Both told Source NM on Monday that they decided to leave office early to give Democratic primary winners in their districts a chance to start early at the Roundhouse.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
County commissions in each House district will meet in the coming weeks to select a replacement before sending their preferred candidates to Lujan Grisham, a Democrat, for approval. 
Herrera’s District 41 covers parts of four different counties, so county commissions from Taos, Santa Fe, Sandoval and Rio Arriba will meet separately to name their own preferred replacements. 
Commission chairs in each of those four counties did not respond to Source NM’s request for comment Monday about when they might meet and who they are considering. But Sandoval County spokesperson Wayne Johnson told Source NM that the commission could meet in mid-August at the earliest. 
Herrera, who served in the Legislature since 2019, told Source NM that she strongly prefers the June 2 Democratic primary election winner Yolanda Jaramillo to serve out the rest of Herrera’s term in the Roundhouse. 
“That gives her a head start,” she said. “It’s good for her. It’s good for the district.”
Herrera previously endorsed Jaramillo during her primary election against Debbie Rodella. Jaramillo won the race with 55% of the vote out of roughly 5,500 ballots cast. 
Jaramillo told Source NM she is looking forward to making her case to all four county commissions and, if approved, to starting early in the Roundhouse. She is running unopposed in the general election Nov. 3. 
As for Ferrary’s House District 37, only the Doña Ana County Commission will need to weigh in on a replacement, because the district sits entirely within that southern New Mexico county’s boundaries.  
Ferrary told Source NM that she is hopeful commissioners, who are all Democrats, will submit Lori Martinez’s name to the governor. Martinez defeated Tilly Villalobos in the Democratic primary in June.
But unlike Jaramillo, Martinez has an opponent in the November election. She will face Republican Isabella Solis. 
Solis told Source NM on Monday that she thinks Ferrary is unfairly advantaging Martinez by dropping out early and paving the way for Martinez to be a sitting House 37 representative when the election occurs. 
“Her goal is to put her finger on the scale, like a switcheroo,” she said. “I think that oftentimes there could be advantages of incumbency, but frankly, New Mexico is in such bad shape and constantly ranking last. In this political environment, being an incumbent is not necessarily helpful.”
Ferrary told Source NM that Martinez being in office during the election may benefit Martinez, but not by much. She’s confident Martinez will win regardless.   
“It could [help], but I also believe that Democrats are going to have a really good turnout in the November election,” she said. 
Martinez did not respond to Source NM’s request for comment Monday.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Rob Sand advocates for more Iowa wetlands and grazing land
description: FORT DODGE — Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand discussed plans to combat Iowa’s water quality issues and advocated for more mental health funding Monday at a town hall in Fort Dodge. Sand, who currently serves as state auditor, said he is “not satisfied” with Iowa’s efforts to address water quality. He  advocated for a data-driven […]
text:
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand speaks at a town hall at the Webster County Fairgrounds in Fort Dodge, July 27, 2026. (Photo by Kadin Luhmann/Iowa Capital Dispatch)FORT DODGE — Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand discussed plans to combat Iowa’s water quality issues and advocated for more mental health funding Monday at a town hall in Fort Dodge.
Sand, who currently serves as state auditor, said he is “not satisfied” with Iowa’s efforts to address water quality. He  advocated for a data-driven approach to tackle the issue, and more wetlands that would improve soil health, water quality, biodiversity and recreational activities.
“I want us to have the single biggest expansion of wetlands and grazing land that we have ever seen in the state of Iowa,” Sand said. “You can fish, you can photograph, all kinds of fun stuff that you can do in wetlands. We want our kids to take part.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The town hall came hours after the announcement that he supports banning social media for children under 16-years-old, citing the negative effects social media can have on mental health, saying the platforms can be as “addictive as nicotine.”
“They’re hurting people’s mental health. They’re making our kids sicker and more depressed. I think that’s a place where the government needs to take action because these are companies that are harming people,” Sand said.
Mental health
Sand said Iowa families face too many barriers when seeking behavioral health treatment, adding that Iowa has restructured its efforts to treating mental health three times in six years,
“It’s like surviving a shipwreck in the dark, with brief flashes of lightning showing possible help, but no consistent path to actually reach it,” Sand said.
Sand argued that mental health providers are in high demand, and must be paid competitive wages so they don’t leave Iowa, saying that providers may receive less compensation for telehealth appointments, causing them to leave Iowa for better opportunities.
“Number one, we should be making sure that mental health professionals in the state of Iowa are paid a competitive wage,” Sand said. “What we do not want is a situation where they can say, ‘Boy, I could make a lot more money if I was just doing this somewhere else,’ but oftentimes, we have that.”
Sand also connected Iowa’s issues to privatized Medicaid, proposing the reversal of privatized Medicaid to lower costs.
“Here’s the other thing that we can do. I just heard from a longtime [acquaintance] of mine that they are closing their mental health clinic in Iowa because of privatized Medicaid,” Sand said.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida judge refuses to boot Fishback from the ballot, won’t ‘decide the race’
description: A Leon County judge refused Monday to kick Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback off the ballot, agreeing that he hadn’t meant to establish residency in D.C. and pointing out that it’s not the court’s job to decide who becomes Florida’s next governor. “This Court will not be deciding the race between the Lieutenant Governor and […]
text:
James Fishback and Anthony Sabatini talk to reporters after their July 21, 2026, court hearing. (Photo by Liv Caputo/Florida Phoenix)A Leon County judge refused Monday to kick Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback off the ballot, agreeing that he hadn’t meant to establish residency in D.C. and pointing out that it’s not the court’s job to decide who becomes Florida’s next governor.
“This Court will not be deciding the race between the Lieutenant Governor and Mr. Fishback. That will be in the very sound hands of the voters,” Judge David Frank wrote in his 25-page order, issued just before 5 p.m. Monday.
Collins sued last month, arguing Fishback is breaking Florida law by running for governor because he bought a home and voted in D.C. in 2020. The state Constitution requires gubernatorial candidates to have lived in Florida for seven years.
But Frank ruled that Collins failed to prove Fishback had established residency outside Florida, crediting Fishback’s testimony last week that he didn’t know voting and living in Washington, D.C., could amount to establishing residency there. He insisted he always intended to remain a Florida resident.
“‘The best proof of one’s domicile is where [the person] says it is,’” Frank wrote, quoting a 1947 Florida Supreme Court case. “That law may be imprudent, or it may give too much leeway to a person seeking or maintaining residency. 
“But it is the law.”
Although the ruling was a blow to Collins’ already-struggling campaign, it’s likely to have little effect on the consistent leader in the polls: Trump-endorsed U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds. 
A two-term House member, Donalds has raked in upwards of 40% in most polls compared to Collins’ and Fishback’s battle for both second place and to climb out of single-digit polling support.
Fishback remains optimistic, tying Collins’ attempt to strike him from the race to Donalds.
“It’s official. The disgraceful lawfare brought by Jay Collins and fueled by Byron Donalds has failed,” Fishback said in a written statement. “This isn’t just a victory for our campaign. It’s a victory for the Constitution and for every Floridian who believes elections should be decided by voters, not politicians trying to rig the system.”
“Jay Collins and Byron Donalds tried to stop our campaign because they know they can’t beat us. Today, they lost in court, and in 22 days they’ll lose at the ballot box.”
A Collins representative did not respond to a request for comment.
What else did the judge say?
Fishback’s Florida roots, including being born and raised here, holding a Florida driver license, operating a Florida company, and voting in Florida every election except 2020, showed he never intended to set up domicile outside of the Sunshine State, Frank said.
And while Fishback could face regulatory or even “severe legal repercussions” for voting in D.C. with a Florida license and receiving a homestead exemption on his D.C. property, it doesn’t negate Fishback’s intentions or his “continued residency” in Florida, the judge concluded.
“Simply put, plaintiff has not brought forth enough substantial and competent evidence to rebut these important presumptions,” he said.
Frank struck a cautious tone in his order, pointing out the importance of walking a “fine line” in “this distinctly political process.” 
Quoting from a 1980 Florida case, he wrote, “If two equally reasonable constructions might be found, this Court in the past has chosen the one which enhances the elective process by providing voters with the greater choice in exercising their democratic rights.”

name: VTDigger
title: End of immigration program forces difficult choices for Vermont residents
description:
“As much as I can stay inside, I will stay inside,” one Haitian on the program in Vermont said, referring to his apartment in Chittenden County.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  End of immigration program forces difficult choices for Vermont residents.
text:
People hold Haitian flags and signs during a rally in support of immigrants living in the United States with temporary protected status, or TPS, Thursday, July 9, 2026, in San Diego. Photo by Gregory Bull/AP

A decades-old federal immigration program that allowed more than 200 residents in Vermont to live and work in the state ends today, meaning many on the program will have to decide whether to stay in the country illegally or return to countries marred by violence. 
“It is hard to imagine any human being choosing to return to a place that our own State Department describes as rife with kidnapping, gang activity, violent crime, terrorism, and poor health care,” Erin Jacobsen, senior staff attorney at the Vermont Asylum Assistance Project, wrote in a statement to VTDigger. 
The U.S. Supreme Court struck down the program, known as Temporary Protected Status, for Haitians and Syrians in a ruling on June 25, though the decision did not go into effect until Monday. 
In the past month, Vermonters on the program — and around 350,000 people nationally — have been scrambling to secure other forms of immigration protection, such as asylum. Many from Haiti who are in the state on TPS have either secured other legal pathways or are currently exploring them, according to Jacobsen. Those without that option, however, face the decision to remain and risk deportation, or return to the countries they fled due to dangerous conditions. 
Yvonne Lodico, co-founder and executive director of Grace Initiative Global, a Vermont-based humanitarian organization, said that some Haitian protected status recipients she has been assisting are currently considering leaving the U.S. — but they are not planning to go to Haiti, due to the safety risks. She said her organization is working with another humanitarian group in another country to facilitate a possible move this month. She declined to name the other country until more details are ironed out. 
“As much as I can stay inside, I will stay inside,” one Haitian on the program in Vermont said, referring to his apartment in Chittenden County. He declined to give his name for fear of deportation due to ongoing immigration proceedings. 
The Haitian man has other possible immigration pathways pending, such as a green card application. But he said that because of the ongoing cases and a fear of being targeted on the street, he is forced to remain in his home. 
After the Trump administration first announced it would end the program for Haitians in February, the man’s former employer, a Chittenden County manufacturer, canceled his work permit, he said. That’s made it difficult to find financial stability. 
“I try to support them,” the man said, referring to his family still in Haiti. “Unfortunately, based on what happened after I lost my employment, I can’t help them.” 
Following the official termination Monday, all employers will have to end work permits for those on the program, leading to a potential blow to industries supported by the immigrants, advocates say. Haitian protected status recipients specifically have been concentrated in the healthcare industry, according to industry leaders and national research.
Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark, in a group of 19 attorneys general, challenged the attempted termination in an amicus brief to the Supreme Court in April. 
“These are our neighbors, our coworkers, and our friends who came to this country seeking safety and the opportunity to build better lives for themselves and their families,” Clark wrote in a statement to VTDigger Monday. “Forcing these community members to return to countries facing extraordinary hardship is contrary to our values and hurts the communities that rely on and value these community members.”
Since President Trump took office in 2025, the Department of Homeland Security has ended protected status for about a dozen countries. The administration has argued that the program, created by Congress in 1990 under Republican President George H.W. Bush, has extended beyond a temporary form of protection, and that the countries are safe to return to. 
Haiti was designated for the program in 2010 following catastrophic earthquakes. The country has for years been engulfed in gang violence, and the U.S. State Department maintains a do-not-travel advisory due to violent crime, kidnapping and civil unrest. 
Referring to Haitian protected status recipients in the state, Lodico, the director of Grace Initiative Global, said that “for many, their houses have been burnt, family members killed.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  End of immigration program forces difficult choices for Vermont residents.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: GOP leaders say the NC budget offers ‘historic’ raises. A top education panel says it’s not enough.
description: Just weeks after the North Carolina General Assembly passed a $34 billion state budget that included 8% average raises for teachers over two years, the state’s Blue Ribbon Commission on Public Education said it’s not enough. The bipartisan panel, assembled in March by Democratic N.C. Gov. Josh Stein, Senate President Pro Tem Phil Berger, R-Rockingham, […]
text:
Thousands of N.C. teachers rallied on May 1, 2026 outside the legislature to say their pay has not kept up with rising inflation or healthcare costs. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)Just weeks after the North Carolina General Assembly passed a $34 billion state budget that included 8% average raises for teachers over two years, the state’s Blue Ribbon Commission on Public Education said it’s not enough.
The bipartisan panel, assembled in March by Democratic N.C. Gov. Josh Stein, Senate President Pro Tem Phil Berger, R-Rockingham, and House Speaker Destin Hall, R-Caldwell, has been working on recommendations to improve teacher training, student advancement, and administrative operations.
Bipartisan education panel unites NC Gov Stein, Republican leaders amid budget rift

At Monday’s meeting, the commission devoted much of its discussion to strengthening the state’s teacher pipeline and its compensation schedule.
“Very simply, we need to pay our teachers more,” said state Superintendent Mo Green during Monday’s commission meeting.
Hall said the new budget offers “historic raises” for teachers, though the largest percentage gains heavily favor early-career educators. Veteran teachers’ salaries have remained relatively stagnant over the past few budget cycles.
Green said teachers at all levels of experience need to be paid more for the state to become the top state for educators in the Southeast.
According to the N.C. Department of Public Instruction, more than 9,100 teachers decided to leave the state’s public schools in 2024-25. That represents a little more than 10% of the public school teachers employed statewide. Beginning teachers left at a much higher rate of 14.7%.
Lisa Godwin, a former North Carolina Teacher of the Year, told her fellow commission members the state should revisit retention bonuses for each year of service. Currently, teachers with 15 to 24 years’ experience don’t get an annual raise for nearly a decade.
“I’m one of those [whose salary] is frozen,” said Godwin, a beginning teacher coach and mentor coordinator for Pender County Schools.
Godwin said North Carolina did not face a perennial teacher shortage in the past.
“See what worked and what was good in the heyday of teaching and education. And let’s bring these things back,” Godwin said.
Brenda Berg, president & CEO of BEST NC, criticized the state budget for eliminating recurring funding for TeachNC, an online platform used to recruit teachers and teacher candidates.
“Teach NC recruited 3,700 candidates last year to educator preparation programs,” Berg said, “which was a 20% increase in EPP enrollment.”
Berg said the commission should recommend that the program be fully funded in the next budget.
Edgecombe Early College High School Principal Matt Bristow-Smith said the panel should consider recommending the indexing  of teacher salaries to inflation to help them keep up with the cost of living.
“What we’ve effectively done is we have lowered the quality of living for teachers because the earning power of what teachers actually make is less than it was a decade ago,” said Bristow-Smith.
House Bill 1178, which proposed indexing teacher salaries starting in 2033-34, didn’t get a hearing in the short session.
Dr. Robert Taylor, superintendent of the Wake County Public School System, summed up what many on the commission were thinking.
“There just needs to be an acknowledgement that if we are going to address teacher compensation, that it’s going to cost us to fix the problem that has been built over the last several years,” said Taylor. “The longer we take to fix it, the harder the problem becomes to fix.”
The Blue Ribbon Commission on Public Education did not take a vote at Monday’s meeting. The bipartisan group, which is also discussing recommendations to strengthen literacy and modernize accountability, meets again August 31, 2026.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC aluminum smelter back to full production after a decade of lower capacity
description: The aluminum manufacturer started operating at half capacity in 2015 amid a dispute over power rates and foreign production.
text:
US Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick praises the reopening of an idle portion of the Mt. Holly aluminum smelter in Goose Creek, South Carolina, on Monday, July 27, 2026. Standing beside him on the left is CEO Jess Gary. On the right is Attorney General Alan Wilson. (Photo courtesy of Jeff Leieritz/Compass Global Communications)A Lowcountry aluminum plant is back to running at full capacity for the first time in over a decade, leaders announced Monday.
Century Aluminum’s Mt. Holly smelter in Berkeley County spent about $50 million to restart an idle portion of the plant, adding back 150 jobs, said company CEO Jess Gary during a Monday ribbon-cutting ceremony. That means the full facility is running for the first time since 2015.
“American aluminum keeps our country running,” Gary said.
The plant, which has more than 600 workers, will create about 50,000 more metric tons each year, increasing the country’s aluminum output by 10%, Gary said. The smelter is already responsible for about 30% of the nation’s aluminum production.
“That is something we should be proud of,” said state Attorney General Alan Wilson, who attended the celebration.
In 2015, the plant slashed its production in half, laying off about 300 workers amid a dispute with state-owned utility Santee Cooper over how much it paid for electricity. Compounding the crisis, Gary said, was an influx of aluminum imported from China and Canada.
The Obama administration in January 2017 filed a complaint with the World Trade Administration saying China illegally subsidized its aluminum industry, leading to overproduction. The complaint is still ongoing.
Five years later, again pointing to power costs and foreign competition, Century Aluminum warned its remaining 295 employees the plant might close. But the smelter survived after the company made a deal to increase its power supply, bringing the plant back to three-quarters of its initial capacity.
The company inked another contract with power company Santee Cooper last year, paving the way for the expansion back to full capacity.
SC now requires American-made steel for roads, bridges and other public projects

Gary also credited the Trump administration’s taxes on aluminum imports with saving the plant.
During President Donald Trump’s first term in office, in 2018, he instituted a 10% tariff on aluminum from most countries. He increased that tariff to 50% last year, increasing the cost for other countries to supply the pliable metal used for smartphones, airplanes and cars.
“President Trump has made clear that unfair trade practices will not decide the future of American aluminum,” Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick said Monday.
While aluminum manufacturers have praised Trump’s tariffs as helping return production to the United States, other businesses, including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, have criticized them for increasing prices at an unsustainable level.
Promoting the production of aluminum at home is important for American jobs and national security, Lutnick said. The metal is an essential component of fighter jets, naval vessels and body armor, he said.
“By increasing the production of aluminum here at home, we are reducing our dependence on foreign supply chains and fortifying our national security,” Lutnick said.
As China and other countries manufactured the metal at high rates, America’s smelters suffered, Lutnick said. The smelter just north of Goose Creek is one of four nationwide still in production, compared to 24 in 2000, according to The Aluminum Association. The Mt. Holly plant was the most recent to open, in 1980.
The other three smelters are in Massena, New York; Evansville, Indiana; and Sebree, Kentucky.
For workers like Mark Schlag, manager of the smelter’s carbon plant and an employee for 22 years, closing a plant means “taking the American dream that I’ve been able to live away from families like mine, away from communities like ours, all across the country,” he said.
Century Aluminum and Dubai-based Emirates Global Aluminum announced plans this year to build a $4 billion smelter in Oklahoma, the first new plant built since then. The plant is expected to employ 1,000 people and produce 750,000 tons of aluminum each year, according to a news release.
“The future of America’s aluminum industry is bright,” Gary said.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Lawyer says Elon Musk’s PAC won’t turnover docs in lawsuit over pay-for-signatures scheme in Pa.
description: The cases against Musk and America PAC stem from a promise to pay $47 for every successful referral of a registered swing state voter to sign a petition in favor of “free speech and the right to bear arms.”
text:
CEO of Tesla and SpaceX Elon Musk speaks last year at the Conservative Political Action Conference in Maryland. Last week’s SpaceX IPO, which made Musk the world’s first trillionaire, is a vivid illustration of wealth concentration in the United States, which has been accelerating since 2022. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)Lawyers trying to mount a class action lawsuit against Elon Musk and America PAC, a super PAC he funded to support President Donald Trump and other conservatives, say the defendants aren’t cooperating in turning over key documents.
“We’re getting the run-around,” said attorney Shannon Liss-Riordan, who is based in Massachusetts. “We’ve been delayed in getting discovery.”
The cases against Musk and America PAC stem from a promise to pay $47 for every successful referral of a registered swing state voter to sign a petition in favor of “free speech and the right to bear arms.” The amount was later raised to $100 per signature.
“Easy money,” Musk posted on the social media site X, which he owns, in October 2024.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
One proposed class action case was brought by an anonymous plaintiff who says, while working as an hourly canvasser for America PAC, he was encouraged to refer people to sign the petition for additional pay. The plaintiff, listed as John Doe, says he’s owed more than $20,000 and is aware of others in similar situations.
Another case was brought by Lancaster man Anthony Maglietta and two other swing state voters who say they were never paid for signing the petition or referring others.
Liss-Riordan, the attorney for both cases, is trying to get them approved as a class action. They’re moving forward together in the U.S. District Court in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania. 
She says she’s heard from dozens of people who could qualify if the court allows it.
“These are generally people who are followers of Elon Musk, and believed in what he was doing and are aligned politically with a goal here,” she told the Capital-Star. “The fact that they weren’t even paid what they were told they would be paid — I don’t know if it’s surprising or not, but it’s very disappointing.”
The Capital-Star reached out to lawyers for Musk and America PAC, an email associated with Musk’s family office, and a public relations firm that employs a spokesperson for America PAC. None responded.
America PAC’s website says, “America PAC has already mailed the overwhelming majority of checks owed to eligible referrers and petition signers. If you haven’t received payment yet, that does not necessarily mean you won’t … We continue to review and process outstanding payments that have been flagged for mismatched information or require additional action.”
Musk is reported to have spent around $290 million helping Trump and Republicans get elected in 2024, making him the largest single political donor of the election cycle. Following the election, he was made a special government employee by the Trump administration, serving as the de facto head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).
“Going in circles”
In a letter to U.S. District Court Judge Wendy Beetlestone, Liss-Riordan explained that her clients requested documents from the defendants in December 2025, part of the discovery process.
She said her team was told by America PAC that they did not have the documents, and should seek them from third-party vendors they’d contracted. But when they went to those vendors, they were told that America PAC had them.
“​​Plaintiffs are frustrated that they have been going in circles to obtain the discovery that is essential to their case – with Defendants claiming the vendors have the documents and the vendors claiming Defendants have the documents – and neither agreeing to produce them,” Liss-Riordan wrote.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Moreover, she alleges that some of the vendors may not be as independent as they seem. She says, for example, United States of America Inc. and Group America, LLC were established by Musk. And other vendors she sought documents from had principal members who were also high-ups at America PAC.
A conference has been set up between Eastern District Judge Wendy Beetlestone and lawyers for both parties on Tuesday, but it will not be streamed to the public.
Both parties have requested an extension of the deadline to certify a class action case from July 31 to November 30. It would mark the third such extension.
According to Liss-Riordan, class certification can’t be done until more documents are turned over in discovery.
Musk and America PAC are also being sued in a Texas U.S. District Court over an alleged $1 million giveaway to swing state voters who signed a petition to support the U.S. Constitution. Plaintiffs allege that Musk and America PAC misled voters into thinking winners would be chosen randomly, but were actually predetermined. 
The bipartisan Wisconsin Elections Commission also agreed in a 5-1 vote in July to refer two complaints against Musk to the Brown County district attorney’s office, finding probable cause that he violated the state’s election bribery statute with another million dollar giveaway during the state’s 2025 state supreme court election.

title: Lawmakers to vote on $250k infusion for WisEye streaming service
description: Wisconsin lawmakers are voting this week to fund WisconsinEye through the end of 2026 with $250,000. The funding would support the service, which provides livestream coverage of floor sessions in the Legislature as well as public hearings and votes held by Senate and Assembly committees, as it continues to seek long-term funding to operate. Members […]
text:
WisconsinEye Board of Directors Chair Mark O’Connell testifies at a hearing in February in favor of funding for WisconsinEye, the state streaming service that covers the Wisconsin Legislature. That legislation has died, but this week lawmakers are voting on $250,000 to fund the service through the end of 2026. (Screenshot via WisconsinEye)Wisconsin lawmakers are voting this week to fund WisconsinEye through the end of 2026 with $250,000.
The funding would support the service, which provides livestream coverage of floor sessions in the Legislature as well as public hearings and votes held by Senate and Assembly committees, as it continues to seek long-term funding to operate.
Members of the Joint Committee on Legislative Organization received paper ballots Monday to vote on a proposal to send WisconsinEye $50,000 per month starting in August and ending in December. The cost would be split between the Assembly and the Senate.
The ballots are due at 5 p.m. Tuesday. Funding would come from appropriations in the budget to carry out the functions of each chamber, including expenses for legislative documents, according to the Wisconsin Legislative Council, a nonpartisan service agency for the Legislature.
WisEye CEO Jon Henkes could not be reached for comment Monday on the potential impact of the funding if it is approved as expected.
WisconsinEye launched as an independent nonprofit in 2007 to livestream and archive government meetings and legislative sessions. The service has operated on donations and runs independently from the state Legislature.
WisconsinEye’s management announced in November 2025 that it needed additional revenue to support the service’s $900,000 annual budget after donations fell behind in the last couple of years.
Henkes told the Wisconsin Examiner at the time that contributions haven’t kept up with expenses since the COVID-19 pandemic. WisEye temporarily halted coverage Dec. 15, 2025. It resumed coverage Feb. 2, 2026, after the Joint Committee on Legislative Organization authorized $50,000 to cover the service for that month.
Two separate proposals to fund the service passed earlier this year, one in the Assembly and the other in the Senate, but neither one got a vote in the opposite chamber.
WisEye launched a GoFundMe campaign in January with a goal of raising $250,000. In a July 15 fundraising email, WisEye said it had raised nearly half of that goal and needed $130,000 “to maintain operations for the next few months.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont’s tax burden is driving families away
description:
High property taxes and a shrinking population point to a state that's pricing out its middle class.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s tax burden is driving families away.
text:
Dear Editor,
My wife and I recently moved our part-time residence from Moretown to Bennington. And we noticed that the relatively new anti-tax fervor has grown here in Bennington, too.
I don’t see the Legislature rolling back funding for any departments or programs. That means property taxes will remain wickedly high. More and more, the state will become a home for the poor and seniors, who are unable to move, and for the rich, who can afford a luxurious second home. The working middle class will be hard-pressed.
I find it ridiculous that my Bennington property taxes on my $160,000 condo are the same as my $500,000 Florida home. Plus, there is no state income tax in Florida.
Last year, Vermont experienced a 0.29% annual population decline because more people are dying than being born and there is an outflow of residents to other states. I would guess that trend will accelerate as more boomers like me die and smart middle-class people give up on paying $5,000 to $10,000 a year for property taxes, plus exorbitant income taxes. Double ouch!
As people wake up, they’ll realize life will be easier, taxes lower, their savings and investments much greater, if they move from Vermont to, say, North Carolina or Tennessee.
Vermont touches the heart but empties the wallet. It doesn’t have to be that way.

READ MORE

There is great pride and loyalty among Vermonters, a profound love and loyalty to the state. But excessive property taxes could cost many Vermonters an extra $100,000 to $400,000 over 20 years compared with living in other states. This is insanity.
If state policies, funding and taxes don’t change for the better soon, that little dribble in population outflow will grow to a flowing stream, then a torrent. It’s inevitable.
Peter Rinaldi
Bonita Springs, Fla., and Bennington, Vt.

title: Blake Hill Preserves prepares to move after employee furloughs
description:
The business says it has a buyer for its Windsor site and is moving to an undisclosed location that’s not in Windsor or any adjacent towns.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Blake Hill Preserves prepares to move after employee furloughs.
text:
A Blake Hill Preserves employee, who declined to be identified, locks the door to the jam manufacturer’s retail store after moving furniture out of the building at Artisan’s Park in Windsor, Vt., on Monday, July 20, 2026. The store was closed in March. Photo by: James M. Patterson/Valley News

This story by Sofia Langlois was first published in the Valley News on July 26, 2026.
WINDSOR — Blake Hill Preserves is preparing to move to an undisclosed location following a furlough of nearly 30 employees that may prove permanent.
Blake Hill Preserves, a family-owned company founded by couple Vicky Allard and Joe Hanglin in 2009, operated a jam shop, tasting room, kitchen and warehouse for a decade at Artisans Park in Windsor.
In March, the owners, who live in Woodstock, closed their shop to the public and temporarily laid off dozens of nonseasonal employees because they’d lost a large customer. Allard specified that company was being purchased and no longer needed their services. Allard declined to name the customer.
In 2024, Blake Hill took out a $50,000 loan from the town of Windsor to nearly double the size of its building. The company still owes $43,700 on the loan, with a monthly fee of $530 that the town’s assistant treasurer confirmed Tuesday has not been paid since December. The company also owes more than $4,000 in taxes.
Allard said the payments “would be handled appropriately in an orderly manner” but declined to comment further about the company’s debt. While she declined to say where Blake Hill is moving, she said it’s not in Windsor or any adjacent towns.
Despite being in debt, the company has kept up with online orders, which it is filling with products that were already in its inventory. In recent weeks, Blake Hill paused all its manufacturing to prepare for its upcoming move.
Now, Blake Hill is selling its 13,000-square-foot building to a “foodie business” that Allard declined to name, but she confirmed it will continue selling Blake Hill products in the store. The property at 60 Artisans Way is currently listed online for $1.75 million, and Allard said they have a buyer.
The new business will provide job opportunities in Windsor and will be great for Artisans Park and the wider community, Allard said.
The owners have decided to work with another manufacturing company to produce their jam and will no longer operate a facility on their own. Allard declined to provide the name of the manufacturing company or the terms of the agreement.
The collaboration and new manufacturing platform will offer “even better footing going forward,” with increased manufacturing capacity, she said.
Allard added that shipping prices from the new spot will not change and she anticipates minimal impact on customers. Though some products are out of stock at the moment, they won’t be for long.
“It will only be good news because we will be able to resume full-scale manufacturing, making all of the jams,” Allard said.
As for the furloughed employees, Allard believes many of them are likely not interested in returning because they’ve found other opportunities, and the new location isn’t within commuting distance from Windsor, she said.
However, Allard said they are reaching out to current and former team members to see if Blake Hill’s new plans interest them.
After the initial furlough, Allard provided guidelines to help staff members respond to questions about the employee downsizing, and she asked them to keep the guidelines discreetly in the jam shop for reference, as noted in a message obtained by the Valley News.
Allard clarified Friday that employees were not obligated to say anything about Blake Hill to members of the public.
“It was merely a guide to support team members, should they find it helpful,” Allard said.
According to a copy of the guidelines, which contained a question about layoffs, Allard included a reply that “no one has been laid off” but rather employees were placed on a short-term furlough, similar to how seasonal businesses are run. It specified that “everyone is being welcomed back over the next few weeks,” with a final return date toward the end of April.
But that didn’t happen.
“This was provided back in March when furloughs had just been announced and we very much hoped everyone on furlough would be invited back,” Allard said Friday.
In an email, Allard said the team is now down to four people: her, Hanglin, an employee in sales and an employee in fulfillment.
Production is slated to begin early in August at the new facility, with details available to customers in the coming days, Allard said.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Doug Jones calls for affordability measures, government reforms in policy speech
description: BIRMINGHAM — Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones unveiled an ambitious policy agenda in a speech Monday, saying Alabamians deserve “three real opportunities” for health, government participation and economic prosperity.  In an hourlong speech delivered to at least 100 people, the former U.S. senator called for traditional Alabama Democratic policies[...]
text:
Democratic gubernatorial nominee and former U.S. Sen. Doug Jones delivers a policy speech on July 27, 2026 in Birmingham, Alabama. Jones Monday outlined an ambitious policy agenda touching on healthcare, affordability and governmental reform. (Andi Rice for Alabama Reflector) 


Key points

Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones said he would work for “three real opportunities” for Alabamians in health outcomes, government participation and economic prosperity.
In an hourlong speech, Jones mixed traditional Alabama Democratic calls for Medicaid expansion and a lottery vote with new proposals like a demand for a data center moratorium, new investments in housing and child care and citizen ballot initiatives.
If Jones were to win election, Jones would likely have to work with a Republican-controlled Legislature not inclined to advance his agenda.




BIRMINGHAM — Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones unveiled an ambitious policy agenda in a speech Monday, saying Alabamians deserve “three real opportunities” for health, government participation and economic prosperity. 
In an hourlong speech delivered to at least 100 people, the former U.S. senator called for traditional Alabama Democratic policies like Medicaid expansion, a lottery vote and the abolition of the state grocery tax. But Jones also called for a one-year moratorium on data centers; a state ballot initiative process; more powers for local governments; constitutional protections for in-vitro fertilization and contraception and additional investments in housing and child care. 
Jones said the state is being governed by “a small circle of people in Montgomery who learned that the surest way to hold power is to cut ordinary Alabamians out of the decisions that shape our life.”

“In this year, in 2026, we’re witnessing perhaps the greatest example of what is wrong with state government in Alabama and how big money works in our state. Not only that it gets in the way, but (it also) buys the willing support of Montgomery and any politician they need,” he said.
Alabama’s governor has limited power, and if Jones won election he would likely have to work with a Republican-controlled Legislature hostile to his proposals.  Jones said after the speech he’d work to ensure his campaign promises much like he did when he was a U.S. Senator.
“You work with people. You talk to them, you listen to them, you don’t just dogmatically tell them this is the way it’s got to be,” he said. “You hear them out. That’s how you get things done.”
Jones’ proposals were a contrast with those of Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville, Alabama’s senior U.S. senator widely considered the favorite in the race, whose platform has largely focused on business development and culture war issues. 
In a statement Monday, Jordan Doufexis, Tuberville’s campaign manager, accused Jones of standing “with the Obama-Biden agenda to bring open borders, socialized healthcare, radical gender policies, and reckless spending” and touted Tuberville’s record in Washington, citing his support of President Donald Trump’s job cuts and his work to bring Space Command to Huntsville, among other items.
“Alabama voters fired DC Doug once already,” the statement said. “Now he has come crawling back from Washington with the same failed liberal ideas, and they are going to reject him again.”
Jones denounced culture war rhetoric, saying that “every one of us — Republican, Democrat, and independent — is being sold the same lie so that a very few can keep the run of the place.” 
“While they had us arguing over pronouns, they were cutting deals on our utility bills,” he said. “While they had us fighting about library books, they were quietly rewriting the tax code to fatten their own portfolios. It takes a lot of fear and a lot of closed doors to keep people from getting angry.” 
Another major contrast was Jones’ support for a data center moratorium. Tuberville has been a vocal advocate for building data centers. AL.com reported earlier this month that Tuberville said people who are opposed to data centers and artificial intelligence are being influenced by China and called concerns about the environmental effects of data centers “bullcrap.”
Doug Jones kicks off Alabama gubernatorial campaign with vision of ‘crowded table’

Jones said a moratorium would allow the state to have “guardrails and policies in place to protect our people and our communities.”
“Those concerns are not bullcrap; they’re real, and they’re being heard in communities across the South,” he said.” 
Jones also alluded to multiple candidacy challenges and a lawsuit challenging Tuberville’s eligibility to run for Alabama governor and allegations that the nominee lives in Florida.
“I guess maybe he also sees the concerns about housing costs as bullcrap, but it’s easy to do when you spend most of your time at a multi-million-dollar beach house in north Florida,” Jones said.
Earlier this month, a Montgomery  judge dismissed a lawsuit over Tuberville’s residency, saying she lacked jurisdiction over the case. The plaintiffs later appealed the lawsuit to the Alabama Supreme Court. Briefs from plaintiffs in the case will go to the Supreme Court early next month. 

Affordability, health care

Democratic gubernatorial nominee and former U.S. Sen. Doug Jones delivers a policy address on July 27, 2026 in Birmingham, Alabama. (Andi Rice for Alabama Reflector)
Jones also said he plans to tackle affordability through eliminating the state’s grocery, tip and overtime taxes; decreasing housing costs through the new federal housing bill and increasing wages for workers across the state. 
Jones also said he wants to expand Medicaid “one way or another.”
“The fact is, Alabama is a poor state. It’s an unhealthy state, and Medicaid expansion is not a handout, it’s a hand up,” he said. “Thirty-nine other states, red and blue, have already figured out that it’s a good thing. It’s time for the 40th state to catch up.”
Alabama is one of only 10 states who have not expanded Medicaid. 
Staying in the theme of healthcare, Jones said he would work to protect contraception and in vitro fertilization (IVF) through a constitutional amendment along with fighting for other policies that would help women across the state. In 2024, the Alabama Legislature passed a law restarting IVF services in the state after the Alabama Supreme Court ruled that frozen embryos were children and parents could file civil suits if they were destroyed, leading several IVF clinics to stop operations. 
Democrats argued at the time that because the Alabama Supreme Court relied on a 2018 state constitutional amendment on the “rights of unborn children” to make its IVF ruling, the only way to protect IVF was a constitutional amendment. 
Alabama passed a new IVF law. But questions remain.

“Republican women, Democratic women, independent women, you watch politicians in Montgomery and Washington decide that they know better than you do about your own body, your own family and your own life,” Jones said. “I’m going to fight to protect access to contraception. I’m going to fight for paid family leave, for affordable childcare, for lower maternal mortality rates, and for wages that reflect the value of your work.”
Government reform
One of the last campaign proposals Jones made was to protect voting rights for Alabamians. Conversations surrounding voting rights re-emerged after an April SCOTUS ruling in Louisiana which ruled the state’s congressional map a racial gerrymander. The opinion had a ripple effect across the South where states including Alabama and Tennessee redrew congressional maps.
One way Jones wants to help protect voting rights is through implementing early voting in the state. Early voting bills have been brought by multiple Democratic members of the Legislature, but none of the bills have ever made it through either chamber for a vote. 
“Voting rights are not a chapter in the history book anymore. We don’t get to close that vote. They’re a living promise that must be defended in every generation, and we are seeing it right now today,” he said.
Jones also called for an initiative process to allow citizens to put issues up for a vote, saying that “when Montgomery refuses to listen, the people have a way to act for themselves.” He also called for more power for local governments, “because the mayor of Clanton knows more about what Clanton needs on any Wednesday morning than a state bureaucracy learns in a year.”
Key points box written by Editor Brian Lyman.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota judge weighs decision in Beef Commission membership lawsuit
description: A North Dakota judge is set to decide whether the process for who serves on the state’s Beef Commission is unconstitutional. South Central Judicial District Judge Jackson Lofgren heard arguments Monday from attorneys for the state and the Ranchers Rights Initiative. The group’s directors – Kenneth Graner, Michael Heaton and Jeremy Maher – are three […]
text:
Cattle roam in a pasture near Killdeer in southwest North Dakota.  (Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)A North Dakota judge is set to decide whether the process for who serves on the state’s Beef Commission is unconstitutional.
South Central Judicial District Judge Jackson Lofgren heard arguments Monday from attorneys for the state and the Ranchers Rights Initiative. The group’s directors – Kenneth Graner, Michael Heaton and Jeremy Maher – are three cattlemen who say the law plays favorites over who serves on the board that decides how to use cattle sale fees from ranchers to promote beef.
The group wants the judge to strike down the law. The state wants the judge to dismiss the challengers’ claims. The judge said he will work to get an opinion out as quickly as he can.
The Beef Commission consists of nine members, including three beef producers, one cattle feeder, one dairy producer, one representative of a public livestock market and three at-large members, all appointed by the governor. The North Dakota Stockmen’s Association submits names for the beef producers and the association’s feeder council submits names for the cattle feeder.
The lawsuit filed last year names Republican Gov. Kelly Armstrong, the commission and the state. 
Ranchers sue to revamp North Dakota Beef Commission appointment process

An attorney for the challengers, who don’t currently belong to any of the organizations set in the law, say the law unconstitutionally elevates the Stockmen’s Association “and other favored associations” above other groups.
“Ultimately, this case is about the simple principle that government is to be by the people, not by the privileged and not by those with influence,” Ranchers Rights Initiative attorney Robby Dube said.
The commission decides how to use the money raised from fees on cattle sales of $2 per head – $1 apiece to the state and federal government – known as the beef checkoff. The money is mainly used for beef promotion, education and research. The commission raised more than $1.5 million of assessment revenue in 2024-2025, according to an annual report.
Dube said the law includes “legislatively favored private associations” and creates a “closed class” for the commission’s beef producer positions of solely the North Dakota Stockmen’s Association, amounting to a special law, which unfairly treats similar entities differently and is prohibited by the state constitution.
Of the 24 beef producer nominations since 2009, 21 were Stockmen’s Association or auxiliary group members at the time, and it’s unclear the membership status of the other three, Dube said. Additionally, the Stockmen’s Association has supported at least 16 people for the at-large positions since 2009, including 10 of its own or auxiliary group members, according to court documents. 
“You have private organizations that are going to only be beholden to themselves who are appointing their own people and then turning around and funding themselves. That is exactly what has happened here over and over again,” Dube said.
The challengers haven’t shown that the law is unconstitutional, Special Assistant Attorney General Zachary Pelham said. The law doesn’t require membership in the Stockmen’s Association or the Milk Producers Association, but commission members must be a North Dakota resident and a U.S. citizen actively engaged in the part of the industry they represent for five years, he said.
State says North Dakota Beef Commission lawsuit should be dismissed

“We have a law that applies equally to all,” Pelham said.
The law has “meaningful at-large access” in that people can nominate themselves or others for the commission’s at-large seats, he said. And ultimately, the governor selects the members, he added.
Additionally, the challengers don’t have legal standing to bring their claims, Pelham said. A three-year statute of limitations bars the claims of the challengers, who have tried to change the commission selection process for at least 20 years via the Independent Beef Association of North Dakota, the state said in court documents. And Maher nominating himself for an at-large seat and not being selected is not a legal injury for standing, Pelham said.
The challengers also say a requirement that commissioners cannot have received a checkoff refund in the last three years is punitive and discriminatory. Pelham said the requirement is appropriate as “skin in the game.”
“The act is constitutional because it reflects rational legislative choices about how to administer a specialized agriculture commodity program,” Pelham said. The challengers’ arguments are essentially “policy objections and dissatisfaction with the appointment outcomes,” he said.
The judge said he will take the matter under advisement. The case had been set for a court trial in August, which has been canceled and may or may not be rescheduled.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura can be reached at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.
